en: I salute Pārvatī and Parameśvara, the parents of the world, who are joined together like speech and its meaning, for the purpose of communicating both speech and meaning.
Where is the lineage originating from the Sun, and where is my intellect of such limited scope?
Out of delusion, I desire to cross the impassable ocean with a mere raft.
"Being dull-witted yet desiring the fame of a poet, I shall become an object of ridicule,
like a dwarf who, out of greed for fruit reachable only by the tall, stretches out his arms."
Or rather, since the gateway of speech has been opened for this lineage by former sages,
my way is as easy as that of a thread through a gem already perforated by a diamond.
Thus, from my very birth, I have [recorded] the deeds of those kings— purified until the attainment of their fruits—
who ruled the earth as far as the ocean and whose chariot tracks reached to the very mines of the earth.

They had offered oblations into the sacred fires according to the prescribed rules; they had honored supplicants according to their desires; they had meted out punishments according to the offenses committed; and they had exercised their sovereign power at the appropriate times.
For those who have accumulated wealth for the sake of giving; for those of measured speech for the sake of truth;
for those desiring victory for the sake of fame; and for those who kindle their households for the sake of progeny.
Having mastered the sciences in childhood, seeking the objects of the senses in youth,
living the life of sages in old age, and finally casting off the body through yoga at the end.
Though my power of speech is meager, I shall recount the lineage of the Raghus;
for their virtues, having reached my ears, have impelled me toward this rashness.
The virtuous, who are the means for discerning the real from the unreal, ought to hear this;
for in fire, both the purity and the impurity of gold are clearly perceived.
There was a son of Vivasvat named Manu, honored by the wise,
who was the first among kings, just as the syllable Om is the first among the Vedic meters.
Born in that pure lineage was one even purer—
Dilīpa, a moon among kings, like the moon born from the ocean of milk.
Broad-chested, with shoulders like those of a bull, tall as a *śāla* tree, and long-armed,
he possessed a body suited to his own deeds, as if he were the very dharma of the warrior class incarnate.
With a vital essence surpassing all others, outshining all splendor,
he stood upon the earth as if he were Mount Meru itself, towering above everything.
His wisdom was equal to his appearance; his sacred learning was equal to his wisdom;
his undertakings were equal to his learning; and his success was equal to his undertakings.
By his royal qualities, which were both formidable and attractive,
he was both unassailable and approachable to his dependents, like the ocean with its jewels that are both fearsome and delightful.
Under that ruler, his subjects did not deviate even by a hair’s breadth from the path established by Manu; they moved only within its bounds, like the revolutions of a wheel's rim.
For the sake of the prosperity of his subjects alone, he accepted tribute from them;
for the sun takes up moisture only to release it back a thousandfold.
His army and his equipment—these two alone were the means for accomplishing his purpose:
an intellect unimpeded in the sciences, and a bowstring drawn upon his bow.
The undertakings of that king, who kept his counsel secret and concealed his outward gestures and facial expressions,
could be inferred from their results, just like past karmic formations (*saṃskāra*).
Fearless, he protected himself; free from affliction, he practiced dharma;
without greed, he acquired wealth; and unattached, he experienced happiness.
Silence in wisdom, forbearance in power, and the absence of self-praise in renunciation—
his virtues, because they were linked with other virtues, seemed as if they were accompanied by their own offspring.
Unattracted by the objects of the senses, having reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge,
and devoted to dharma, he attained the state of old age without the physical decay of senility.
Because he disciplines, protects, and sustains his subjects, he is their father;
their biological fathers are merely the cause of their birth.

For that wise king, even his pursuit of wealth and pleasure was rooted in righteousness alone— righteousness which he maintained by punishing those deserving of punishment for the sake of stability, and which he wedded for the sake of progeny.
That generous lord milked the earth for sacrifice and the heavens for grain;
through an exchange of their respective abundances, the two sustained both worlds.
Indeed, other kings did not follow the fame of that protector,
for since he had turned away from the property of others, the practice of thievery remained only in the ears [of reports].
To him who was thus afflicted, even a learned man who was normally disliked was esteemed like medicine;
whereas a wicked person, though beloved, was to be shunned like a finger bitten by a snake.
Surely the Creator fashioned him through the meditative absorption of the great elements;
for thus all his qualities had as their sole fruit the welfare of others.
He ruled the earth— which had the ocean as its moat and was encircled by the ramparts of its shores—
as if it were a single city, under his sole authority.
He had a wife born of the Magadha lineage named Sudakṣiṇā, so called because of her extreme courtesy; she was like the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of a ritual.
The lord of the earth considered himself possessed of a wife by virtue of that high-minded lady, even though he already had a great harem, just as one is possessed of prosperity through true fortune.
Eager for the birth of a son from her, who was worthy of himself,
he passed the time with desires whose fulfillment was long delayed.
For the sake of ensuring the continuity of his lineage,
he took from his own arm the heavy burden of the world and entrusted it to his ministers.
Just as Bhagīratha once entrusted the Gaṅgā— capable of purifying his ancestors—
to his ministers, so did he entrust Kosala to them, desiring a lineage.
Then, having worshipped the Creator with self-restraint out of a desire for a son,
the couple went to the hermitage of their preceptor Vasiṣṭha.
Seated together upon a single chariot that emitted a smooth and deep resonance,
they resembled lightning and Airāvata upon a rain-cloud during the monsoon.
Lest there be any disturbance to the hermitage, they were accompanied by only a limited number of attendants;
yet, due to the excellence of their majesty, they appeared as if surrounded by an entire army.
They were served by breezes pleasant to the touch, fragrant with the resin of *śāla* trees,
scattering the pollen of flowers, and shaking the rows of forest trees.
Delightful to the mind, they listened as the peacocks, with heads turned toward the sound of the chariot wheels,
uttered cries divided into two tones that harmonized with the *ṣaḍja* note.
They beheld pairs of deer, which had recently left the path, resembling one another as they watched from their chariot.
In some places, with their faces raised by cranes whose sweet-sounding cries formed, as it were, a pillarless archway-wreath through their flight in rows; Ragh_1.41.
Because the wind was favorable, foretelling the fulfillment of their prayers,
the two of them had their garments untouched by the dust kicked up by the horses.
In the lakes, they inhaled the fragrance of the lotuses, cooled by the agitation of the ripples and resembling their own breath.
In the villages surrendered to them by the sacrificers, marked by sacrificial posts,
they received infallible blessings following upon the respectful offerings.
Taking fresh butter, they approached the elder cowherds who were standing by,
inquiring after the names of the wild trees along the path.
As those two, dressed in pure attire, proceeded together, there was a certain splendor about them,
like that of the moon and the star Citrā joined in conjunction when freed from the clouds.
In the evening, that king of pleasing appearance, accompanied by his queen, showed all those things to his wife as he approached the great sage who was observing his vows.
Having achieved a fame difficult to attain, he reached the hermitage in the evening with his weary horses,
accompanied by the queen of that great seer who was self-restrained.
It was being filled by ascetics returning from the depths of the forest, carrying sacrificial wood, kusha grass, and fruit,
who rose up to meet the fire that remained invisible to them.
It was crowded with deer that blocked the doors of the hermits' huts,
like offspring accustomed to receiving their share of wild rice.
At the edge of the watering-place, the young daughters of sages had just at that moment abandoned their saplings so that the birds,
coming to drink from the water in the basins, might feel secure.
In the courtyards of the leaf-huts, the deer sat upon the ground where wild rice had been gathered from the heat of the sun,
chewing their cud.
He purified those guests who were setting out for the hermitages with smoke wafted by the wind— smoke that bore the fragrance of oblations and was heralded by the rising of the sacrificial fires.
Then, having instructed the charioteer to let the draft animals rest,
he helped his wife descend from the chariot and himself alighted.

To him, the protector who was accompanied by his wife, the sages— whose senses were most thoroughly guarded— offered the honors due to one worthy of them, for he possessed the eye of political wisdom.
At the conclusion of his evening rites,
he beheld that ocean of asceticism seated beside Arundhatī, like the consumer of oblations (Agni) with Svāhā.
The king and the Magadhan queen took their feet;
the preceptor and his wife greeted them with affection in return.
The sage questioned that sage of the royal order about his welfare in the kingdom— his fatigue from the jolting of the chariot having been stilled by the performance of hospitable rites.
Then, before that repository of the Atharva Veda, whose cities of enemies had been conquered,
the Lord of Wealth— the best among speakers— uttered these meaningful words.
Is it not indeed fitting that prosperity has come to me, whose seven limbs have you as the dispeller of both divine and human calamities?
By the mantras composed by you, my arrows— which strike their targets at a distance— seem to be repelled from afar by enemies who have likewise employed mantras against them.
O Hotṛ priest, because the oblation has been offered by you into the fires according to the prescribed rites,
there shall be rain for the crops that were withered by drought.
That my subjects live out their full span of life, free from affliction and calamity,
is due to the spiritual luster of your sacred knowledge.
When I am thus meditated upon by you, my preceptor who is the source of the Veda,
how could my prosperity not be free from calamity and accompanied by its proper consequences?
But since this daughter-in-law of yours has not yet borne a son equal to her,
even the earth— with its continents and its yield of jewels— does not comfort me.
Surely my descendants, seeing that the offering of funeral cakes will cease with me,
will no longer eat their fill at the *śrāddha* ceremony, being intent instead on the accumulation of ancestral offerings (*svadhā*).
Considering that which is beyond me to be difficult to attain,
my ancestors surely drink the water I have offered, made lukewarm by their own sighs.
Thus, with my soul purified by sacrifice, yet obscured by the lack of progeny,
I am like the mountain Lokāloka— both light and dark.
Merit arising from austerity and charity brings happiness in other worlds;
indeed, a lineage of pure descent leads to well-being both here and in the hereafter.
O Creator, how is it that you do not grieve upon seeing me deprived of her,
like a sapling in a hermitage that has been watered by your own affection yet remains barren?
"O Blessed One, know that my final debt causes me unbearable pain,
like a goad piercing the tender flesh of an elephant that has not yet attained liberation."
Therefore, my dear father, you ought to arrange matters so that I may be released;
for in this matter difficult to achieve for the Ikṣvākus, success indeed depends upon you.
Thus addressed by the king, the sage, his eyes motionless in meditation,
remained for a moment like a lake whose fish are asleep.
Then, through his meditative resolve, he whose self was purified perceived the cause of the obstruction within the king's mental continuum; he then awakened the lord of the earth to this fact.
Formerly, as you were returning toward the earth after attending upon Śakra,
Surabhi was resting on the road beneath the shade of a Kalpa tree.
Out of fear of violating dharma, you did not act rightly toward this queen, who was worthy of being circumambulated, while remembering that she had bathed after her menses.
"Because you despise me, therefore offspring shall not be born to you without having propitiated me"—thus did she curse you. (Raghuvamśa 1.77)
O King, that curse was heard neither by you nor by the charioteer,
as the sky resounded with the roar of the celestial Gaṅgā while the wild elephants of the quarters plunged into its current.
Know that through the disregard of him, your desired goal is effectively barred;
for the neglect of honoring those worthy of honor obstructs one's spiritual welfare.
That daughter of the wise one now presides over Pātāla, whose gates are guarded by serpents, for the sake of the oblation of the long sacrificial session.
Having made her daughter a substitute for Surabhi, you, being pure, should worship her together with your wife; for she, when pleased, is indeed the cow of plenty.
Even as the Hotṛ priest was speaking thus,
a blameless cow named Nandinī, the means for his sacrificial oblation, returned from the forest.
With her forehead slightly curved upward, she was like the twilight bearing the new moon marked by white hair, as rosy and smooth as a fresh sprout.
She sprinkled the earth with lukewarm, purifying water even after the ritual bath,
raining down from her udder as it flowed forth at the sight of her calf.
By the particles of dust raised by their hooves that touched his body from close at hand,
the king attained the purity born of bathing in sacred waters.
Having seen her, whose appearance was auspicious, the knower of signs and treasure-house of asceticism spoke again to his patron, whose prayers were now destined to bear fruit.
O King, consider that success is not far off for you,
since this auspicious lady has appeared as soon as her name was uttered.
Living on forest fare, you ought to propitiate this cow by constantly following her, just as one seeks to master knowledge through constant practice.
When she has set out, you should set out; when she has stopped, you should take your stand;
when she is seated, you should sit down; and when she has drunk water, you should drink water.
And let the devoted bride, having honored her [the cow] until she reaches the penance grove,
follow her with self-restraint in the morning, like a father at the head of those who possess sons.
Thus, until she is won over by your favor, remain devoted to her service;
may you meet with no obstacles, and stay there even if you must return at evening.
"So be it," replied the disciple with joy, together with his retinue; knowing the proper place and time, he, bowing low before his teacher, accepted the command of his instructor.
Then at twilight, the son of the Creator, who knew the faults [of the day] and spoke with pleasant truth, dismissed the Lord of the People for rest, as his own splendor had already arisen.
Although he possessed the perfection of asceticism, the sage,
who was skilled in ritual procedures, ordained for him a forest dwelling in accordance with the rules of discipline.
Having occupied the leaf-hut pointed out by the head of the clan, accompanied by his devoted wife as his second companion,
he spent the night lying on a bed of *kuśa* grass, its end signaled by the recitation of his pupil.

Then at dawn, the lord of subjects, whose wealth was his fame, released for the forest the cow belonging to the seer— her calf having been tied up after drinking— and whose scent and garlands had been received by his wife.

The lawful wife of the lord of men, who was herself irreproachable, followed her path— the dust of which was purified by the placement of her husband's hooves— just as the Smṛti follows the meaning of the Śruti, she being worthy of praise at the forefront of those who are free from worldly stain.
Having turned back his beloved wife, the compassionate king— fragrant with his own glories—
protected that daughter of Surabhi as if she were the earth herself in the form of a cow, whose udders were the four oceans.
By him, who was following for the sake of his vow, even the rest of the retinue of followers was dismissed;
nor did he require protection for his person from any other source, for the progeny of Manu is guarded by its own prowess.
With mouthfuls of grass that were flavorful, by scratching her to relieve her itching, and by warding off gadflies,
the emperor devoted himself to pleasing her with unhindered freedom of movement.
Standing when she stood, moving when she moved, and sitting down with steady composure when she sat upon her seat,
the king followed her like a thirsty man following one who carries water.
Though he bore royal fortune stripped of its outward emblems, it was inferred by his extraordinary splendor;
he remained like a lordly elephant in a state of internal rut, whose flow of ichor has not yet been manifested.
With his bow strung by creepers and climbing vines, he roamed through the forest;
under the pretext of guarding the sage’s sacrificial cow, he seemed as if to discipline the wild beasts.
As he proceeded with his attendants left behind, the trees by his side— equaling Varuṇa, the wielder of the noose—
seemed to utter the cry of "Look! through the warbling of birds intoxicated with joy.
And young creepers, impelled by the Maruts, covered him— who resembled a friend of the Maruts— as he approached nearby,
with their blossoms and with the cries of birds that sounded like the word "Aloka" (behold!).

Even though he was a wielder of the bow, the does, their hearts having been made fearless, perceived his compassionate nature; gazing upon his form, they attained the full fruit of the wide expansion of their eyes.
In the groves, he heard his own fame being loudly sung by the forest deities, while the hollow bamboos, their interiors filled with the wind, produced the effect of a flute as they whistled.

The wind, fragrant with the scent of flowers shaken from the trees by mountain torrents and carrying cool drops of spray, attended upon him— who was purified by his conduct, who lacked a parasol, and who was weary from the heat of the sun.
Even without rain, the forest fire was extinguished; there was an extraordinary increase in fruits and flowers;
and while he, O cowherd’s daughter, was entering that forest, no one of superior strength oppressed those who were weak among the creatures.
Having purified the quarters of the sky with her movement,
as that cow-pen-woman, copper-red as a young leaf, was entering the forest at the end of the day to go to her dwelling, she set out.
The protector of the middle world followed her for the sake of performing rites for the gods, the ancestors, and guests;
and she shone with him, who was esteemed by the virtuous, like Faith herself visibly accompanied by the prescribed ritual.

He proceeded, beholding forests turning dark with the onset of night— forests where herds of boars had emerged from the ponds, where peacocks looked up toward their roosting trees, and where deer lay resting upon the sward.
Due to the effort of bearing the weight of her full udders, the young cow and the king, on account of the heaviness of his body,
both graced the path of their return from the penance grove with their elegant gaits.
As he returned from the edge of the forest following Vasiṣṭha’s cow, his wife drank him in with her eyes—
the lashes of which were slow to blink— as if they had been fasting.
Honored on the path by the king and welcomed by the king’s lawful wife,
that cow shone between them like the twilight between day and night.
Having circumambulated that milch-cow, Sudakṣiṇā, with a vessel of parched grain in her hand,
bowed down and worshipped its broad space between the horns, which was like a gateway to the fulfillment of her desires.

Although she was anxious for her calf, she received the ritual service with composure; thus the two rejoiced, for among those endowed with devotion, the signs of favor from such beings are the precursors of the fruit.
Having massaged the feet of his preceptor and his wife and completed the evening rites, Dilīpa—
who had severed the enemy with his own arms— attended once more to the milch cow as she sat down after the milking was finished.
Having sat beside her, where offerings and lamps were placed nearby, the protector, accompanied by his wife,
lay down after she had gradually fallen asleep; and in the morning, he rose when she rose from sleep.
Thus, as he of illustrious fame— who was ever intent on uplifting the distressed— observed this vow for the sake of progeny together with his queen,
seven times three days passed away.
On another day, the sage’s sacrificial cow, wishing to ascertain the disposition of her attendant,
entered the cave of the Lord of Gauri, where young grass grew at the edge of the fall of the Ganges.
While the king’s gaze was fixed upon the beauty of the mountain,
the lion— his leap unnoticed by the monarch— seized her and dragged her away by force.

The king’s gaze, which was fixed upon the lord of mountains, he turned back as if drawing it in by its rays— the wailing of that distressed and virtuous man, made long by the echoes reverberating within the caves.
Standing on the Pāṭalā cow, that archer beheld the lion,
like a blossoming Lodhra tree upon a mountain peak made of minerals on a high plateau.

Then the king, who moved like a lion among lions, who was a refuge for the distressed, and who had forcibly uprooted his enemies, felt a surge of passion for the slaughter of his victim and desired to draw an arrow from his quiver.

The other hand of that archer, its fingers still clinging to the feathered shaft of the arrow— its flight depicted in a painting— remained fixed upon the heron-feather, adorned with the luster of his fingernails.
His fury increased by the obstruction of his arms,
the king burned within with his own vital energies, unable to touch the offender who stood so near, like a serpent whose power is neutralized by mantras and medicinal herbs.

The lion, his cow having been seized, addressed that banner of Manu’s lineage— who was a noble protector, who had mastered himself, and who was of lion-like courage— in human speech, astonishing him who was already amazed at his own conduct.

"Enough of your exertion, O protector of the earth; even a weapon discharged against him would be in vain. The power of the wind's force to uproot trees does not prevail against a mountain. (Raghuvamśa 2.34)

"Know me to be Kumbhodara by name, a friend of Nikumbha and a servant of the Eight-formed Lord (Śiva), whose back has been purified by the grace of your footstep as you desire to ascend Mount Kailāsa, white as the mountain itself."
Do you see that deodar tree ahead? It has been adopted as a son by the bull-bannered god [Śiva], for it alone knows the flavor of the milk flowing from the golden-pitcher breasts of Skanda’s mother.
Once, while scratching his flank, the skin of this [tree] was torn away by a wild elephant;
then the Daughter of the Mountain grieved for him, as if for a general pierced by the weapons of the Asuras.

From that very time forward, the wielder of the trident, having transformed me into a lion whose livelihood consists of preying upon creatures that come into his clutches, appointed me to this vast belly for the purpose of terrifying the wild elephants.
This [offering], ordained by the Supreme Lord at the appointed time, is sufficient for the satisfaction of me who am hungry;
it has arrived as my feast of blood, just as the nectar of the moon is for the enemy of the gods.
Therefore, casting aside shame, return; you have demonstrated devotion to your guru.
That which is to be protected by weapons but cannot be protected does not diminish the fame of those who bear arms.
Having heard these bold words of the king of beasts, the king of men,
his weapons rendered ineffectual by the power of Śiva, relaxed the self-contempt he had felt within himself.
And he replied to him at the moment of discharging the arrow— his effort rendered futile by that previous encounter,
paralyzed by the glance of the Three-Eyed God— like the wielder of the thunderbolt wishing to release his vajra.
He replied to him: "Let me not, by the failure of my arrow's release, incur a change of voice from the friction of the feathers;
let me not be weighed down by this autumnal cloud, which is devoid of essence and has lost its former resonance."
"Since laughter is the cause for one whose actions are restrained, I shall speak that which I desire to say;
for you know all the internal states of living beings, and therefore I shall address you."
"He is venerable to me as the cause of the creation, preservation, and dissolution of all things mobile and immobile;
this wealth of my preceptor, who maintains the sacred fires, must not be neglected by me as it perishes before my eyes."
Therefore, be gracious enough to sustain my bodily existence with your own body;
let this cow of the great seer be released, for her young calf is anxious at the close of day.
Then, shattering the darkness of the mountain caves with the rays from his fangs,
that attendant of the Lord of Beings once more spoke to Arthapati with a slight smile.
"Your sovereignty over the world under a single umbrella, this fresh and lovely body, and [your youth]—
you appear to me to be bewildered by lack of reflection, desiring to abandon so much for the sake of a trifle."
If this compassion for living beings were yours, then at your end this single cow would be safe;
yet, O Lord of Subjects, you protect your people from constant calamities like a father protects his children while he himself lives.
Now, you fear your teacher, who is fierce in his resentment toward a single cow and resembles a consuming fire;
yet it is possible for you to appease his wrath by presenting him with millions of cows with udders as large as jars.
Therefore, protect your own vigorous body, the enjoyer of a succession of auspicious deeds;
for they say that a prosperous kingdom, which differs from the station of Indra only by its contact with the surface of the earth, is indeed the state of Indra himself.

When the king of beasts had ceased speaking after saying this much, the mountain itself, through the echo returning from its caves, seemed to address that very same purpose to the protector of the earth with loud affection.
Having heard the words of the celestial attendant, the god among men spoke once more;
he was moved to even greater compassion as he gazed upon the cow, whose eyes were distressed by his presence.
The exalted word *kṣatra* is indeed established throughout the worlds as meaning "one who protects from injury.
Of what use is sovereignty, or life itself, stained by infamy, to one whose conduct is the opposite of that?
How indeed could the great seer be won over by the gift of other milch-cows?
Know this cow to be no inferior to Surabhi; rather, she was seized from you by the power of Rudra.
Therefore, it is right for me to release her from you by paying the ransom of my own body;
in this way, your breaking of the fast will not be frustrated, and the purpose of the Sage’s ritual will remain unimpaired.
Your Majesty also understands this dependence on another, for great indeed is your effort regarding the Devadāru tree;
for it is not possible for one who desires to protect a charge to stand before its destroyer without himself remaining unharmed.
If you consider me someone not to be harmed, then show compassion for my body of fame;
for those like me have truly no attachment to physical lumps of matter that are destined for absolute destruction.
They say that friendship is preceded by conversation; that has occurred between us two as we met at the edge of the forest.
Therefore, O follower of the Lord of Beings, you ought not to reject the affection of one who is my kinsman.
Having said "So be it" to the cow, Dilīpa immediately released his arm from its paralysis;
laying down his weapons, he offered his own body to Hari like a morsel of meat.
At that moment, as the protector of his subjects beheld the fierce descent of the lion,
a rain of flowers released from the hands of the Vidyādharas fell upon him as he sat with his face cast downward.
Hearing the words "Rise, my child! which were like nectar, he rose;
and having risen, the king beheld before him not a lion, but his own cow, yielding milk like a mother.
To him who was thus amazed, the cow said: "O virtuous one, you have been tested by me through the manifestation of an illusion.
By the power of the sage, not even Death himself is able to strike me, much less other predatory beasts."
"Out of devotion to my guru and out of compassion for me, I am pleased with you, my son; choose a boon.
Know me, when I am propitiated, to be the wish-fulfilling cow, not merely the source of milk."
Then, having summoned him, he who honored his purpose and had earned for himself the title of "Hero" by his own hand,
requested from Sudakṣiṇā a son who would be the founder of his lineage and possess infinite fame.
Having promised the king—who desired progeny—that his wish would be granted, that milch-cow milked her own milk into a leaf-cup and instructed him: "My son, drink this."
O Mother, having obtained the permission of the Sage for the remainder of the calf after the rules for the oblation have been fulfilled,
I wish to enjoy the milk from your udders, just as one enjoys the sixth part of a protected earth.
Thus addressed by the lord of the earth, Vasiṣṭha’s cow became exceedingly pleased;
accompanied by him, she returned from the slopes of the Himalayas to the hermitage without any fatigue.
The preceptor of kings, his moon-like face radiant with serenity, having communicated his favor to the Guru,
declared it to his beloved wife through words that were like a mere reiteration, as it had already been inferred from the signs of his great joy.

Having been granted permission by Vasiṣṭha, that blameless soul, who was ever affectionate toward his subjects, drank the milk of Nandinī— the remainder of what had been offered to the calf— with great thirst, as if it were pure fame incarnate.
In the morning, at the conclusion of the breaking of the fast according to the prescribed vow,
the self-controlled Vasiṣṭha performed the rite for a safe journey and sent the couple back toward their own capital city.

Having circumambulated the sacrificial fire into which oblations had been offered, and immediately thereafter his lord’s wife Arundhatī and a cow with her calf, the king set forth, his majesty further intensified by these auspicious signs.

Accompanied by his lawful wife, the patient king traveled along a road made pleasant by the absence of obstacles on a chariot whose sound was delightful to the ear, as if upon his own fulfilled desire.

The subjects, distressed by his absence and their own bodies emaciated by vows for the sake of progeny, drank him in with eyes that could not reach satiety— him whose longing had been aroused [for them], and whose limbs were thinned by the vow for offspring, like the lord of medicinal herbs at his first rising.
Having entered the city, which was adorned with raised banners and where he was greeted with joy by the citizens, he— possessing the splendor of Indra—
once again placed the burden of the earth upon his arm, which was equal in strength to that of the king of serpents.
Then, as the sky receives the light arising from the eyes of Atri, or as the celestial river receives the splendor of Śiva spat forth by fire,
the queen conceived a fetus for the prosperity of the royal lineage— a fetus infused with the weighty majesties of the world-protectors.

Then Sudakṣiṇā bore the signs of pregnancy— the very cause for the continuity of the Ikṣvāku lineage, the fulfillment of her husband’s desire, and the moonlight-like beginning of the glances of her circle of friends.
With her ornaments incomplete due to the exhaustion of her body, and with a face pale as the *lodhra* flower,
she appeared like a night at dawn when the stars have been sought out by their faint light, accompanied only by the moon.

Then the beloved wife of the lord of the people— whose lineage was unbroken, whose affection was shared by no other, and who was naturally sweet-spoken— experienced a longing that was like a pregnancy-craving for her husband’s desire, which was now somewhat inclined toward fulfillment.
With her face as pale as a ketaka petal, her slender frame adorned with but a few ornaments,
she emulated the night at dawn when the moon’s orb is faint and only a few stars remain.
Then the lord of the earth, having secretly kissed her face, fragrant with clay, found no satiety,
just as an elephant at the end of the hot season finds no satisfaction in sniffing a pond at the edge of a forest row that has been sprinkled by the droplets of rain clouds.
"For his son, with his chariot resting at the ends of the quarters, shall enjoy the earth as the Lord of the Maruts enjoys heaven;
therefore, she first fixed her mind upon such a desire, bypassing all other pleasures."
Out of modesty, the Magadhan princess did not express any desire she might have for various objects;
for even in the third heaven, that lord of the earth would not have desired what was not dear to his beloved friend, the ruler of Uttarakośala.
Having approached her state of longing and distress, whatever she chose, that very thing she saw brought to her;
for there was nothing desired by this king—even in the third heaven—that remained unattainable when his bow was strung.
Having gradually overcome the distress of her pregnancy longings, she shone with her limbs increasingly full,
like a creeper that, immediately after the falling away of its old leaves, is covered with beautiful new shoots.
As the days passed, her two breasts, becoming exceedingly full and dark-tipped,
eclipsed the beauty of two well-formed lotus buds with bees settled upon them.

The king regarded his queen as the ocean-clad earth containing hidden treasures, like a *śamī* tree with fire latent within its heart, or like the river Sarasvatī filled with water; he perceived her as being truly pregnant.

That steadfast king performed the *puṃsavana* and other rites appropriate to his affection for his beloved, his mental exaltation, the wealth acquired by his arms from the ends of the earth, and his own fortitude, in their proper sequence.

The king rejoiced when she entered the house, her body heavy with the burden of the womb resting upon the lap of Surendramātṛ; she had risen from her seat with great effort, her hands were weary from the gesture of respectful salutation, and her eyes were tremulous.
Then, when the care of the pregnancy had been attended to by trusted physicians skilled in pediatrics,
the husband, full of confidence, beheld his beloved at the time of delivery, like the sky freed from clouds at the proper season.

Then, at the auspicious time, she who was equal to Śacī gave birth to a son whose abundant fortune was indicated by five planets situated in their exaltations and not in the sun’s path— just as the triple-powered Śakti brought forth the imperishable Artha.
The quarters became serene, the winds blew pleasantly, and the fire accepted the oblation with its flames turning to the right;
at that moment, everything became auspicious, for such is the nature of the birth of those destined for the world's exaltation.
By the innate splendor of that noble-born one, which spread all around his deathbed,
the midnight lamps were suddenly robbed of their luster and became as if fixed in a painting.
To the person of the inner apartments who announced the birth of the prince in words equal to nectar, there was only one thing that the king could not give:
his moon-bright parasol and the two fly-whisks.
Beholding his son’s face after so long, the father— like a destitute man who has found a jar of treasure—
was so overcome with joy that he could not contain himself within his own body, just as the ocean swells at the rising of the moon.
As the king drank in his beloved son’s face with eyes as motionless as a lotus in a windless place,
a profound joy arose within him— so great that it could not be contained, like the swelling tide of the great ocean at the sight of the moon.
When the entire birth-rite had been performed by the ascetic family priest who had come from the penance grove,
the son of Dilīpa shone with even greater luster, like a jewel produced from a mine that has undergone the proper refinement.
The sounds of auspicious musical instruments, pleasant to hear, accompanied by the joyful dances of courtesans,
resounded not only within the palace of the Lord of Magadha, but also along the path of the gods.
The protector did not restrain anyone whom he might have released, being overjoyed at the birth of his son;
at that time, he himself was liberated from the bondage of his ancestors solely by virtue of what is called the "debt."
Considering that this child would reach the end of what is heard— that is, master the Vedas— and likewise reach the end of others in battle, the king,
who understood the meaning of words, gave his son born of himself the name Raghu, for the root *ragh* signifies "to go."
Through his father’s efforts and the fulfillment of all prosperity, he grew day by day with auspicious limbs,
like the young moon increasing in size through the entry of the rays of the sun.
Just as Umā and the Bull-bannered Lord [Śiva] rejoice with Śarajanman [Kārttikeya], and as Śacī and Purandara with Jayanta,
so did the King and the Magadhan princess rejoice with their son, who resembled them and was their equal.
The mutual affection between them, which was like that of the two birds named *rathāṅga* (cakravāka) bound by the ties of love,
increased all the more toward one another even though it was divided by their single son.
The child spoke the words first uttered by his nurse, walked while holding her finger, and became humble through the instruction of prostration; thus, that infant spread joy for his father.
Placing him upon his lap, as if drenching his skin with nectar through the bliss born of physical contact,
the king, with eyes half-closed, finally attained the experience of the taste of his son's touch.
Having placed him upon his lap, the protector of his lineage— who never deviates from the proper conduct— embraced that steadfast boy with the touch of his own body,
just as the Lord of Creatures embraces his own creation through the excellence of his own form.
Having had his tonsure ceremony performed, he was accompanied by sons of ministers of his own age who wore the sidelocks of youth;
through the proper acquisition of writing, he entered the ocean of literature as a river enters the sea through its mouth.
Then, once he had been initiated according to the prescribed rites, the teachers instructed him—who was dear to his elders—in the sciences;
their efforts toward the boy were not in vain, for he mastered the branches of knowledge with a speed surpassing that of the wind.
With all his virtues complete, that noble-minded one gradually crossed over the four branches of learning— which are like the four oceans—
just as the Lord of the Monkeys [Hanumān] crossed the quarters of the sky with his bay horses that outstripped the wind.
Having donned the sacred skin of the Ruru deer, he practiced the science of weapons with his father’s mantras;
for not only was his father the sole sovereign on earth, but he too became the sole wielder of the bow upon the world.
Like a young calf reaching the state of a great bull, or like a young elephant attaining the condition of a lordly tusker,
Raghu— his childhood gradually supplanted by youth— cultivated a body that was captivating in its majesty.
Then, immediately after the rite of the Godāna ceremony, the preceptor performed the initiation for his marriage;
having obtained that virtuous husband, the princesses shone like the daughters of Dakṣa who have attained the dispeller of darkness.
Though Raghu— youthful, with arms as long as a yoke, muscular, with a chest like a door-panel and a thick-set neck—
surpassed his elder in physical excellence, he appeared humble because of his modesty.

Then, because he was naturally disciplined by his refined upbringing, the king appointed him to the title of crown prince, intending thereby to lighten the exceedingly heavy burden of the subjects which he himself had long borne.
Immediately after the primary abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
she who desired his virtues went forth with a portion of herself, like the sun emerging from the clearing of thick clouds, or as a fresh lotus-stalk issues from an old one.
Like fire fanned by the wind, or the sun at the end of the rainy season,
or an elephant with its temples bursting, the king became exceedingly difficult to endure because of him.
Having appointed that archer, followed by the princes, to guard the sacrificial horse,
he who was equal to Indra completed one hundred sacrifices without obstacle, lacking only one.
After that,

Śakra, it is said, having assumed a concealed form, seized the horse that had been released again without restraint for the sacrifice by that wielder of the thunderbolt, right before the eyes of the archers who were its guardians.

When she heard these words uttered by the cow, Nandinī, whose power was known through sacred tradition, then appeared; for it was she who, her resolve obscured by distress and filled with wonder, beheld the horse here before me.
"Wipe my eyes with the water from your sweat, my son, so that you may see the horse here,"—
hearing these words uttered by the cow, the son of Dilīpa attained the highest joy.
Then, having wiped his eyes with the holy water flowing from her body, the son of Dilīpa, honored by the virtuous,
became one who possessed the power of vision even regarding things that transcend the senses.
To the east, the son of a king beheld the god who shatters the wings of mountains;
he was repeatedly restraining the horse—which had been freed from its reins by the chariot’s ropes—though its restlessness was being checked by the charioteer.
Recognizing from the east that Hari, the shatterer of the wings of mountains, was there with his bay horses,
Raghu addressed him in a deep voice, as if calling him back, using a tone that reached even the Ganges.
O Lord of the Gods, you alone are always declared by the wise to be the foremost among those who partake of the sacrificial offerings;
how then do you proceed to obstruct the ritual of my preceptor, who is ever-diligent in his consecration?
"Surely the Lord of the Three Worlds, possessing divine vision, must always be restrained by you against those who are enemies of sacrifice;
yet if you yourself become an obstacle to those practicing dharma, the established order has fallen away."
Therefore, O Maghavan, it behoves you to release that horse, which is the foremost limb of this great sacrifice;
for lords who show themselves as protectors of those who seek refuge do not tread upon a path stained by impurity.
Having heard these bold words uttered by Raghu, the lord of the gods,
filled with wonder, turned his chariot back and proceeded to offer a reply.
"O Prince, what you have said is true; however, fame must be guarded against others by those for whom fame is their wealth.
Your father is now prepared to violate that entire world-renowned [fame] through his sacrifice."
Just as Hari alone is remembered as Puruṣottama, and Maheśvara alone as Tryambaka and none other, so do the sages know me as Śatakratu; for this title of ours does not apply to a second person.
Therefore, this horse was carried off by me from your father, who was imitating Kapila.
Enough of this effort; do not set foot upon the path of Sagara’s progeny.
Then, laughing and free from fear, the protector of the horse spoke again to Purandara:
"Take up your weapon if this is your intent; indeed, you shall not achieve your purpose without first conquering Raghu."
Having spoken thus to Maghavan, he stood with his face turned upward, about to fix an arrow upon his bow;
by the excellence of his physical form, made beautiful by the *ālīḍha* stance, he rivaled the Lord Śiva himself.

Wounded in the heart by Raghu’s arrow— which was composed of his very defiance— even the impatient Indra, the breaker of mountains, fixed an unerring shaft upon his bow, which was marked for a moment by the approaching host of fresh clouds.
Having entered the broad chest of Dilīpa’s son, that swift arrow— accustomed to the blood of terrifying demons— drank human blood such as it had never tasted before, as if out of sheer curiosity.

The prince of Hari, possessing the prowess of a youth, also fixed an arrow marked with his own name upon the arm of Indra— that arm which was hardened by the lashing of the celestial elephant's trunk and adorned with decorative patterns of Śacī’s leaves.
And with another feathered arrow, he struck down Śakra’s great thunderbolt-banner;
the god raged violently at him, as if his very hair had been forcibly shorn from the Goddess of Fortune.

Between those two, who were stationed near each other and eager for victory, there occurred a tumultuous battle with arrows— some facing downward and some facing upward— that was terrifying to behold due to the presence of Siddhas and soldiers, as well as Garuḍas and venomous serpents.
With showers of weapons discharged in an incessant stream, Indra was unable to extinguish that body of unbearable splendor,
just as a cloud cannot extinguish with its waters the fire that has issued forth from within itself.
Then, with an arrow whose head was like the crescent moon, Raghu— whose voice was as deep as the churning ocean— snapped the bowstring of Indra upon his forearm marked with yellow sandalwood paste.

Casting aside his bow, his envy having intensified, he took up a weapon that was capable of lopping off the wings of mountains— a weapon that emitted a shimmering halo of light— in order to destroy his powerful adversary.
Struck violently in the chest by him, Raghu fell to the ground along with the tears of his soldiers;
yet, shaking off that pain in the mere twinkling of an eye, he rose up together with the shouts of joy from the troops.

Nevertheless, even though he had long remained in the state of an enemy—a condition harsh with the practice of weapons—the Slayer of Vṛtra was gratified by his extraordinary valor; for a position is established everywhere through one's virtues.
"Even among the mountains, no one other than you has withstood my weapon because of its inherent power;
know that I am pleased—what do you desire, except for the horse? Thus did Vāsava speak clearly.
Then, withdrawing from his quiver the arrow that had not been fully drawn out— its golden-feathered shaft coloring his fingers—
the prince, speaking with kind words, replied to the Lord of the Gods.
O Lord, if you consider the horse to be unreleasable, then, once the ritual is completed according to the prescribed rules,
let my preceptor— who has been purified by an unceasing consecration— be endowed with the entire fruit of the sacrifice.

O Lord of the World, let it be so arranged that the Sovereign of the Universe, who is difficult to approach due to being a portion of the Three-eyed One, may hear this account from you himself as he sits in the assembly, through a messenger sent by you.
Saying "So be it," Mātali, whose charioteership was Raghu’s pleasure, departed for the way he had come;
and the son of Sudakṣiṇā also returned to the king’s assembly hall, his mind not entirely at ease.
First awakened by the messenger of Hari, the lord of subjects greeted him,
stroking with a hand numbed by joy his body marked by the scars of the thunderbolt.
Thus the lord of the earth, whose command was honored, having performed ninety-nine great sacrifices,
as his life drew to a close, desired to ascend to heaven and thereby created, as it were, a succession of steps.

Then, his soul freed from poison, having according to the prescribed rites bestowed the white royal umbrella upon his young son as the preeminent mark of sovereignty, he took refuge with that queen in the shade of a tree in the sage’s forest; for this is the family custom of the Ikṣvākus when their age has declined.
Having accepted the kingdom bestowed by his elder, he shone even more brightly,
like the sacrificial fire when the light of the sun has been deposited within it at the close of day.
And they heard that Dilīpa had laid down his weapons and that he was the lord of those kings whose hearts, from which the iron arrows had been extracted, felt as if a dart had been implanted.
Having heard that he had been established in the kingdom after Dilīpa,
the fire that had previously smoldered in the hearts of rival kings flared up like a blaze.
Like the rows of banners on Indra’s standard,
his subjects rejoiced at the sight of him as he rose for the first time after his birth.
Simultaneously, his rows of eyes ascended upon both his ancestral throne and the entire circle of his enemies.
It is said that Padmā herself, remaining invisible, attended upon him who had been consecrated for imperial sovereignty, using her own shadow as a lotus parasol.
And from time to time, as the bards were present, Sarasvatī attended upon him who was worthy of praise with meaningful hymns of praise, appearing as if personified.
Although the earth had been enjoyed by venerable kings beginning with Manu, nevertheless, it seemed as if it had never belonged to anyone else before him.
For he won the hearts of the entire world through his just administration of punishment, just as the southern breeze, being neither too cold nor too hot, wins the hearts of all.
Because of his superior virtues toward his teacher, he caused the people to feel only mild longing for him, just as the fruit of a mango tree causes the fading of longing for its blossoming flowers.
When those skilled in statecraft presented both the right and the wrong course to the new king, his former position alone remained; his subsequent [opinion] did not exist.
The qualities of even the five elements flourished in excellence;
under that new protector of the earth, everything seemed as if new once more.
Just as the moon is so called because it gladdens, and the sun because it heats,
even so did that king truly bear his name because he delighted his subjects.
Granted that his large eyes reached as far as his ears,
yet his true possession of vision was through the scripture, which allows one to perceive the meaning of subtle matters.
Then, royal fortune, marked by lotuses, approached him who was established in the well-being of having attained tranquility, like a second autumn.
When the clouds had shed their rain and become light, the unbearable heat, having found its path clear,
pervaded all directions at once, as if by his own bow drawn by one filled with apprehension.
Having cleared his path, the unbearable god of a hundred sacrifices drew back his own bow, as if apprehensive, in order to string his weapon.
Indra withdrew his rain-bringing bow, while Raghu took up his victorious one;
for those two were like a pair of bows raised in turn to accomplish the welfare of their subjects.
With its white lotus as a parasol and its blooming kāśa grass as fly-whisks, the season imitated him; thus, there was equality between the two.
With the white parasol of his favor held aloft and the moon of clear radiance shining,
the delight of those with eyes was then equal toward both.
Upon the rows of swans, upon the stars, and upon the waters filled with white lotuses,
the glories of his kinsmen seemed to have been scattered as a display of their splendor.
Seated in the shade of sugarcanes, the women guarding the rice fields sang of the fame of that protector, which arose from his virtues and extended back to the stories of his childhood.
At the rising of the great-spirited Agastya, the waters became clear;
yet at the sight of Raghu, the minds of his enemies were agitated with fear of defeat.
Intoxicated by rut, humped, and tearing up the banks of rivers,
the elephants of his enemies approached his prowess with playful ease, yet they were brought to ruin.
Struck by the blossoms of the *saptaparṇa* trees, which were fragrant with ichor,
those elephants exuded [ichor] from seven parts of their bodies as if out of envy.
Making the rivers fordable and the roads free from mud,
the autumn season first urged him toward his expedition by means of its power.
The fire, duly poured into it during the rite of the Horse-sacrifice purification,
gave him victory as if with its own hand under the guise of its clockwise-turning flames.
With his frontiers and rear-guard well-protected, his flanks pure,
and endowed with speed, he set out taking the sixfold army with him, desiring to conquer the quarters.
The city women, advanced in years, strewed parched grain over him,
just as the waves of the milk-ocean scatter droplets tossed up by Mount Mandara over Acyuta.
Equal to Prācīnabarhis, he first set out toward the east,
as if threatening his enemies with banners fluttering in the wind.
With dust raised by his chariot and with elephants resembling clouds,
he made the sky appear like the surface of the earth, and the earth like the sky.
First came the majesty, then the sound, then the dust, and finally the chariots and the rest; thus that army marched as if in four divisions.
By virtue of his power, he made the mountain ridges abound with water, the navigable rivers easy to cross, and the forests illuminated.
The rivers along his path were made turbid by those who preceded him, shallow by those who traveled with him, and muddy by those who followed behind.
Leading that great army toward the eastern ocean,
he shone like Bhagīratha leading the Gaṅgā as it falls from the matted locks of Śiva.
With kings deprived of their fruits, uprooted, and broken in many ways,
his path became formidable, like that of an elephant through trees.
Thus conquering various eastern provinces as he advanced,
the victorious king reached the shore of the great ocean, dark with groves of palm trees.
Therefore, the Suhmas protected themselves by adopting the behavior of a reed, like one escaping from the current of a river, in order to uproot those who were not submissive.
Having swiftly uprooted the Vaṅgas, who were arrogant in their naval forces,
that leader erected pillars of victory within the channels of the Ganges' current.
Bowing down as far as their lotus-feet like rice stalks,
they caused Raghu to flourish with fruits, having been uprooted and replanted.
Having crossed the Kapiṣā with his armies by means of a bridge constructed of bound elephants, he proceeded toward Kaliṅga, the path having been shown by the people of Utkala.
He planted his sharp prowess upon the head of Mahendra,
just as a driver fixes a goad upon the forehead of a deep-sensing elephant.
The King of Kaliṅga, whose force was his elephants, countered him with missiles,
just as a mountain raining down boulders opposes Indra when he prepares to clip its wings.
Having endured there the storm of iron arrows from his enemies, the descendant of Kakutstha attained the glory of victory as if he had bathed in an auspicious rite.
From the elephant host of the Kalinga king, which had been shaken by the Vāyavya weapon and scattered like the great ocean by its wings, he seized him as Tārkṣya seizes a serpent.
There, having prepared their drinking grounds with the leaves of betel vines,
the warriors drank coconut liquor and the fame of their enemies.
That king, victorious through righteousness, took away the sovereignty of the lord of great Indra once it had been seized and then relinquished, but he did not take the earth itself.
Then, along the very shore lined with rows of fruit-bearing betel-nut trees,
he whose victory was beyond doubt proceeded toward the quarter frequented by Agastya.
By the use of his army, fragrant with the ichor of elephants,
he made the Kāverī river seem as if it were a rival to the lord of streams, the ocean.
The foothills of the Malaya mountain, where green parrots fly about among the pepper shrubs, were traversed by the forces of that king who was intent on conquest after he had completed his journey.
The rising pollen of cardamom fruits,
crushed by the horses and sharing a similar fragrance, clung to the temples of the rutting elephants.
The dust arising from the fields of ripe paddy trampled by the hooves of well-bred horses suddenly pervaded the sky, even for those who could take three steps at a time.
The neck-chains of the elephants, though they tore through their foot-tethers, did not break even as they were entangled in the paths of the sandalwood trees.
In that very southern quarter, even the brilliance of the sun grows dim;
yet it was there that the Pāṇḍyas could not endure the majesty of Raghu.
Having descended, they presented to him the finest pearls from the great ocean where it meets the Tāmraparṇī river,
as if offering their own accumulated glory.
Having enjoyed himself as he desired on the slopes where sandalwood trees grew,
he beheld the Malaya and Dardura mountains, which were like the breasts of that region, with their sandalwood clinging to them.
With his advancing armies intent on conquering the western regions,
he was like the ocean, though driven back by Rāma’s arrows, yet clinging to the Sahya mountains.
By him, the dust of the army was made to serve as a substitute for scented powder upon the tresses of the Kerala women, who had cast off their ornaments out of fear.
The pollen of the *kaitaka* flowers, stirred up by the wind from the banners,
became the effortless *paṭavāsa* powder for the armor-clad garments of those warriors.
It was surpassed by the jingling of the limbs of the moving horses and by the sounds of their armor,
which resembled the rustling of groves of royal palm trees shaken by the wind.
From the *puṃnāga* trees, arrows fell upon the temples of the elephants— temples bound with the trunks of date-palm trees and fragrant with the outpouring of rut.
It is said that the ocean, being entreated by Rāma, granted him space;
under the pretext of being the king of the western frontier, he paid tribute to the descendant of Raghu.
There, he made Mount Trikūṭa itself a lofty pillar of victory, its distinct marks of prowess carved by the tusks of his intoxicated elephants.
Then, like a self-controlled ascetic who sets out to conquer the enemies known as the senses through the knowledge of reality, he set forth by land to conquer the Persians.
He could not endure the intoxication of the wine from the lotus-faces of the Yavana women,
just as the rising of an unseasonable cloud cannot endure the morning sunlight of the lotuses.
A tumultuous battle took place between him and his western cavalry opponents amidst a cloud of dust, in which the enemy warriors could only be identified by the twanging of their Śārṅga bows.
With their bearded heads severed by his arrows,
he covered the earth as if with honeycombs swarming with bees.
The survivors, having removed their helmets, sought refuge with him;
for the anger of great-souled men is appeased by prostration.
There, those warriors dispelled the fatigue of their victory with honey-wines upon grounds covered with precious deer-skins and encircled by vineyards.
Then Raghu set out toward the northern quarter like the sun,
intending to extract the essence of the northerners with his arrows, as the sun draws up the fluids with its rays.

Having made those very conquered peoples his subjects, he— invincible himself— placed them at the forefront of his chariots and entered the Northern Region like a forest fire entering the great ocean.
Having their fatigue from the journey relieved by the splashing of the waters at the riverbank,
his horses shook their manes, upon which saffron filaments were clinging.
There, among the Hūṇa women, the actions of Raghu— whose prowess was clearly manifest toward their husbands— produced a flush upon their cheeks.
In battle, the Kambojas were unable to withstand his prowess;
they submitted along with their acorns, which had been worn down by rubbing against the tethering posts of their elephants.
To the Lord of Kosala, there constantly arrived as tribute vast heaps of wealth consisting mostly of excellent horses; yet these never gave rise to pride.
Then, mounted on his steed, he ascended the mountain that is the father of Gaurī,
as if making its peaks grow taller with the rising dust of the minerals.
He described how even amidst the roar of the army, the lions dwelling in their caves remained undaunted, turning back to gaze with eyes equal in courage to his own.
On the way, breezes attended upon him— breezes that rustled the birch leaves, caused the whistling of the hollow bamboos, and carried the spray of the Ganges.
The soldiers rested,
taking shelter in the shade of *nameru* trees upon rocks whose surfaces were scented by the musk of deer reclining thereon.
At night, the nearby medicinal herbs served as oilless lamps for their leader, their radiance shimmering upon the neck-chains of the elephants tethered to the *sarala* trees.
In the dwellings abandoned by him, the deodar trees, their bark scarred by neck-ropes,
indicated to the Kirātas the presence of the elephants' bodies.
There, a terrible battle ensued between Raghu and the mountain-dwelling hosts,
in which fire was produced by the sparks from the clashing of iron arrows, slings, and stones.
Having caused the festivities known as the *utsavasamketa* to cease with his arrows,
he had the Kinnaras sing of the triumph of his arms.
When they had recognized one another, with presents in their hands,
the king received the essence of the Himalayas, and the Himalayan mountain received the essence of the king.
There he descended, having established Akṣobhya— that mass of glory—
thereby causing the mountain, which had been lifted by the descendant of Pulastya, to feel as if it were ashamed.
When he had crossed the Lauhitya, the Lord of Prāgjyotiṣa trembled along with the black aloe-wood trees that had been bent down by his passage.
He could not even endure the path of the chariot, where the sun was obscured and the sky was overcast by incessant rain; how much less, then, could he face his army with its banners?
The Lord of those who can assume forms at will, whose prowess surpassed that of Indra,
resorted to elephants with temples rent open— those very ones by which he had previously restrained his other enemies.
The Lord of Kāmarūpa worshipped the shadow of his feet— the presiding deity of his golden throne— with an offering of jeweled flowers.
Having thus conquered the quarters, the victorious one turned back on his chariot,
laying to rest the dust raised by the wheels upon the crests of kings now shorn of their umbrellas.
He performed the Viśvajit sacrifice, in which his entire possessions were given as the sacrificial fee;
for the accumulation of wealth is indeed for the sake of distribution, just like the gathering of clouds by rain-bearing winds.

At the conclusion of the sacrificial session, the descendant of Kakutstha, accompanied by his ministers, permitted the kings— who had their humiliation of defeat assuaged by weighty honors and whose queens were longing for him due to their long separation— to return to their own cities.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, the kings— purified by the final ablution (*avabhṛtha*), their humiliation and resentment at defeat assuaged by marks of honor—
took their leave of him and departed for their respective cities, as they were sent forth by the eager women who had been left behind.

With their foreheads bowed low in prostration at his departure, they placed upon the toes of the Emperor’s pair of feet—marked by the signs of the lute, the banner, the thunderbolt, and the parasol—that which was obtainable only through his grace: a mass of pollen and nectar fallen from the garlands on their crowns.

At that sacrifice, the Viśvajit, Kautsa— the disciple of Varatantu, who had acquired all branches of learning and was seeking a teacher’s fee— approached the lord of the earth after he had bestowed his entire treasury upon the people.
Having placed that guest-offering in an earthen vessel because he had discarded all golden ones, the king— who was of priceless character,
radiant with fame, and hospitable by nature— went out to meet his guest whose splendor was revealed by his learning.

Having honored that ascetic according to the prescribed rites, the lord of the people— who was foremost among those whose wealth is honor and who knew the proper procedure— stood nearby with palms joined in reverence and, knowing his duty, spoke as follows.
O you of sharp intellect, is your preceptor—the leader of the seers who composed the mantras—well?
For from him you have obtained complete knowledge, just as the world receives consciousness from the sun.

I hope that the threefold austerity of the Great Sage— which, though it constantly consumes his fortitude like fire, has been accumulated through body, speech, and mind— is not being brought to waste by obstacles.

I hope that no calamity, such as from wind or other elements, has befallen the trees of your hermitage— which dispel fatigue and have been nurtivated by your efforts beginning with the construction of their foundations— as if they were your own sons.

Out of affection even for those things used for ritual purposes, the sages have not thwarted the desires of the deer; thus, I hope that the birth of the does remains unblemished, their umbilical cords having fallen away upon the beds of kusha grass where they lay.

I hope those auspicious waters of the holy fords—by which the ritual ablutions are performed according to rule, from which the handfuls of funeral offerings are cast for the ancestors, and whose sandy banks are marked by grains gathered by the *uñcha* method—are well-being unto you? (Raghuvamśa 5.8)

I hope that the forest produce— the means for maintaining your bodies— which you receive as a portion for guests arriving at the proper time, such as the ripening wild rice and other grains, is not being seized by the rustlers of the countryside.
Has the great seer, being well-pleased, permitted you to return home after having properly instructed you?
For now is the time for you to proceed to the second stage of life, which is capable of providing all assistance.
My mind is not satiated by merely visiting you, the Arhat; it yearns for the performance of service.
Whether by the command of your teacher or of your own accord, you have come from the forest to honor me.

Having heard Raghu’s noble speech regarding the cow—whose wealth was inferred from the vessel for the guest-offering—the disciple of Varatantu, his hopes for the fulfillment of his own purpose now weakened, spoke to him thus: *Ragh_5.12*
"Know, O King, that all is well with us; for while you are the protector of the subjects, how could anything inauspicious exist?
When the sun is shining, how could darkness possibly serve to obstruct the vision of the world? (Raghuvamśa 5.13)
"O illustrious one, devotion toward those worthy of honor is appropriate for your lineage; by it, you excel your ancestors.
Yet, my regret is this: that I have approached you as a petitioner after the proper time has passed."
O lord of men, standing there with nothing but your body, you shine with the splendor bestowed by sacred fords;
you appear like a stalk of wild rice remaining after its grain has been gathered by forest-dwellers.
It is fitting that you, being the sole lord of men, manifest this state of possessing nothing born of sacrifice;
for the waning of the digits of the moon after it has been drunk by the gods in succession is indeed more praiseworthy than its waxing.
Therefore, I shall strive to procure the preceptor’s requirement from elsewhere, provided it does not interfere with my other duties.
May it be well with you; even the cātaka bird does not trouble an autumn cloud whose interior has already shed its water.
Having said this much, the king restrained the disciple of the great seer who was desiring to depart, and questioned him:
"O learned one, what object should be given by you to the teacher, and of what value?"
Then that wise student related the matter at hand to him— the teacher of the castes and stages of life— who had duly performed the sacrifice and was entirely free from the influence of pride.
When I had completed my studies, I requested the great seer for the teacher’s fee;
he, however, first took into account only that devotion of mine which had been offered to him unceasingly over a long time.
Disregarding the emaciation of my purpose caused by the anger born of his persistence, I was told by my preceptor:
"Bring me fourteen crores of wealth, according to the number of sciences I possess. (Raghuvamśa 5.21)
Therefore, perceiving that the title of "Lord" remains as my only possession while everything else has been consumed by the ritual of worship,
I do not venture now to detain you, for the price of my learning is no small matter.
Thus addressed by the twice-born, the best among the knowers of the Vedas, whose splendor was like that of the moon,
the sole lord of the world, his sensory activities turned away from sin, spoke to him again.

May this new onset of scandal not arise against me: that one who was seeking wealth for his preceptor and had mastered the Vedas departed for another country because he did not obtain his desire from Raghu.
Therefore, O Worthy One, dwelling in my praiseworthy and honored fire-sanctuary like a fourth sacred fire,
you ought to endure two or three days while I strive to accomplish your purpose.

Saying "So be it," the noble-born Raghu, having confidence in his word, accepted that unerring pledge; and perceiving that the earth had been drained of its essence, he desired to extract wealth from Kubera as well.
Due to the power arising from the sprinkling of Vasiṣṭha’s mantras, the movement of his chariot was not obstructed over the oceans, the sky, or the mountains,
just like that of a cloud accompanied by the wind.

Then at nightfall, the resolute Raghu, desiring to conquer the Lord of Kailāsa by his own prowess through the mere expectation of his being a vassal, lay down upon his chariot which was filled with prepared weapons.
In the morning, as he was preparing for his departure, those appointed to the treasury, filled with wonder,
reported that a shower of gold had fallen from the sky into the middle of the treasury house.
The king bestowed that entire heap of radiant gold, obtained from Kubera who was being assailed [by him],
upon Kautsa in its entirety, like a portion of Mount Sumeru split by the thunderbolt.
Both of those two became objects of veneration for the people dwelling in Sāketa:
the petitioner, who was free from desire for more than what was due to his preceptor, and the king, who bestowed even more than the petitioner desired.

Then, his purpose accomplished by a hundred female camels and mares, the great seer Kautsa, with a joyful mind, touched the lord of subjects—who had bowed his upper body—with his hand as he set forth, and spoke these words: Ragh_5.32.
What wonder is there in this, that the earth yielded all desires for you, the sovereign of subjects, while you remained steadfast in righteous conduct?
But your power is truly inconceivable, by which even the heavens were milked according to your wish.
Any further blessing would be redundant for you who have already attained all auspicious things;
may you obtain a son worthy of your own virtues, just as your father obtained you, O venerable one.
Having thus offered his benediction to the king, the Brahmin returned to the presence of his preceptor;
and the king, for his part, quickly obtained a son from him, just as the world of living beings receives light from the sun.
It is said that during the *brāhma* hour, his queen gave birth to a son who was like a young Kumāra;
therefore, his father named that self-born son Aja after the very name of Brahmā.
His form was majestic, his very vigor was such, and his natural loftiness was just so;
the prince did not differ from his father in his qualities, just as a lamp lit from another lamp does not differ from it.

Although Fortune was eager to depart from him— who had duly acquired knowledge from his teachers and who was rendered especially beautiful by the dawning of youth— she waited for her teacher’s permission, just as a steadfast maiden awaits her father’s consent before leaving.
Then King Aṅga, desiring to bring his nephew to the svayaṃvara of his sister Indumatī,
dispatched a trusted messenger to Raghu, accompanied by Bhoja, who was eager for the prince’s arrival.
Reflecting upon that praiseworthy alliance and considering his son to have reached an age suitable for marriage,
he dispatched him with an army to the prosperous capital of the Lord of Vidarbha.

The halting places of the prince’s son along the road— where hospitality was provided by specially constructed guest-houses and by the various offerings of the local people— became like pleasure gardens for his recreation.

Having traversed the road, he caused his army— exhausted and its banners grey with dust— to encamp on the bank of the Narmadā, where the *naktamāla* trees were made to dance by breezes moist with spray.
Then another elephant emerged from the river, its entry into the water previously signaled by bees hovering above,
its broad temples free of rut and washed clean.
On the slopes of the Ṛkṣavat mountain, even though his physical elements had been washed away without remainder,
he revealed the traces of his dwelling by means of two teeth, mottled with dark upward streaks and blunted against the rocks.
With a hand capable of swift withdrawal and extension, he shone as he moved toward the shore with a splash,
cleaving the great waves like one who has begun to break through a water-barrier.

With his hand, thick and more massive than the coils of a serpent, he stretched toward the shore and cast forth long waves like iron bars, which, raised and then released with a roar, seemed to strike against the water.
Like a mountain, he first drew the masses of mossy clusters toward himself with his chest;
thereafter, the river current, its waters previously compressed by him, surged back toward the bank.
Dragging along the river weeds that clung to his shoulders— those weeds which were like the soft, ancient girdles of Pulinda women who had been sporting in the water— he moved toward the bank.
The splendor of the rutting-fluid, which had been momentarily stilled on the temples of that solitary elephant by its immersion in the water,
blazed forth once again at the sight of other wild elephants.
Having inhaled his unbearable rut, which flowed with a pungent stream like the milk of the seven-leaved *saptacchada* tree,
the lordly elephants of the army turned away, disregarding the strenuous efforts of their drivers.

In an instant, he threw that military camp into a tumultuous state: its yoke-animals were broken loose and fled from their severed bonds, its chariots had their axles shattered and overturned, and its soldiers were rendered helpless as they sought to protect the women.
Hearing that it was a wild elephant, which could not be slain by a king,
the prince drew his bow-string not too far and struck it on the forehead with an arrow as it charged toward him, intending to turn it back.
As soon as he was pierced, it is said that he cast off his serpent form; watched by the astonished army, he assumed a beautiful celestial body standing in the midst of a shimmering halo of light.
Then, having showered the prince with flowers produced from the wish-fulfilling trees that had appeared through his power,
the eloquent sage spoke, the pearl necklace upon his chest enhanced by the radiance of his teeth.
"Due to the curse of Mataṅga, rooted in my own arrogance, I have attained the state of a forest elephant;
know me, O Lord of Gandharvas, to be Priyaṃvada, the son of Priyadarśana."
And when I subsequently entreated that great seer with prostrations, he became gentle; for just as water attains coolness through contact with fire and sunlight, yet its true nature is coolness.
"When Aja, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, shall break your jar with an iron-tipped arrow,
you will be reunited with your own bodily majesty"— thus did that treasury of asceticism speak to me.
"I have been liberated from a curse by you, a man of courage, whose sight I have long desired;
for if I were not to perform a service in return for you, my attainment of my own station would indeed be in vain."

"Friend, take up my Gandharva weapon named Sammohana, whose mantras for its employment and withdrawal are clearly distinguished; for by its use, there is no injury to enemies, and victory remains in the hand of the wielder."
Enough of this shame toward me, since even while striking me you were for a moment intent on compassion;
therefore, as I entreat you with a purpose, do not meet me with the harshness of refusal.

Saying "So be it," that moon among men, having sipped the purifying water of the river born from Soma while facing north, received from him— the one whose curse had been withdrawn— the mantra of the weapon, being himself an expert in missiles.
Thus, as they traveled along the road, a friendship arose between them through the power of destiny, its cause beyond thought;
one proceeded toward the regions of Caitraratha, delightful with their excellent governance, while the other went to Vidarbha.
As he stood on the outskirts of the city, the King of Krathakaiśika— filled with profound joy upon his arrival—
went forth to meet him, like a surging ocean with its waves rising toward the moon.

Having led him into the city as his foremost guest, he attended upon him with humility, offering all his royal splendor; thus, the people gathered there believed that the Lord of Vidarbha had come to his own home to visit the unborn Aja.

There, as the assembled people beheld the palace— its eastern gate adorned with full water-jars set upon the altar by bowing officials— he, Madana, felt as though he had entered the final stage of life due to his childhood.

There, sleep—clouded by the awareness of his inner state—after a long time appeared before the eyes of Aja, who desired that lovely jewel of a maiden for whom the assembly of kings had been gathered by her own choice; it was like a beloved woman appearing at night.

At dawn, the sons of the charioteer, of similar age and eloquent speech, awakened him— whose broad shoulders were pressed by his ear-ornaments, whose body-unguents were thinned by friction against the bedspread, and whose wakefulness was already renowned— with words of noble import.
