The night has passed, O best of the wise; leave your bed. Surely the Creator has divided the burden of the world into two parts:
your father, remaining awake, bears one portion alone, while you are the one who supports the position of his other successor.

Under the sway of sleep, even you, disregarding her, have left the young woman in a state of longing like one who has been spurned; and even that moon, hanging at the edge of the horizon, loses its luster before the radiance of your face, as it seeks to dispel the gloom of night.

Therefore, let these two— the eye within you, with its pupil now quivering and soft from being suddenly opened, and the lotus with its bee in motion— attain an immediate and mutual likeness through their simultaneous and beautiful blossoming.
The morning breeze loosens the flowers from the stalks of the trees and mingles with the lotuses split open by the rays of the sun;
it seems to desire, as it were, the natural fragrance of your breath through the excellence of another.
Upon the copper-red bellies of the tree sprouts, the snow-water— clear as a washed pearl from your necklace—
shines like your playful smile with its gleaming teeth, having attained a secondary luster upon your lower lip.
Before the sun, the treasury of heat, can even begin its course, the darkness has already been dispelled by Aruṇa;
for when you, O hero, have gone to the vanguard of battle, why should your preceptor himself destroy the enemies?
Having shaken off sleep on both sides, those elephants abandon their beds while dragging their clanging chains;
their tusks shine with the hue of the young dawn, appearing like the slopes of mountain cliffs streaked with red ochre.
O lotus-eyed one, these horses from the Vānāyu region, tethered within the long cloth pavilions, have abandoned sleep;
the steeds are blackening with the heat of their breath the licks of rock-salt placed before them.
Devotion has grown thin, the offerings of flowers have withered, and the lamps are devoid of the halo cast by their own flames;
moreover, this sweet-voiced parrot of yours, staying in its cage, repeats our words intended to awaken you.
Thus addressed by the sons of bards with well-composed words, the prince suddenly cast off his sleep and abandoned his bed;
awakened by the royal swans warbling with the skill of intoxication, he was like the elephant Supratīka rising from the sandy bank of the Ganges.

Then, having completed the rites prescribed by the scriptures appropriate for the beginning of the day, he— whose eyelashes were curved and who was dressed in attire skillfully arranged to suit the occasion— went to the assembly of kings gathered for the *svayaṃvara*.

There he beheld the guardians of the world of men, appearing like the gods of the celestial chariots (vaimānika-maruts), seated upon thrones on couches with charming attire, possessing the grace of those drawn [to him] by the objects of service.

As the kings gazed upon the descendant of Kakutstha— who seemed like his own body returned to him by the Lord after having been seized by Rati through her entreaties— their hearts became hopeless regarding Indumatī.
Following the path pointed out by Vaidarbha, the prince ascended the dais by means of the constructed staircase,
just as a young lion cub climbs a lofty mountain peak by means of rock fissures.
Seated upon a jewel-studded throne covered with a most excellent spread of cloth,
he possessed a splendor that was almost equal to Guha, who rests upon the back of a peacock.

Among those royal successions, he shone as a thousandfold self divided by his splendor— a sight difficult to behold due to the emergence of such extraordinary radiance— just like lightning flashing amidst rows of clouds.
Seated upon costly thrones and arrayed in magnificent attire, the son of Raghu shone in their midst by his splendor alone, like the Pārijāta tree among the Kalpa trees.
The eyes of the city folk fell upon him, leaving behind all other kings,
like wild bees deserting flowering trees when a scent-elephant, intoxicated with rut, has entered the forest.

Then, while the world of kings—descendants of the lunar and solar dynasties—was being praised by bards skilled in genealogy, and while the incense produced from the heartwood of agaru rose up, wafting toward the victory banners; Ragh_6.8.

While the conch was blown and the sound of musical instruments, intended for auspicious purposes, swelled in all directions, the peacocks dwelling in the groves on the outskirts of the city began their wild dance.
Seated upon a square carriage drawn by men, the maiden— adorned with her retinue,
arrayed in wedding attire, and choosing her own husband— entered the royal highway between the rows of platforms.
At that extraordinary creation of the Creator, consisting of a maiden who was the sole target for hundreds of eyes,
the kings fell with their inner hearts, remaining on their seats only by means of their bodies.
To those kings whose desires were made manifest toward her, various amorous gestures became the foremost messengers of their affection,
like the beauty of young shoots on trees.
Someone whirled a play-lotus, its stalk grasped in both hands, which struck bees with its trembling petals and formed a halo within by means of its pollen.

Another elegant man, turning his beautiful face slightly to one side, drew up the jeweled necklace that had slipped from his shoulder and caught upon the tip of his armlet, restoring it to its proper place.
Then another, with the tips of his fingers slightly curled and the beauty of his eyes somewhat cast down,
scratched the golden footstool with a foot whose nail-lustre spread obliquely across its surface.
Having placed his left arm upon half of the seat, his shoulder raised higher by that positioning,
with his necklace displaced as his triple-jointed back was turned, a certain man became intent on addressing his friend.
Another youth tore with the tips of his nails a pale ketaka petal— serving as a decorative leaf-pattern for the teeth of a playful woman— which had been arranged upon his beloved’s hip.
With a hand whose palm was copper-red like a lotus and marked with the sign of a bannered line,
someone playfully cast the dice, which were illuminated by the luster of jeweled rings upon his fingers.
One [of them], although remaining in his assigned place, as if transgressing his own position,
extended one hand— its fingers containing rays of diamonds— toward the crown.
Then Sunandā, the guardian of the inner apartments, who was as bold as a man and well-versed in the learning, conduct, and lineages of kings,
led the princess into the presence of the Lord of Magadha and spoke to her.
He is a refuge for those seeking shelter, possessed of unfathomable courage, established in Magadha;
a king who has won renown by delighting his subjects, named Parantapa—a name truly meaningful to his character.
Granted that there may be other kings by the thousands; yet they say this earth possesses a true king only because of him.
For though a night is crowded with constellations, stars, and planets, it is radiant only through the moon.
Through the continuous performance of sacrifices, this king— whose thousand eyes were incessantly summoned—
long rendered Śacī’s curls devoid of mandāra flowers, as they hung down from her pale cheeks.
If you desire that your hand be taken by this most excellent groom during his entry,
then cause yourself to become the object of the eyes of the women of Puṣpapura as they lean against the palace windows.

When she had spoken thus, the slender maiden, her garland of dūrvā grass and madhūka flowers slightly loosened as she looked at him, rebuked him by means of a simple gesture of salutation alone, without speaking a word.
The very same woman appointed to hold the cane led the princess to another king,
just as a line of waves stirred by the wind leads a royal swan from one lotus to another on Lake Mānasa.
And this lord of women, whose youthful splendor was coveted by celestial damsels, spoke to her:
"Indeed, according to the authors of the Sūtras, one who has subdued his senses enjoys the status of Indra even while remaining on earth."
By scattering drops of tears as large as pearls upon their breasts,
he presented the enemy queens with necklaces that were, in effect, already unstrung, though without the thread.
In this world, Fortune and Sarasvatī—though by nature occupying different abodes—dwell together in one place;
O auspicious lady, you alone, through your beauty, your speech, and your truthfulness, are the third worthy of them both.
Then, withdrawing her gaze from the King of Aṅga, the maiden said to her female companions:
"It is not that he is not desirable, nor that she does not know how to see him properly; for the world is indeed of diverse tastes."

Thereafter, the female doorkeeper stationed at the entrance presented to Indumatī the king, who was difficult for enemies to withstand and exceptionally beautiful to behold, like the newly risen moon.
This lord of Avanti, with his uplifted arms, broad chest, and slender, rounded waist,
shines like the sun whose heat is fierce, having been fashioned with great effort by Tvaṣṭṛ after being mounted upon the revolving lathe.
In the expeditions of this king of complete power, the dust raised by the horses leading the way causes the setting of the sprouting rays from the crest-jewels of the subordinate chieftains.
Dwelling not far from the abode of Mahākāla, the moon-crested Lord,
he indeed enjoys the evenings with his beloveds even during the dark fortnight, as if they were filled with moonlight.

O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, do you perhaps find pleasure in your heart in wandering together with this young prince through the succession of gardens shaken by the breezes from the ripples of the Siprā?
In him— who had illuminated the lotus of his kinsmen and dried up the mire of his enemies with his prowess— she,
possessed of unsurpassed delicacy, did not fix her affection, just as the night-lily does not fix its state upon the sun.

Having placed before her that lovely creation of the Creator, who shone like the interior of a lotus and was not inferior in virtues to the king of Anūpa, Sunandā spoke again to the fair-toothed maiden: Ragh_6.37.
It is said that the yogi Kārtavīrya possessed a thousand arms deployed in battle, had erected sacrificial posts throughout the eight subcontinents,
and held the title of "King" in a manner not shared by any other.
Appearing before him at the very moment he thought of improper action,
the wielder of the bow— who as a leader restrains the misconduct even within the bodies of his subjects— rebuked that impropriety.

In his prison, the Lord of Laṅkā— having conquered Indra— dwelt until [Rāma’s] favor was granted, his arms rendered motionless by the binding of the bowstring and his rows of mouths sighing incessantly.

In his lineage was born this king named Pratīpa, who served the elders learned in the scriptures; by him the infamy that clings to Fortune because she is fickle by nature was wiped away by his being her refuge.
Having obtained as his ally in battle Kṛṣṇagati, who was the night of destruction for the kṣatriyas,
he regarded the sharp edge of Paraśurāma’s axe as having the softness of a lotus petal.

O you whose beauty is like that of the crescent moon, become the consort of this long-armed king; if you have the desire to behold the river Revā, which is charming with its water-weeds and whose banks are girdled by the mounds of the ramparts of Māhiṣmatī, visible through the lattices of its palaces.
Although he was exceedingly pleasing to behold, that lord of the earth did not please her,
just as the full moon, though its obstruction by clouds has been cleared away by autumn, does not please the night-lily.

Addressing Suṣeṇa, the lord of the Śūrasenas— whose fame was sung in the other world and who was a lamp illuminating both his lineages through purity of conduct— the maiden, guarded by the women of the inner apartments, spoke.
This king is of the Nīpa lineage; by relying upon his virtues, even natural enmity was cast aside by creatures who, like those at the peaceful Siddhāśrama, came together in mutual harmony.
In his own home, a splendor as delightful to the eyes as the moon was established;
yet an irresistible radiance was present in the palaces of his enemies, where blades of grass had grown upon the rooftops of their mansions.
At the time of his water-sports, because of the washing away of the sandalwood paste from the breasts of the women in his harem,
the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā), though having reached Mathurā, appeared as if her waters were mingled with the waves of the Gaṅgā.
That jewel, which was reportedly released by Kāliya, the inhabitant of the Yamunā, as he was dragged away in terror,
bears a luster that spreads across his chest and seems to put to shame Kṛṣṇa, who wears the Kaustubha gem.
O beautiful one, having won this youth as your husband, enjoy the splendor of your youth in Vṛndāvana— a place not inferior to Caitraratha— upon beds of soft sprouts covered with flowers.
And having occupied the rocky surfaces scented with bitumen and sprinkled with droplets of water,
behold the dance of peacocks in the lovely caves of Govardhana during the rainy season.
With her charming navel like a whirlpool, she passed by that king— who was destined to become another man's wife— just as a river flowing toward the ocean passes a mountain encountered on its course.
Then, as she approached the Lord of Kaliṅga named Hemāṅgada— whose arms were embraced by his attendants,
who had subdued the factions of his enemies, and whose face was like the full moon— the maidservant spoke to that young woman.
This lord of Mahendra and the great ocean, whose strength is equal to Mount Mahendra,
appears as if Mahendra himself were marching before him on his expeditions under the guise of the rutting elephants of his army.
The lord of archers, whose handsome arms bear the scars of bowstring strokes,
carries two lines that resemble the tracks of tear-stained mascara on the captured fortunes of his enemies.

In battle, he is radiant through his conquest of enemies; with his two arms, which serve as a touchstone for the string of his bow, he bears two distinct marks that are like the paths leading to the extinction of the fire of his foes' valor.
The ocean itself, close to his palace, awakens him as he sleeps— its waves visible through the palace windows, its deep rumbling having silenced the drums that mark the end of the night.
Dwell with him on the shores of the ocean, rustling with groves of palm trees,
where the drops of perspiration are dispelled by breezes carrying the fragrance of clove blossoms brought from other islands.
Though enticed by the king of the city named Uragapura, whose form was so captivating, she turned away from him as if drawn far off by fate, like the goddess Lakṣmī repelled by adverse destiny.

Then, having obtained as her husband one who was like a king of the gods, the lamp of both lineages purified by their conduct, the maiden— guarded by the women of the inner apartments— spoke to the lord of the city named Uragapura.
Then, the female gatekeeper spoke to the princess of the Bhojas, who had been previously instructed: "O Cakora-eyed one, look here at the lord of the city of Ayodhyā, who resembles a god."
This Pāṇḍya king, with long necklaces resting upon his shoulders and his body anointed with yellow sandalwood paste,
shines like the king of mountains, whose peaks are reddened by the morning sun and from which waterfalls are gushing forth.
Agastya, who brought the great mountain Vindhya to a standstill and drank the king of rivers until it was entirely exhausted,
becomes his ritual bath-attendant out of affection, as he is moistened by the concluding purificatory bath of the horse sacrifice.
Having obtained from Hara that weapon so difficult to acquire, the proud Lord of Laṅkā,
fearing a future assault upon Janasthāna, once set out for the conquest of Indra’s realm after having fixed it to his bow.
When he, of noble lineage, has taken your hand according to the rite, become the co-wife of the southern quarter— the earth-like weightiness of which has the ocean for its jeweled girdle.

Be pleased to sport forever upon the plateaus of the Malaya mountains, where areca palms are entwined with betel vines, where sandalwood trees are embraced by cardamom creepers, and where the ground is strewn with the leaves of the tamāla.
This king has a body dark as a blue lotus, while you have a slender frame fair as yellow orpiment;
may your union be for the mutual increase of your splendor, like that of lightning and a rain-cloud.
That instruction did not find a place in the heart of his father-in-law, the lord of Vidarbha,
just as the rays of the moon cannot enter a lotus that has closed its petals due to the absence of the sun.
Like a moving flame of a lamp at night, as that maiden choosing her own husband passed by one after another,
each king fell into a state of pallor, like a turret on a royal highway in the dark.
When she appeared before him, the son of Raghu was overwhelmed by the thought, "Shall I choose her or not?";
his right arm dispelled this doubt with the throbbing of its armlet-fastenings.
Having obtained him, whose every limb was faultless, the maiden turned away from the pursuit of others;
for a swarm of bees, having reached a blossoming mango tree, does not long for another tree.
Observing Indumatī, who was as radiant as the moonlight and whose mental faculties were fully absorbed in him,
Sunandā, who knew the proper sequence of events, began to speak these words in detail.
Born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, he was Kakutstha, the preeminent among kings, endowed with the marks of royalty;
from him the lords of Uttarakosala, their aspirations lofty, derive their praiseworthy title of Kākutstha.
Mounting Mahendra in the form of a great bull,
he who had attained the grace of Pinākin in battle rendered the cheeks of the asura women pale with the marks of collyrium by means of his arrows.
He who, by clashing his own armlet against Airāvata’s armlet— which had become loosened by the elephant’s flapping—
attained even a foremost form as he approached, and occupied half the throne of the Splitter of the Mountains.
Born into that lineage was King Dilīpa, of vast renown and the lamp of his family;
he remained one short of a hundred sacrifices in order to avoid provoking the envy of Śakra.

While he ruled the earth, even the wind did not disturb the garments of the women who had fallen asleep halfway to their pleasure-grounds; for who would have ventured to stretch out a hand to take them away?

His son Raghu now governs his station; he is the performer of the great Viśvajit sacrifice, who reduced all royal fortune—gathered from the four quarters—to nothing but the clay vessel used for the ritual.
His fame— climbing mountains, crossing oceans, entering the abode of serpents,
and ascending to the heavens— is such that it is impossible to measure its extent.
That unborn prince was born after him, just as Jayanta was born after the lord of heaven;
he, being a youth fit for training, bears the heavy yoke of the world in a manner worthy of his father, who is himself a bearer of that burden.
By virtue of your lineage, your beauty, your youth, and those various qualities preeminent in discipline, choose him as a match for yourself; let this jewel be united with gold.
Then, at the conclusion of Sunandā’s speech, the princess, casting aside her modesty,
welcomed the prince with a gaze pure with favor, as if with a garland of choice.
Due to her modesty, she was unable to express her bond of longing for that youth;
yet, through the visible sign of horripilation, it emerged from the slender body of the lady with curling locks.

To her friend Tathāgatā, who was speaking with playful intent, a female attendant holding a cane said, "Noble lady, let us go elsewhere. Then the bride looked at her with a glance crooked with resentment.

And she, whose thighs were like the trunk of an elephant, fastened that powder-white string around the neck of the joy of the Raghus in its proper place with her two hands, as if it were his affection incarnate.
With that garland made of auspicious flowers hanging from his broad chest,
that most excellent man considered the younger sister of the King of Vidarbha to have already cast the noose of her arms around his neck.

"This Kaumudī moonlight has reached the moon; it has reached the ocean, its worthy receptacle, now freed from clouds"—thus, delighted by the union of matching virtues, the citizens there uttered this single voice, harsh to the ears of rival kings.
On one side was that circle of kings with their excellent factions delighted, while on the other was the canopy;
at dawn, it was like a lake with full-blown lotuses, while the groves of water-lilies have not yet awakened from sleep.
Then the Lord of Vidarbha, taking his sister— who was joined with a husband worthy of her like Devasenā herself united with Skanda— set out toward the entrance of the city.
The lords of the earth also departed for their military encampments at dawn, when the light of the planets was dim;
they were filled with envy regarding the beauty and attire [of the enemy] due to the frustration of their desires concerning the banquet.
It is said that due to the presence of Śacī there, there was an absence of those who would cause disturbances at a svayaṃvara;
thus, even though they were full of envy toward the descendant of Kakutstha, the assembly of kings was pacified by him.

Meanwhile, the bridegroom, together with his bride, reached the royal highway, which was strewn with fresh offerings, marked by gateways radiant with rainbows, and where the heat was warded off by the shade of banners.
Then, in the palaces adorned with golden lattices, the activities of the city's beautiful women— who were intent on beholding him— became such that they abandoned all other duties.
As one woman was suddenly proceeding along the path of light,
her mass of hair— its flowers already disgorged from being untied— was not even noticed as she tried to bind it, for it was held fast by her hand.
Another, having cast aside her forefoot which had been held by her maid, went toward the window with a graceful gait, carrying the applicator-stick even as the red lac-dye was still dripping.
Having adorned her right eye with collyrium while leaving her left eye deprived of it,
another woman, carrying the applicator-stick, likewise approached the vicinity of the window.
Another woman, her gaze directed through the lattice window, did not fasten her girdle which had slipped during her departure;
she stood holding up her garment with a hand whose brilliance was enhanced by the ornament resting upon her navel.
The half-strung girdle of a certain woman, slipping at every misstep as she rose in haste,
was then reduced to a mere thread held between her big toes.

Leaving behind her infant son who was still nursing, a certain woman hurried away to gaze [at him]; as she went, she drenched his path with milk from her breasts, which were overflowing with milk, as seen through the window.

With their faces, filled with the scent of wine, filling the interiors of the windows, those women— filled with intense curiosity and possessing eyes like wandering bees— made the windows appear as if adorned with thousand-petaled lotuses.
Drinking in the sight of Rāghava with their eyes, those women did not turn toward other objects;
for the functioning of their remaining senses had entered, as it were, entirely through their eyes alone.
It was fitting that the daughter of the Bhojas chose a self-choice marriage (svayaṃvara), though she had already been selected by kings who were out of her sight;
for otherwise, how could she have obtained a husband as worthy of herself as Nārāyaṇa obtains Padmā?
If the Creator had not joined this pair, whose mutual splendor is so desirable,
then his effort in fashioning their beauty would have been in vain.
Surely these two were Rati and Smara in former births among kings, for thus has this maiden found one exactly like herself; the mind indeed knows its associations from previous lives.
Hearing these words, pleasant to the ear, emerging from the mouths of the Paurava women, the prince reached the residence of his relative,
which was illuminated by auspicious preparations.
Then, having quickly descended from the female elephant with the hand of the Lord of Kāmarūpa supporting him,
he entered the inner quadrangle pointed out by the King of Vidarbha, as if entering the hearts of women.
Seated upon that most precious lion-throne, he accepted the jewel-encrusted guest-offering mixed with honey-milk,
as well as the pair of fine silk garments presented by Bhoja, all while being met with the sidelong glances of women.
Clad in fine linen, he was led by humble guards of the inner apartments into the presence of his bride,
just as the ocean, its rows of foam clearly visible, is led toward the shore-guarding moon by its fresh rays.

There, the honored priest of the Lord of Bhoja, who was skilled in the rites of the sacred fire, having offered oblations of clarified butter and other substances into the fire according to the ritual manuals,
established that very fire as a witness to the marriage and brought the bride and groom together.
Taking his bride's hand in his own, that prince shone most brightly,
like a mango tree in full bloom upon receiving a new sprout from an adjacent ashoka creeper.
The bridegroom’s forearm bristled with horripilation and his fingers perspired; the maiden became still.
At the joining of their hands, the conduct of the two seemed as if it were a single portion divided between them by the Lord of Love.
Their eyes, glancing from the corners and moving with the grace of ritual action and meditative absorption, were mutually restless and attained a charming restraint born of modesty.
As he proceeded in circumambulation around the blazing fire,
that pair shone forth like day and night joined together at the slopes of Mount Meru.
Instructed by that preceptor, who was like the Creator himself, the bride—
whose hips were heavy and whose eyes were like those of an intoxicated cakora bird— cast the parched grain offerings into the fire with modesty.
The holy smoke of the sacrificial fire, fragrant with oblations, śamī leaves, and parched grain, rose up;
with its crest trailing over her cheek, it momentarily assumed the likeness of an ear-lotus for her.

From the inhalation of ritual smoke according to custom, the bride’s face became one whose eyes were clouded by the moisture of collyrium, whose ear-ornaments of fresh lotus shoots were withered, and whose cheek-lines were turned pale-red.

Seated upon golden thrones, the maiden and the prince successively underwent the ceremony of receiving fresh grains of rice, as performed by the Snātakas, the king accompanied by his kinsmen, and the matrons of the city.
Having thus performed his sister’s marriage ceremony, that king, the lamp of the Bhoja lineage and preeminent in glory,
commanded his officials to provide separate hospitality for each of the sovereigns.
Concealing their agitation through outward signs of joy, those lakes, like clear waters with hidden crocodiles,
took leave of the King of Vidarbha and departed under the pretext of returning his hospitality.
That assembly of kings, having previously made a compact for the success of their undertaking,
stood blocking the path of Aja, intending to seize the sacrificial victim as soon as the appointed time arrived.
The husband of the Krathakaiṣikas, having performed the marriage of his younger brother,
sent forth the descendant of Raghu— who had acquired wealth in accordance with his character— and followed after him.
Having dwelt upon the path with the Unborn One, who is renowned throughout the three worlds, for three nights,
the Lord of Kuṇḍina turned back from him, like the moon at the end of its conjunction with the sun.
Even before the Lord of Kosala, those princes had each attained their own sovereignty;
therefore, when assembled together, they could not tolerate the acquisition of that jewel of a woman by his son.
As he was carrying away the daughter of the Bhoja king on the road, that arrogant host of kṣatriyas blocked him,
just as the enemy of Indra obstructed the foot of Viṣṇu in his three strides while it was taking away the fortune bestowed by Bali.
Having appointed his father’s minister, who possessed many warriors, for her protection,
the prince received that royal army of Jyotīratha like the surging red river Śoṇa receives it.
The foot-soldier rushed against the foot-soldier, the chariot-lord against the chariot-lord, the horseman against the horseman, and the elephant-driver against the rider of the elephant;
thus the battle became one of equal oppositions.
While the musical instruments resounded with indistinct sounds, they did not utter their family lineages;
instead, bearing their bows, they proclaimed to one another their names and noble lineage through the very letters inscribed upon their arrows.
The dust raised in battle by the horses was thickened by the wheels of the rows of chariots;
spread abroad by the flapping of the elephants' ears, it gradually obstructed the sun with its mass.
With their mouths opened wide by the force of the wind, the fish-bannered clouds,
like true fish, appeared as they drank in the thick dust raised by the advancing army, as if drinking turbid fresh water.
In the thick dust, the chariot was recognized by the sound of its wheels, the elephant by the ringing of its swaying bells,
and the distinction between one's own side and the enemy was made by the calling out of their respective masters' names.
As the darkness of dust, having expanded, obstructed the path of vision in the battle,
a stream of blood arose like the morning sun, born from the weapons-wounded horses, elephants, and heroes.
That dust, its root severed, was shaken upward by the wind upon him who was covered in blood;
it shone like smoke rising from a fire that has been extinguished, leaving only embers behind.

When they had recovered from their swoon caused by the blows, the charioteers reproached them; then, having turned back the horses, they slaughtered with fury those very men who had previously struck them, even though they recognized their banners.
Even arrows severed by the shafts of other dexterous archers midway along their flight reached their target by means of their feathered front halves, following the momentum of their own speed.
In the clash with the elephants, the heads of the elephant-riders, though struck by sharp, razor-edged discuses,
fell only after a long time, as their hair remained caught upon the tips of the riders' extended claws.
The horseman, who had previously struck him, did not strike again;
he waited for his enemy, who was seated upon the neck of his steed and recovering his breath, as he was incapable of returning the blow.

On the field of battle, the earth became a stream of blood-wine from the unsheathed swords falling upon the great tusks of armored warriors who had cast off their bodies; the elephants were agitated by the spray from their trunks.
Abounding with the fruit of heads severed by arrows, and with fallen helmets as if they were goblets,
the battlefield— filled with rivulets of blood as its wine— shone like the drinking hall of Death.
Although she was fond of flesh, the jackal, having torn away from the birds the pieces carved from the edges [of the arm],
and with the surface of her palate wounded by the tip of Keyūraka’s armlet, caused the severing of the arm to be averted.
A certain man, his head severed by an enemy’s sword, immediately attained mastery over a celestial chariot;
with a divine maiden clinging to his left side, he beheld his own headless trunk dancing in the midst of battle.

From the mutual crushing of their charioteers, those two became both charioteers and chariot-warriors; then, deprived of horses, they engaged in a protracted battle with maces, and finally, armed with their arms as weapons, they were intent on crushing each other with their bare hands.
When the two combatants had wounded one another and their vital breath had simultaneously departed,
a dispute arose between them— though they were now immortal— regarding the possession of a single lake.
Both those battle arrays achieved victory and defeat from one another in an unstable manner,
like the surging waves of the great ocean driven by alternating winds from behind and from the front.
Even when his own forces were broken by the enemy, the mighty Aja advanced against the hostile army itself;
for smoke may be driven back by the wind, but fire always moves toward the dry grass from which it originated.
Armed with a chariot, a quiver, armor, and a bow, that proud and peerless hero held back the host of kṣatriyas,
just as the Great Boar had checked the ocean waters tossed up at the end of an aeon.
In that battle, he was seen employing his right hand while his left rested at the mouth of the quiver;
from him, the warrior, the bowstring drawn back to his ear produced arrows as the *riguphnā* repeatedly gave birth to sons.

He covered the earth with the heads of his enemies— heads whose lips were reddened even more by the bite of rage, which bore clearly upward-arching frowns, and which were severed at the necks by crescent-headed arrows while still containing the sound of the roar "hum."
With all their forces, led by elephants, with all weapons capable of piercing armor,
and with every effort, all those kings indeed struck at him in that battle.
With his chariot concealed by the volleys of missiles from the enemies, he became visible only by the tips of their banners,
like the early part of the day when the sun is obscured by mist and is visible only by its faint light.

From Priyamvada, that prince received it; the son of the sovereign king, who was as lovely as the flower-arrowed god, employed the Gandharva weapon, "the Sleeper," which causes those whose greed for pleasure has ceased to fall asleep.

Then the army of the king of men stood subject to sleep, their hands bewildered as they drew the bows, the mass of their turbans fallen over one shoulder, and their bodies leaning against the flagstaffs.
Then the prince placed his lips upon the lower lip of his beloved, which had already tasted her passion, and drank the water;
by this act, that peerless hero appeared as if he were drinking his own fame, acquired by his own hand, in bodily form.
Recognizing him by the sound of his conch, his own warriors beheld that fallen enemy,
shimmering like the reflection of the moon amidst closed lotuses.
By him, with the tips of his blood-stained arrows, these letters were inscribed upon the banners of the kings:
"Rāghava has now taken away your fame, but not your lives out of compassion."
With one arm resting on the tip of his bow, his turban loosened as he pulled it from his head,
and drops of perspiration clinging to his forehead, he approached his frightened beloved and spoke these words.
"O Princess of Vidarbha, behold these others whose weapons are wielded by children; you have my permission to look.
By such deeds in battle as these, you are sought after by those who have you already within their grasp."
Her face, suddenly freed from dejection caused by its opposite, shone forth;
it attained its own natural clarity, like a mirror when the mist of breath has vanished.
Though thrilled, she, overcome by modesty, did not openly welcome her friend’s pleasant words with speech;
she was like a stretch of land drenched by fresh raindrops, which does not respond to a mass of clouds with the cries of peacocks.
Thus, placing his left foot upon their heads, he who was free from reproach led away that faultless princess from the kings.
With the dust raised by his chariots and horses, the tips of her curls became rough; she herself appeared like the very goddess of victory in battle incarnate.

Having welcomed his victorious brother who had returned accompanied by his praiseworthy wife, Raghu—having entrusted the family responsibilities to him and being intent on the path of tranquility—no longer remained at home; for when there is one capable of bearing the burden of the lineage, those of the Solar dynasty do not stay at home.
Then, while he was still wearing the graceful marriage-thread,
the king made the earth itself come into his possession, as if it were another Indumatī.
For although princes strive to bring even misfortunes under their own control,
the Unborn One accepted what was presented to him as his father’s command, and not out of a thirst for enjoyment.
Having experienced the consecration together with him by means of the waters prepared by Vasiṣṭha,
the earth, through its clear breathing, seemed to declare that its purpose had been fulfilled.
Having received the consecration from his preceptor, who was a knower of the Atharva Veda, he became unassailable by enemies;
for this was the union of fire and wind, when the sacred power (*brahman*) is joined with the energy of a missile.
The subjects regarded that very Raghu as one whose youth had returned when he became the new lord;
for he inherited not only his father’s royal fortune, but all of his virtues as well.
The two auspicious things, when united with their respective counterparts, shone all the more:
his father’s inherited station with the Unborn One (Viṣṇu), and his own new youth with discipline.
The mighty-armed king enjoyed the earth, which had recently come under his sway, with compassion, fearing lest it should suddenly experience distress, as if she were a bride newly taken by the hand.
"Only I am esteemed by the lord of the earth"—thus everyone among the subjects thought;
like the ocean amidst hundreds of submerged mountains, he met with no disrespect anywhere.
Neither harsh nor excessively mild, like the wind that bends the trees of the earth,
he caused the kings to bow down without uprooting them, following the honored middle course.
Then, seeing that his son was firmly established among the subjects through his self-possession, Raghu became indifferent even toward those celestial realms,
which are subject to destruction despite their being situated in heaven.
For those born of Dilīpa’s lineage, having transferred their royal splendor to virtuous sons,
at the end of their lives devotedly entered the path of self-restrained ascetics clad in tree bark.
As his father was intent on taking refuge in the forest, the son, bowing his head adorned with its turban at his father’s feet, entreated him not to abandon him.
Raghu, who was so fond of his son, fulfilled that desire of the tearful man;
yet he did not, like a snake casting its skin, resume the royal fortune he had relinquished.
Having undertaken his final exertion as a stakeholder, he dwelt in a residence outside the city;
with his senses unimpaired, he was attended by royal splendor as if by a daughter-in-law fit for his son.

That lineage, which had previously been established in tranquility by former kings, now rose to a state of equality with the sky containing the steady moon, as a new sovereign was exalted while the sun had already risen.

Raghu and Rāghava, bearing the emblems of both ascetics and kings, were beheld by the people like two portions of Dharma descended to earth for the sake of liberation and great prosperity respectively.
Aja employed counselors expert in statecraft for the attainment of what was yet unattained;
Raghu associated with trusted yogis for the realization of the imperishable state.
Every day, the young king consulted with his ministers for the accomplishment of his goals;
meanwhile, he traveled with self-restrained sages for the sake of escaping rebirth.
The young king took his seat upon the judgment throne to oversee the affairs of state,
while the aged one sat upon a mat purified with kusha grass to practice silent meditative concentration.
The new lord occupied the throne to delight his subjects;
another, seated upon a pure mat, strove to master the meditative concentrations.
One brought the neighboring kings under his control by means of the excellence of his sovereign power;
the other, through the practice of meditation, brought the five winds that range within the body under his sway.
Desiring to see the vulnerabilities of his enemy, Raghu, whose eye was the science of policy, spread his net across the [hostile] circle;
fixing his mind upon his heart, he sought to behold the supreme light.
The lord of the earth reduced the fruits of his enemies' undertakings to ashes;
the other, however, devoted himself to consuming his own past actions with the fire of knowledge.
The Unborn One (Aja) employed the six qualities beginning with treaty after considering their results;
Raghu likewise conquered the three qualities residing in primordial nature, being indifferent to clods of earth and gold alike.
The new king, firm in his resolve, did not desist from his work until its fruit was attained;
nor did the other, who was steadfast in mind, cease from the practice of yoga until he beheld the Supreme Self.
Thus, with the expansion of both their enemies and their senses restrained,
and remaining vigilant while being intent upon both worldly prosperity and final liberation, they both attained their respective success.
Then, having spent some years in the company of goats for the sake of concealment,
Raghu reached the imperishable Puruṣa beyond darkness through the concentration of yoga.
Having relinquished his body and shed tears for his father for a long time, Rāghava,
though he had maintained the sacred fires, performed the final funeral rites for him alongside the ascetics, being now one who no longer maintains a fire.
Then, out of devotion to his father, he who was skilled in the rituals for the ancestors performed the funeral rites;
for by that path, those who have cast off the body do not desire the funeral cakes offered by their sons.
Having his mental anguish assuaged by those who knew the true meaning of reality regarding the irreparable state of his father’s departure to the highest realm,
he strung his bow and issued a command to the world that was never to be disobeyed.
Having obtained that husband of preeminent prowess, Kṣiti and the beautiful Indumatī both flourished;
the former became the mother of many jewels, while the latter gave birth to a heroic son.
The wise know him as one whose splendor is like ten thousand suns, who is renowned for his fame in all ten directions,
who is called Daśaratha, and who is the preceptor of the enemy of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa.
Having attained freedom from his debts through the hearing of the Vedas and the performance of sacrifices for the hosts of seers, gods, and the eaters of *svadhā*,
that king shone like the sun released from its halo.
The strength of the wise is for the pacification of the fear of distress, and their great learning is for the sake of humility;
not only their wealth, but even their possession of virtues is intended for the benefit of others.

Once, having ensured his subjects were well-protected, that king of noble progeny sported with the queen in the city park, like Indra, the protector of the Maruts, accompanied by Śacī in the Nandana grove.
Then Nārada went by the northern return-path of the sun to play the lute for the Lord who had taken up residence at Gokarṇa on the shore of the southern ocean.
It is said that a swift wind, as if longing for its fragrance, carried away from the head of his musical instrument a garland woven of flowers not grown on earth.
The lute of the sage, strewn with bees following after the flowers,
appeared as if shedding tears clouded with collyrium born from its indignation at the wind.
Surpassing the seasonal splendor of the creepers by means of its excessive honey-scent,
that celestial garland found a secure place upon the tips of the large breasts of the king's beloved.
Beholding that [breast-plate], which was but a momentary companion to her well-formed breasts,
the beloved of the best of men closed her eyes in distress, like the moonlight when the moon has been snatched away by darkness.
Falling with a body deprived of its faculties, she caused even her husband to fall;
for indeed, the flame of a lamp descends to the earth along with the drop of oil poured upon it.
At that very moment,
her consciousness utterly eclipsed by profound delusion, she fell to the surface of the earth like the flame of a newly lit lamp.
Agitated by the tumultuous cries of distress from those standing on both sides,
the birds dwelling in the lotus ponds shrieked there as if they were equally pained.
She dispelled the king's darkness with fans and other remedies, yet he remained just as he was;
for a remedy can only bear fruit when there is still a remnant of life remaining.

Then, out of affection for living beings, he who was exceedingly compassionate took the lute— which had fallen into a state requiring repair— into his lap and embraced the woman who deserved such treatment.
Exceedingly affectionate, with eyes overflowing with tears, he placed his beloved on his lap in an instant; she, whose complexion had changed, resembled a lotus stalk uprooted from the water.
Deeply affectionate, he led her away;
with her complexion altered by the loss of her senses, she appeared like the moon at dawn bearing a turbid crescent.
Abandoning even his natural fortitude, he lamented with a voice choked with tears;
for even iron, when heated, yields to softness—how much more so, then, for embodied beings?
If even flowers, by contact with his body, are capable of taking away life,
then alas, what indeed will not serve as a weapon for Fate when it intends to strike?
Alternatively, the Destroyer of Creatures begins to destroy even a soft object with something mild;
in this regard, I consider the lotus plant’s destruction by a frost-spray to be the primary illustration.
If this garland is a taker of life, why does it not kill me when placed upon my heart?
By the will of the Lord, even poison may sometimes become nectar, or nectar may become poison.
Or rather, through the ruin of my own fortune, this thunderbolt was fashioned by the Creator;
for by it the tree was not felled, but the creeper clinging to its branches was destroyed.
Since you have not shown me contempt even when I have long been guilty of offenses,
why do you suddenly consider this innocent person unworthy of being addressed?
O lady of pure smiles, I am surely a rogue, for by fate I have been a lover of deceit toward you;
since you have departed from here without taking leave of me, never to return to the next world.
If he indeed followed after his beloved, why has he now turned back without her?
Let this wretched life of mine endure the intense agony caused by its own deed.
Even a drop of perspiration produced by the fatigue of love-play remains upon your face;
yet, alas, it has vanished—oh, fie on this worthlessness of embodied beings!
The drops of perspiration from the fatigue of love-making have not yet ceased upon your face;
how is it that [the passion] has already subsided? Oh, alas! Shame on this worthlessness of embodied existence!
"Even in my mind I have never before done anything displeasing to you; why then do you abandon me?
Am I not the lord of the earth by right of lineage? My affection for you is bound to the very essence of my being."
O lady with thighs like an elephant's trunk, the wind, stirring your tresses— which are adorned with flowers, wrinkled, and dark as bees— makes my mind suspect that you have returned.
Therefore, my beloved, you ought to dispel my grief quickly through your awakening,
just as the glowing medicinal herb dispels the darkness dwelling in the cave of the Snowy Mountain.
This face, with its disheveled locks and silenced conversation,
pains me like a single lotus sleeping at night, its internal humming of bees having ceased.
The night returns again to the moon, her beloved, and the female bird to her mate who wanders with her;
since even these two are capable of enduring separation, how could you, having gone away forever, not consume me with grief?
Tell me, O lady of beautiful thighs: how will this body of yours, which would suffer even when placed upon a bed of fresh sprouts, endure ascending the funeral pyre?

This girdle, your first companion in solitude, lying here as you sleep in unconsciousness, appears neither through grief nor as if following you in death; it is silent, having lost its graceful movements.

The warbling of the cuckoos was eclipsed by the speech of the female swans; their languid grace, dulled by passion, was surpassed by the glances of the gazelles; and their playful movements were outdone by the swaying of the creepers shaken by the wind.
Although you were longing for heaven, these virtues were truly bestowed upon me by you;
yet, in separation from you, they are not able to sustain my heart, which suffers great pain.
"You have indeed imagined a union between the mango tree and the Phalinī creeper;
yet, it is improper to depart without having performed the auspicious rite of their marriage."
Since this aśoka tree, having been granted its longing by you, will put forth blossoms,
how shall I not carry those flowers to adorn your hair, cherished as they are by your funeral offerings?

O fair-limbed one, you are being mourned by this Ashoka tree, which rains down flowers like tears; it seems to remember the favor of your feet, accompanied by the sound of anklets—a favor difficult for others to obtain.
O Kinnarī-voiced one, why do you sleep now, having left unfinished your ornamental girdle— half-completed by me along with Bakula flowers that mimic the fragrance of your sighs?
Your friends share equally in your sorrow and joy, and this son of yours resembles the moon at the beginning of the fortnight;
yet I alone am of one taste with you, and thus your resolve is cruel in its execution.
Fortitude has set, delight has vanished, song has ceased, the season is without festival;
the purpose of ornaments is gone, and my bed today is utterly empty.
My wife, my counselor, my intimate friend, and my dear pupil in the arts of grace—
tell me, what has not been taken from me by Death, who is indifferent to compassion, in seizing you?

O lady with intoxicating eyes, having drunk the flavorful wine offered from my own mouth, how indeed will you now drink the handful of water for the dead, defiled by tears and brought forth from the other world?
Even though wealth exists, let this much alone be considered the happiness of the Unborn One when he is without you;
for all my objects of sense, which depend upon him, cannot be stolen by other temptations.
Lamenting thus for his beloved in words composed of compassion and meaning, the Lord of Kosala caused even the trees to shed a rainy day of tears in the form of sap flowing from their branches.
Then, somehow removing Sundarī from his lap, his kinsmen sent her away,
having adorned her with final ornaments, to the fire that was smeared with aloe and sandalwood.

The king, overcome with grief for his consort, did not consign his body to the fire along with the queen because he perceived that such an act would be censurable; it was not, however, due to any hope for life.
Then, after ten days had passed, that wise man, having instructed his wife in the remaining duties,
completed the highly efficacious rites in a grove just outside the city.
Without her, he entered the city like the moon at the end of the night; he seemed to see the overflow of his own sorrow in the tears upon the faces of the city’s women.
Then, having been urged by his pupil to perform the sacrifice, the Guru, remaining in his hermitage,
realized that [the prince] was paralyzed by infatuation and thus informed him.
Because the Sage, though he is wise, has not yet completed his ritual,
he has not personally approached you to restore you to your natural state, remaining instead established in his own observance.
O you of excellent conduct, his speech, consisting of brief messages, is directed toward me;
listen to it, O you whose essence of courage is renowned, for you ought to take it to heart.
Regarding the states of a person who is unborn, that which has passed, that which is present, and that which is yet to come—
he indeed perceives this triad with an unimpeded eye consisting of knowledge.
Long ago, it is said that Indra, becoming suspicious of Tṛṇabindu as he was performing difficult austerities,
dispatched to him a celestial nymph in the form of a doe, capable of disrupting his meditative absorption.

The sage, his anger provoked by the obstruction to his asceticism, cursed her— who had displayed her lovely charms before him— saying, "Become a human being," as if with a wave of dissolution at the hour of peace.
"O Blessed One, this person is dependent on another; please forgive my offensive conduct.
Thus she spoke, as she fell prostrate upon the ground, helpless, seeking the means for the cessation of the curse.
Having been your queen for a long time, that princess born of the Krathakaishika dynasty,
now fallen from heaven, has helplessly come to understand the cause for the termination of her curse.
Therefore, enough of worrying about his downfall; misfortune has befallen those who possess prosperity.
You should look toward this earth as your treasury, for kings have the earth as their wife.
Since you have revealed your learning through self-control by abandoning intoxication at its onset,
let it now be manifested once more by your fortitude when this fever of the mind has arrived.
How much less could she be recovered by you through weeping, even if you were to die after her?
For the destinies of embodied beings who have reached the next world follow diverse paths according to their own past actions.
O King, she will not be turned back by your weeping; therefore, it is useless for you.
Even though you pursue her, you shall not obtain her, for embodied beings are subject to their own karma.
Free from sorrow, favor your wife with offerings for the deceased;
for it is said that the unceasing tears of one's kinsmen indeed burn the departed spirit.
Death is the natural state of embodied beings, while life is said by the wise to be an anomaly;
if a creature remains breathing for even a moment, is it not indeed a gain?
One of deluded mind perceives the loss of a loved one as a dart driven into the heart;
but he of steady intellect regards that very same event as having been extracted because it serves as a gateway to spiritual welfare.
When a person of deluded mind perceives the union with and separation from what has been heard and retained,
tell me, how could separation from external objects cause distress to a wise man?
O supreme among those who possess self-mastery, you ought not to fall under the power of grief like an ordinary person;
for what difference is there between trees and mountains if both are shaken by the wind?
Saying "So be it," he accepted the words of the noble-minded Guide and dismissed the sage;
yet that [instruction], finding no footing in his heart which was thick with grief, returned, as it were, to the presence of his teacher.

Thus, because of his son’s childhood innocence and his unfailing truthfulness, he somehow passed eight years with the sight of portraits and likenesses of his beloved wife, and through the joy of momentary reunions in dreams with his son.
It is said that the stake of grief violently tore through his heart, as if a sprout of the Plakṣa tree were piercing the roof of a palace;
and he considered it a gain, though incurable by physicians and even fatal to life, to hasten in pursuit of his beloved.
Then, having duly instructed the prince, the wearer of armor, in the task of protecting the subjects,
the king— desiring to escape his wretched dwelling in a body afflicted by disease— set his mind upon fasting unto death.
At that sacred ford, where the waters of the Ganges and the Sarayu mingle, he immediately attained a place among the ranks of the immortals by casting off his body;
then, reunited with his beloved, whose radiance was now even more intense than her former form, he took delight once again in pleasure-pavilions within the Nandana groves.
Immediately after his father, Daśaratha— having conquered his senses through meditative concentration,
a great chariot-warrior standing at the forefront of both the self-controlled and the protectors— ruled over the northern Kośalas.
Having duly acquired his ancestral circle of vassals, he protected it in accordance with the traditions of his own lineage;
consequently, for that king whose prowess was like the thunderbolt of Indra, the realm including its cities became even more excellent in virtue.
The wise speak of both as the fulfillers of the deeds of those who have performed their duties through timely rain:
of him, the slayer of Bala, the lord of wealth; and of him, the remover of fatigue, born of the lineage of Manu who wields the rod of justice.
In that realm, disease found no footing, much less any defeat born of enemies;
while that king, who delighted in tranquility and possessed the splendor of the immortals, ruled, the earth became fruitful even in the absence of his son.
Just as the earth had flourished with glory under Aja, who surpassed Raghu— the conqueror of the ten directions—
so too did she shine once more upon attaining him, whose prowess was no less than his father’s.
By his impartiality in bestowing showers of wealth and by his restraint of the wicked,
the lord of men followed the paths of Yama, the Lord of the Guhyakas, Varuṇa, and Aruṇa, excelling them all in splendor.
Neither the delight in hunting, nor gambling, nor wine adorned with moon-like ornaments,
nor even his most beloved young wife, could divert him as he strove toward that awakening.
Even when Indra was present, he did not utter a word that was base; even in jesting conversation, his speech was never false;
and even toward those who were his enemies, he never spoke a harsh word with cruel syllables.
The lords of the earth attained both rise and fall from that scion of Raghu;
for he was a friend to those who did not transgress his commands, yet he was like iron-hearted steel to those who challenged him.
With his bow strung, he conquered the earth bounded by the oceans on a single chariot;
yet it was his army—abounding in elephants and swift in its horses—that proclaimed his victory.

He, whose prowess equaled that of the Lord of Alakā, forcibly deprived the wives of his enemies of their girdles from their hips, of the decorative marks on their foreheads due to the unaccustomed shedding of tears, and of their tresses.
It is said that for that archer who had conquered the earth with a single chariot equipped with a protective fender,
the oceans— resounding like clouds and filled with the wealth of men borne on elephants— became his drums of victory.
Purandara, who subdued the strength of the wings with his sharp-tipped thunderbolt against the mountains,
[now] possessed a bow that released showers of arrows at his enemies, while his face was like a fresh lotus.
Indra, whose face is like a fresh lotus, acquired fame with his thunderbolt that radiated thousands of millions of rays;
he, however, acquired it in battle with his resounding bow that rained down arrows.
Touching him with the rays of the jewels on his crown— which were rich in hue like the nails on his feet—
he [confronted] that Indra, the master of a hundred sacrifices, whose prowess remained unimpaired despite being showered with arrows from a bow in battle.

Having shown compassion for the inhabitants of Alakā— who were surrounded by enemies and whose young sons had been made to offer salutations with joined palms by their ministers— he returned from the shore of the great ocean to that city which was no less than Alakā itself.
And although he had reached the center of the circle [of kings], yet without raising his own dark parasol,
he— whose splendor was equal to fire and the moon— remained untiring, thinking, "The royal domain is still unconquered."

By him, who had cast off his crown and seized the wealth of the quarters with his own arms, the banks of the Tamasa river were adorned with sacrificial posts erected during rituals— posts that shone with their golden height and dispelled all darkness.
The Lord illumined that unapproachable body, which was consecrated for the sacrifice, wearing a deerskin and a staff, girdled with kusha grass, restrained in speech, and holding a deer horn.
Having performed his purificatory ablutions and with his senses restrained, he— fit to enter the assembly of the gods—
bowed only his lofty head to the enemy of Namuci (Indra), the taker of the forest (the rain-cloud).

Abandoning that man born of the Kakutstha lineage as well as the Self-born [Brahmā], the goddess Lakṣmī, devoted to her husband, served another king; for what lack of dignity could there be among those who seek a goal?
That great chariot-warrior, having indeed rendered assistance to Indra at the forefront of the battle,
caused the celestial damsels— whose fears had been dispelled by his arrows— to sing of the loftiness of the prowess of his own arms.
On many occasions, by that swift archer who led the vanguard of Indra on a single chariot,
the dust of battle rising toward the sun was laid to rest by the blood of the enemies of the gods.

Those daughters of the illustrious Magadhas, Kosalas, and Kekayas, who held their husbands as their deities, obtained him as their husband— him whose arrows were aimed at his enemies— just as rivers flowing from mountain peaks reach the ocean.

Accompanied by those three beloved wives, he shone like Indra, the slayer of enemies and expert in the application of weapons, who had descended to earth with his three Śaktis, desiring as it were to govern the subjects.
Then Spring returned with fresh blossoms, as if to serve that sole lord of men who was equal in majesty to Yama,
Kubera, Varuṇa, and Indra, and whose valor was honored.
Desiring to go toward the quarter inhabited by the Giver of Wealth, the Sun, having turned his vehicle with his charioteer,
left Mount Malaya while purifying the faces of the days with frosty rays.
Leaving behind the Malaya mountain, whose sandalwood sprouts had been described by Himavat,
the sun turned northward and proceeded slowly, as if out of compassion for the pair of birds who were certain to be separated at the end of the day.
First the blossoming of flowers, then the new shoots, followed by the humming of bees and the warbling of cuckoos—
in this sequence, Spring manifested as it descended upon the forest region of Drumavatī.
The forest garland, born from contact with fragrant blossoms and consisting of fragile fresh palāśa leaves,
was worn by him as if it were a fresh nail-mark bestowed by a young woman whose modesty had been dispelled by intoxication.
The cluster of buds upon the *kiṃśuka* tree, bestowed by the beauty of the departure of winter,
shone like the ornament of nail-marks upon a beloved woman whose modesty has been dispelled by intoxication.
Like a light-tongued female friend to women whose hearts were wounded by love, the cuckoo—
soft-voiced yet making union difficult to attain— caused their lovers to fall out with one another during their quarrels.

The sun was indeed not yet able to dispel the frost entirely; it had merely made it sparse—frost that was unbearable due to the wounds caused by the heavy lip of the young woman, and which had rendered the girdle useless upon her hips.

The winter season made rare that supreme delight of the rainy season— characterized by the rays of the clear moon, pleasant breezes, blossoming trees, and intoxicated cuckoos— which brings forth the essence of enjoyment.
The mango creeper, its shoots trembling in the Malaya breeze as if striving to master the art of dramatic gesture,
intoxicated the minds even of those who had conquered the god of love, for it was now budding with new blossoms.

Seekers of wealth approached the king’s fortune— which was augmented by the virtues of his policy and bore the fruit of good deeds— just as bees and lotus-stalk eaters approach a lotus pond filled with nectar from a lake.
Her smile, illuminated by the moonlight of her teeth and fragrant like wine,
was sought after by the bees— those desiring its pure nectar— which had long been stored within her like a bakula flower.
Not only was the fresh seasonal blossom of the aśoka tree an inflamer of love,
but even the emerging sprouts, when placed upon the ears of beloved women by amorous men, were intoxicating.
Like fresh decorative leaf-patterns fashioned by Spring upon the beauty of the groves,
the *kurabaka* flowers— skilled in bestowing honey upon the bees— became the cause of their humming.
The blossoming of the *bakula* tree, which possessed qualities corresponding to the nectar from the mouth of Suvadanā,
was made agitated by bees greedy for honey as they formed long rows around it.

The night during the spring, possessing the moon, became long as if out of compassion, for it was filled with the wine from the mouths of fair-faced women and possessed the quality of echoing that [wine] like the blooming of flowers.
First, in the fragrant rows of flowering forest groves, sparse words uttered by female cuckoos were heard, like the soft conversations of young brides.
The creepers at the edge of the grove shone with the luster of flower-like tender teeth and songs like the humming of bees pleasant to hear;
they seemed to keep time with their sprouts, which were struck by the breeze as if they were hands.

The women entered into their husbands— the honey [of spring], which is skilled in the composition of graceful amorous dalliances, whose filaments are surpassed by its fragrant scent, which is the companion of the God of Love, and which is devoid of any interruption in its sweetness.

Ten thousand playful bees, companions of the women and united with the god of love, sang sweetly; they had made their home in the palaces that were the tilaka-foreheads of the women, and they were fragrant from their attachment to the honey of flowers.

The palace ponds, with their blooming lotuses and birds restless upon the water as if intoxicated, shone like women whose faces are made more beautiful by smiles and whose girdles jingle softly as they move.

The mango tree, though in full bloom and bent down by intoxicated bees, did not alleviate the resentment harbored by the young woman toward her husband— a resentment born of his offense and intensified by the meditative concentration of the God of Love.
The night-bride, her face pale at its edge by the rising of the moon and her beauty diminished by the spring,
grew thin like a woman whose joy in the union with her beloved has been cut short.
With rays that were clear due to the absence of frost, which dispelled the fatigue of the gods' passion,
the moon sharpened the flower-bowed god whose banner bears the sea-monster.

The young women wore upon their tresses a flower that was as delicate as its petals and filaments, which served as a substitute for golden ornaments and possessed a luster like the blazing fire of a sacrificial offering.
Marked by bees, which were like charming drops of collyrium falling in rows upon the flowers,
the Tilaka tree did not fail to grace the forest glade, just as a sectarian mark (tilaka) adorns a beautiful woman.

The beautiful vine-like woman, the fresh jasmine, delighted his mind with her smile-like luster produced by flowers, which was joined to her sprout-like lower lip and endowed with the fragrance of honey.
The Ashoka creeper— untiring, stirred by a breeze carrying the pollen of lotuses from the minds of other birds,
and bent low under the weight of its blossoms— brought incomparable sorrow to the wives of travelers.
By means of garments that eclipsed the glow of the dawn, by barley sprouts that had found a place upon their ears,
and by the warbling of cuckoos— the very forces of Love— those graceful men were rendered single-mindedly devoted to women.
With its parts built up from pure pollen grains, having attained union with a swarm of bees,
the cluster of blossoms on the *tilaka* tree appeared as beautiful as a mass of hair-ornaments set with pearls.

The swarms of bees followed the pollen of flower filaments, raised by the breeze from the groves, which served as a banner for the bow-wielding God of Love, a complexion-enhancing cosmetic powder for the Beauty of Spring, and a fragrant scent.
Experiencing the seasonal festival of the new swing, the clever women, desiring to grasp the necks of their beloveds,
rendered their vine-like arms limp as they took hold of the ropes of the seats.
"Abandon pride; enough, alas, with these quarrels! Youth, once gone, does not return.
When the female cuckoos had thus announced this, which was pleasing to the God of Love, the women took their delight.
Then, having enjoyed the seasonal festival at his pleasure in the company of his playful consorts,
that lord of men— resembling the spring, honey, and the god of love— longed for the delight of the hunt.

Through mastery of fatigue, he made his body capable of hitting moving targets, of discerning the gestures of fear and anger, and of remaining agile; therefore, with the approval of his ministers, he set forth.
Wearing attire suitable for entering the deer-park, with his bow slung around his broad neck,
that sun among men made the sky appear as if it were possessed of twilight by means of the dust raised by the horses' hooves.
With his crown bound by a forest garland, his body clad in bark garments the color of tree leaves,
and his earrings swaying as he galloped his horse, he shone upon the grounds where the ruru deer roam.
The forest deities, their forms nestled within slender creepers and their movements of the eyes transferred to the bees,
beheld him on the road— the one with beautiful eyes who brings joy to Kosala.
He entered the forest, which was already occupied by packs of dogs and hunters, free from fire and bandits,
possessing ground level for steady horses, and teeming with herds of deer and flocks of birds like a watering place.
Then, like the wielder of the thunderbolt in the sky,
that best of men— free from anxiety and with his lion-like mane bristling at the roar [of the enemy]— took up his bow, which was strung and joined with a golden-brown cord like a streak of lightning.
Before him appeared a herd of deer with mouths filled with *kuśa* grass, led by a proud black antelope; its female deer were repeatedly interrupted in their gait by fawns eager for the mother’s teat.
That desired object was shattered by the king, mounted on a swift horse and with an arrow drawn from the mouth of his quiver;
it darkened the forest with its falling glances, as if with a mass of lotus petals tossed about by the wind.
Seeing his mate standing there, having shielded her body with her own, that archer of lion-like prowess—
his mind softened by compassion— retracted his arrow, even though it had been drawn back to his ear out of desire for the kill.
As he drew his arrows against other deer, even his firm grip was loosened as they reached the tip of his ear;
for with eyes exceedingly tremulous from fear, those deer recalled the amorous glances and playful movements of the mature wives of their lovers.

He perceived the clearly marked path of a herd of swift boars that had emerged from the midst of the mud of a cool-season pond, strewn with fragments of mouthfuls of musta-grass shoots, by means of long rows of fresh footprints.
As he bent his upper body from the mount and pierced them slightly, the boars, with their manes bristling, sought to strike back;
yet they did not realize that they themselves were suddenly pierced by arrows in the flanks from the jaws of the wolves.
With impetuous force, he drew back and released an arrow into the eye-socket of a wild buffalo;
having pierced through its body without its feathers being stained with blood, it first caused the animal to fall, and only afterwards did it drop itself.

The king, appointed to humble the arrogant, generally rendered the rhinoceroses light-headed by stripping away their horns with sharp crescent-headed arrows; he could not endure the uplifted tusks of his enemies, yet not their long lifespans.

With the swiftness of hand characteristic of his specialized training, he rendered in the blink of an eye those tigers— which had rushed headlong from their caves like flowering *asanā* trees uprooted by the wind— into a quiver, their mouths filled with arrows.
Desiring to slay the lions lurking in their thickets with the fierce crashes of his thunderbolt, he agitated them with the twanging of his bowstring;
surely he was full of envy toward those beasts, for the title of "King" is preeminent in their prowess.
Having slain those elephants whose intense enmity was fixed upon the elephant-herd, the descendant of Kakutstha— seeing pearls clinging to the tips of his curved claws—
considered himself to have attained freedom from debt through his arrows toward those elephants who had performed their duty in battle.

Having slain those elephants who harbored intense enmity toward the elephant race, the descendant of Kakutstha perceived himself— through his arrows— as having attained freedom from debt to those beasts whose curved claws had once clung to his pearls during their deeds in battle.
Having set his horses in motion around the camaras, and in some places showering crescent-headed arrows drawn back to his ear,
he immediately parted those kings from their white yak-tail fans and attained peace.
Even when a peacock with its beautiful plumage sprang up near his horse, he did not make it a target for his arrow;
for his mind was instantly fixed upon the mass of hair of his beloved, strewn with variegated garlands and loosened from its ties during their amorous play.
The forest breeze, with its spray of cool dew and its opening of young leaf-buds, drank up the sweat born of his strenuous exertion, which had formed a web-like film clinging to his face.
Thus, while the king had forgotten all other duties and rested his burden upon his ministers,
hunting— like a clever mistress— carried him away with its increasing passion and constant attendance.
In one place, the king spent the night without his retinue on a bed of delicate flowers and sprouts, illuminated by lamps made of glowing great medicinal herbs.
At dawn, his sleep dispelled by the rhythmic flapping of the ears of the elephant herds— sounding like the sharp beat of cymbals—
he took delight there in listening to the sweet songs of the birds, which served as auspicious hymns from bards.
Then, having once taken the path of Ruru, unobserved by his attendants in the forest,
he reached with his horse the river Tamasā, which was frequented by ascetics and was spuming foam from its exertion.
The sound produced by the filling of the jar rose loudly and clearly from those waters;
suspecting it to be the trumpeting of an elephant, Nanda discharged a sound-aimed arrow there.
The son of Paṅktiratha committed that very act which was forbidden by the king;
for even those possessed of sacred learning, when blinded by passion, set foot upon the wrong path.

Hearing the cry "Alas, father!", he became despondent; searching for its source hidden by the reeds, the king beheld the sage’s son transfixed by an arrow along with his water-jar, and like one with an internal thorn, he was pierced by inner anguish.

Having dismounted from his horse, he whose lineage was renowned asked about the other’s ancestry; then, with his body leaning against a water-jar, he began to describe himself to him as the son of a non-twice-born ascetic through faltering syllables and words.
Urged by him, the king led the prince, whose arrow had not yet been extracted, into the presence of his parents, whose vision was failing;
having approached them in that state, the monarch confessed his own conduct out of ignorance regarding their only son.
Having lamented profusely, the couple extracted the arrow that had been driven into their child’s chest by his assailant;
then, as he lay lifeless, the aged man, with tears falling from his hands, cursed the king.
To him who had said, "In your old age, you too shall meet your end through grief for a son,
just as I have," the Lord of Kosala, having committed his first offense, spoke to him who was like a venomous snake that had previously been stepped upon and then released its poison.
This curse, which has been cast upon me by the Blessed One, is actually a favor, since it has not allowed me to behold the lotus-like beauty of my son's face;
for even fire, though it burns the earth while being fueled by wood, produces the growth of seeds through its heat.
When the lord of the earth had thus spoken— "In this situation, what can this pitiless man do to you who are condemned to death?"—
the sage, desiring to follow his deceased son along with his wife, requested fuel from the king for a funeral fire.
Having immediately carried out his command, the king returned, his resolve shattered by the sin [of the deed],
bearing within him that curse which had taken root and was the cause of his own destruction, like the ocean holding the Aurva fire.
Therefore, since the one who knew the truth had departed, did this man condemned to death, casting aside all shame, offer you any instruction?
That king requested for himself the funeral rites with fire, and he performed them for his wife and son as well.
Having reunited with his own troops, the bull of the Raghus returned to his palace with a heavy heart,
bearing within him the weighty curse of the seer like the ocean at the end of time bears the fire of universal destruction.
As he ruled the earth, that sovereign whose splendor equaled Indra’s and whose prosperity was undiminished,
ten thousand autumns passed, falling short by but a little.
And he did not find among his ancestors the means for liberation from debt—
a son as his light— and so he passed ten thousand autumns.
In that [kingdom], the lineage of Manu, its continuity unmanifest for a long time,
became like the Śoṇa river, which, having submerged, was about to rise up once more.
For a long time that king remained with his mental continuum dependent upon external conditions,
like the ocean before the churning when the production of jewels has not yet been manifested.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and the other virtuous priests, who were self-controlled and desirous of his progeny, began the sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son.
At that moment, the gods, oppressed by the descendant of Pulastya, approached Hari like travelers afflicted by the heat of summer seeking the shade of a tree.
And they reached the ocean, while the Primeval Being awoke;
for freedom from distraction is indeed the sign of the accomplishment of a future task.
The inhabitants of heaven beheld him seated upon the coils of the serpent,
his body illuminated by the jewels blazing from the circle of its hoods.
[He saw him] with his feet placed upon the lap of Śrī, who was seated upon a lotus, her girdle concealed by silken garments, and her sprout-like hands spread out as a cushion.
With his lotus-eyes fully opened and his garment resembling the light of the morning sun,
he was like an autumn day, pleasant to behold at its onset.
With his broad chest, he bore the Kaustubha gem— the very essence of the waters— which anointed the Śrīvatsa with its radiance and served as a mirror for the playful charms of Lakṣmī.
With arms resembling branches and adorned with divine ornaments,
