he appeared from the midst of the waters like another *pārijāta* tree.
The sounds of victory were raised by sentient weapons that wiped away the redness of intoxication from the cheeks of the hosts of Daitya women.
Garuda approached him with palms joined in reverence, humble and bearing the marks of wounds from the thunderbolt, yet free from all lingering resentment.
He was favoring the sages who had spent the night in comfortable rest, such as Bhṛgu and others, with purifying glances that were clear at the conclusion of their yogic sleep.
Having prostrated before that pacifier of the enemies of the gods,
the deities then praised him, who is worthy of praise and beyond the reach of speech and mind.
Salutations to you, who first create the universe, then sustain it, and finally withdraw it— the self who exists in these three modes.

Just as divine water, though possessing a single taste, assumes various other tastes according to the different regions it reaches, so too do you, remaining changeless, abide amidst the qualities in each respective state.

You are immeasurable, yet you have measured the worlds; you are free from desire, yet you fulfill the prayers of others; you are unconquered, yet you are the ultimate victor; you are unmanifest, yet you are the cause of all that is manifest.
By means of various causes, you assume this or that state;
your manifoldness is said to arise from contact with passion, just like that of a crystal.
They know you to be dwelling in the heart, yet not near; free from desire, though practicing asceticism; compassionate, untouched by sin; ancient and undecaying.

You are the omniscient one, yet you remain unrecognized; you are the source of all births, yet you are self-born; you are the sovereign lord of all, yet you are without a master; you are the one, yet you assume every form.
They have declared you to be one praised by the seven Saman hymns, reclining upon the waters of the seven oceans,
having the seven-flamed fire as your mouth, and the sole refuge of the seven worlds.

From you, the four-faced one, comes knowledge that bears fruit as the four goals of life, the duration of time consisting of the four ages, and the world composed of the four castes; indeed, everything proceeds from you.
With minds restrained through practice, yogis seek you, who consist of light and abide in the heart, for the sake of liberation.
Who knows your true nature— you who take birth though unborn, who destroy your enemies though devoid of effort, and who remain awake though appearing to sleep?
To enjoy objects such as sound and to practice austerities difficult to perform—you are capable of these; yet you are fit to protect your subjects by conducting yourself with equanimity.
Though the paths leading to perfection are divided in many ways by various scriptures,
they all converge upon you alone, like the torrents of the Ganges falling into the ocean.
For those whose minds are absorbed in you and whose actions are dedicated to you,
you are the goal for those free from passion, leading to the state of no further rebirth.
Even your greatness, such as the earth and so forth, though perceptible, cannot be fully delimited;
what need is there to mention you, who must be established through both authoritative scripture and inference?
Since you purify a person by mere remembrance alone,
all other modes of conduct have their fruits already offered to you.
Like jewels from the ocean or like the splendors of the sun,
your deeds far exceed all praises.
There is nothing remaining for you to attain that has not already been attained;
your sole motive for taking birth and performing actions is indeed the favoring of the world.
That your speech is withdrawn after having proclaimed your greatness is due either to exhaustion or to inability, and not because of any limit to your virtues.
Thus they sought to propitiate you; for that which was spoken was the truth of the matter, not mere praise of the Supreme Lord.
To him, who was filled with joy manifested by his inquiry after their welfare,
the gods reported the danger arising from the ocean of the Nairṛtas, which had overflowed its shores at the end of the dissolution.
Then the Blessed One, whose voice surpassed the sound of the ocean, spoke with a tone that resounded through the mountain caves near the shore.
The speech of that ancient poet, articulated with the proper places and organs of articulation and refined by grammatical purification,
became truly purposeful.
The moonlight of his teeth, issuing from the face of the Lord,
shone like the Ganges flowing upwards after it has emerged from his foot and only a small portion remains behind.
I know that your majesty and prowess, when assailed by the Rākṣasa, were both eclipsed,
like the primary and secondary qualities of embodied beings by darkness.
And by him, the three worlds were perceived as being tormented,
like the heart of a virtuous man by a sin that has come upon it against his will.
And because we share a single purpose in our undertakings, I am not to be entreated by the wielder of the thunderbolt;
for the wind itself spontaneously assumes the role of charioteer for the fire.
By him, the edge of his own sword was spared; thus, he has spared my tenth head at will, as if it were a portion to be left for the Rākṣasa.
But because of the Creator’s granting of a boon, I have endured the excessive arrogance of that evil-minded enemy,
as one might endure a serpent upon sandalwood.
For that Rākṣasa, having turned his back on hope for mortals, requested from Dhātṛ— pleased by his asceticism— invincibility against all beings other than gods.
Therefore, having become the son of Daśaratha, I shall, with my sharp arrows, make that collection of lotus-like heads on the battlefield fit for an offering.
Before long, you shall again take possession, according to the prescribed rites, of that portion ordained by the fire-gods—
a portion untouched by the night-stalking practitioners of illusion.
May the merit-performing Vaimānika gods on the path of the winds abandon their agitation at the sight of the Puṣpaka, remaining intent instead on veiling it with clouds.
You shall undo the unblemished braids of the captive women of heaven,
which were once seized by force by the descendant of Pulastya while his hands were restrained by a curse.
Having showered the rain of nectar-like words upon the crop of Marutta, which was withered by the drought of Rāvaṇa, that dark cloud vanished from sight.
Led by Puruhūta, the gods, intent upon the task of the deities,
followed Viṣṇu with their portions, as trees follow the wind with their flowers.
Then, at the conclusion of that king’s optional rite,
a man emerged from the fire, causing wonder among the officiating priests.
Holding with both arms a golden vessel containing milk-rice,
it was difficult even for him to carry because of his entry into the body of the Primordial Being.
The king accepted that food brought by the son of Prajāpati,
just as a bull accepts the essence of the waters revealed by the ocean.
By him were recounted the king’s virtues, which are difficult for others to attain,
since even he who is the source of the three worlds desired offspring from him.
He divided that Vaiṣṇava splendor, known as the *caru*, between his two wives,
just as the lord of day distributes his fresh heat between heaven and earth.
Kausalyā was honored by him, as was his beloved wife born of the Kekaya lineage;
therefore, the lord desired Sumitrā, who was highly esteemed by those two.
Those two wives of the king, who were both highly learned and knew his mind,
each joined her with half of the remaining half of the sacrificial porridge.
She was equally devoted to both her co-wives,
just as a female bee is drawn to the two streams of ichor flowing from an elephant's temples.
By them, for the sake of the prosperity of progeny, was borne a fetus born of a portion of the gods,
just as the watery essence is held by the solar channels known as the "nectar-flowers."
Those women, having conceived, shone with a pale radiance,
like the excellence of grain-bearing crops when the development of the fruit has begun within them.
In their dreams, they all saw themselves protected by dwarf figures whose bodies were marked with the lotus, sword, mace, Śārṅga bow, and discus.
And they were carried by Suparṇa, who spread a mass of luster from his golden wings across the sky and drew the clouds along with his speed.
She was attended by Lakṣmī, who bore the Kaustubha gem as an ornament hanging between her breasts,
and held a lotus-fan in her hand.
Having performed their ablutions in the celestial river with its triple stream,
the seven Brahman-sages approached him, chanting the supreme Brahman.
Having heard such dreams from them, the king was indeed delighted;
he considered himself most preeminent by virtue of being the teacher of the Teacher of the World.
The omnipresent Lord, whose self is manifoldly divided among them, dwelt in many ways within those various wives,
like the reflected moon in clear waters.
Then, at the time of delivery, the king’s chief queen gave birth to a son who dispelled darkness, just as a medicinal herb produces light in the night.
The preceptor bestowed upon him the name "Rāma"— a name that was delightful, possessed incomparable splendor, and was the foremost auspiciousness in the world.
By him, the lamp of Raghu’s lineage and possessed of incomparable splendor,
the lamps within the protection-chamber seemed as if they had been eclipsed.
As she lay upon her bed, the slender-waisted mother shone like the Ganges in autumn, emaciated by the season, yet graced by an offering of lotuses upon its sandy banks.
To Kaikeyī was born a son named Bharata, who was possessed of virtuous character;
he adorned his mother as humility adorns prosperity.
Sumitrā gave birth to twin sons, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna,
who were like learning and discipline perfectly acquired together with wisdom.
The entire world became free from defect and manifested its virtues;
for heaven, as it were, followed the Supreme Person who had descended to earth.
Upon the rise of that fourfold-formed one, the quarters of space, their lords terrified by the descendant of Pulastya, seemed to breathe a sigh of relief through dustless winds.
Because he was smokeless and radiant, Agni, the maker of light,
appeared as if he had been cast off by his guards after being treated with indignity and left in a state of impurity.
At that moment, from the crowns of the ten-faced one,
the tears of the Rakshasa’s fortune fell upon the earth under the guise of gems.
The celestial drums in the heavens first began to sound for that father of a son, preceding the musical instruments to be entered upon at the birth of a son.
A rain consisting of celestial garlands fell upon his palace;
that very rain became the first arrangement of auspicious offerings.
Having undergone the purificatory rites and drinking the breast-milk of their nurses,
the princes grew up alongside their father’s eldest son, Ānanda, as if he were their own elder brother.
Their innate discipline was further refined by the formal act of ordination,
just as the natural brilliance of fire-gods intensifies when fed with sacrificial oblations.
Mutually non-contradictory, they fully illuminated that sinless lineage of Raghu,
just as the seasons illuminate the grove of the gods.
For although their brotherly affection was equal, just as Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were,
so too did Bharata and Śatrughna form a pair through mutual love.
The unity of each of those two pairs was never divided,
just as that of wind and fire, or of the moon and the ocean.
Those lords of subjects captivated the hearts of the people by their splendor and their humility,
like days at the end of summer when dark clouds have appeared.
That progeny of the lord of the earth, divided into four parts, shone forth like the incarnation of Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa, each assuming its own limb.
Devoted to their teacher, they propitiated him with their virtues,
just as the great oceans satisfy the Lord of the Four Quarters with jewels.

With those shoulders of his, the lord of kings shone like a celestial elephant with tusks that have severed the edges of the swords of Daityas, like the principle of policy (naya) with expedients made manifest through the binding of stakes, and like Hari with arms as long as a yoke. Ragh_10.87.

It is said that Kauśika approached that lord of the earth and entreated him for Rāma—who still bore the side-locks of youth—in order to appease the obstruction to the sacrifice; for in the case of those possessed of spiritual luster, age is not taken into account.
Though it was obtained with great difficulty, he, who possessed a reputation for excellence, bestowed him along with Lakṣmaṇa upon the sage;
for in the lineage of Raghu, the request of even those who were not friends was never denied.
Even as the king was issuing orders for the preparation of the city streets for their departure,
it was quickly carried out by the clouds, friends of the wind, raining down water and flowers.
Ready to carry out their father’s command, those two archers fell at his feet; and from the lord of the earth, too, tears fell upon them as they bowed down, about to depart on their journey.
With the water born from their father’s eyes slightly moistening their topknots,
both archers followed that seer, for whom the citizens had created gateway-arches out of their very glances.
The sage desired to take away only Rāghava, who was followed by Lakṣmaṇa;
thus the king offered him a blessing, but not his army, for that [blessing] alone was sufficient for the task of protecting the two of them.
And those two of great prowess proceeded even more swiftly, following the path of Viśvāmitra,
like the months of Madhu and Mādhava following the sun as it sets out toward the northern quarter.
Having touched the feet of their mothers and entered upon the path of the great-splendored sage,
those two shone as they proceeded by the force of their movement, like the months of Madhu and Mādhava following the course of the sun.

The restless movements of those two, whose arms were as tremulous as ripples, though fickle due to their youth, appeared beautiful; their actions were like the very names they bore, resembling the surging of the two oceans at the arrival of the rainy season.
By the power of the two sciences, Bala and Atibala, which had been imparted to them by the sage on the road,
those two did not falter, appearing like two boys staying by their mother's side upon a jeweled floor.

Accustomed to being carried in a vehicle, Rāghava— conversant with ancient lore as he was— did not even notice that he was walking on foot, though he was being led by his younger brother who recounted the stories of the past concerning his father’s friend.
The lakes served them with their flavorful waters; the birds with their songs pleasant to the ear;
the winds with the pollen of fragrant flowers; and the clouds with their shade.
The ascetics did not derive such joy from the sight of waters adorned with lotuses, nor from trees that dispel fatigue,
as they did from the mere brief sight of those two.
Having reached the penance grove of Sthāṇu, whose body had been consumed by fire, the son of Daśaratha took up his bow;
with his beautiful form he became a likeness of Madana, yet not in his actions.
On the road, which had been rendered impassable by the daughter of Suketu— who was aware of the curse from Kaushika—
they effortlessly restored their two bows to a state of being strung, as the riverbanks were settled upon dry land.
Then Tāḍakā appeared, seizing the twang of their bowstrings;
she possessed the luster of many nights, with dangling skull-earrings, like a dense storm cloud filled with cranes.
With her path shaken by the force of her intense speed, wearing the rags of a preta and possessing a fierce voice,
she overwhelmed the elder brother of Bharata like a whirlwind rising from a cemetery.
Beholding her with one arm raised like a staff and a girdle of human entrails hanging from her hips, Rāghava cast away his compassion for the slaughter of a woman along with his arrow.
That arrow of Rāma, which had made a breach in the solid rock-like chest of Tāḍaka,
became the gateway for Death to enter the realm of the Rākṣasas.
Falling with her heart pierced by the arrow, she not only shook her own land,
but also made even the sovereignty of Rāvaṇa tremble— a sovereignty once thought secure due to his conquest of the three worlds.
Struck in the heart by the unbearable arrow of Rāma’s love, that night-stalker woman,
anointed with fragrant blood-sandalwood, departed for the abode of the Lord of Life.
Then, from the sage— who was gratified by his noble deed— the slayer of Tāḍakā received a weapon accompanied by a mantra that destroys the followers of Nirṛti,
just as a sun-stone receives light from the sun that falls upon its fuel.
Then, having heard of the further purifying hermitage of Vāmana, Rāghava approached the sage;
though he did not consciously remember the deeds of his former birth, his mind became uplifted with longing.
Then the sage reached his own penance grove, where hospitality had been prepared by the assembly of disciples,
where the trees held their hands joined in cupped leaf-petals, and where the deer stood with faces upturned, eager for a sight of him.
There, the two sons of Daśaratha protected the consecrated seer from obstacles with their arrows,
just as the moon and sun, rising in succession, protect the world from blinding darkness with their rays.
Then, seeing the altar defiled by drops of blood as large as bandhujīva flowers,
the officiating priests— having abandoned their rites and dropped their ladles made of *vikaṅkata* wood— were seized with agitation.

Turning his face upward, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa immediately drew the arrow from the mouth of its sheath and beheld the army of the rākṣasas in the sky, their banners fluttering in the wind stirred by the wings of the vulture.
There, he made those two—the lords of the haters of sacrifice—his target, but not the others;
for does the Garuḍa, whose prowess spreads even over great serpents, ever direct his efforts toward mere water-snakes?
Skilled in the use of weapons, he fixed upon his bow that missile presided over by Vāyu, which possessed a fierce velocity;
with it, he struck down even the son of Tāḍakā, though as heavy as a mountain, like a withered leaf.
Another rākṣasa there, named Subāhu, who had been prowling here and there by means of his illusory power,
was cut into pieces with razor-sharp arrows by the skillful king and distributed outside the hermitage.
Thus, having praised the martial prowess of those two who had warded off the obstacles to the sacrifice,
the officiating priests performed the rites for the patriarch, who remained silent according to the prescribed order.
The sage, having emerged from his ritual bath, touched the two brothers— whose side-locks of hair moved as they bowed—
with a hand whose palm was scarred by the darbha grass, immediately following his words of blessing.

Having prepared his sacrificial rites, the self-controlled King of Mithilā invited him; as he was traveling toward Mithilā, he also brought the two descendants of Raghu, who were filled with curiosity born from hearing of that bow.
Having completed their journey, they took up residence for the evening among the trees of the hermitage belonging to Śiva,
where Dīrghatapas’s wife had once served as the momentary consort of Indra.
That the daughter-in-law of Gautama, who had long been turned into stone,
should once again assume her own beautiful form was indeed the grace of the dust from the feet of Rāma, which cuts away all sins.
Hearing that the sage had arrived accompanied by the descendant of Raghu, Janaka, the lord of men, approached him with offerings of hospitality,
as if approaching Dharma itself embodied in physical form for the sake of both worldly prosperity and spiritual merit.
As they went to Videha’s city like the two Punarvasu stars descended from heaven to earth,
the minds of the inhabitants felt that even the blinking of their eyes while drinking them in was a deprivation.
When the sacrificial rites involving the sacrificial post had been completed, that knower of time, the enhancer of Kuśika’s lineage,
spoke to the King of Mithilā concerning Rāma, who was eager to behold the bow.
Beholding the graceful form of that child born of a renowned lineage,
and reflecting upon his own bow which was so difficult to bend, the king was distressed by the condition set for his daughter's dowry.
And he said: "O Blessed One, even that deed which is difficult for great elephants to perform, I am not able to approve of it; it is the conduct of a young elephant whose efforts are in vain."

For many lords of men, those wielders of the bow, were put to shame by that bow, my dear; shaking their own arms whose skin was hardened by the striking of the bowstring, they departed, crying, "Shame! (Raghuvamśa 11.40).
The sage replied to him: "Listen to this in its essence, or rather, enough with words;
your bow itself shall manifest its power, like a thunderbolt upon a mountain."
Thus, from the words of the authoritative one, he believed in the manly prowess of the descendant of Raghu, though he still wore the side-locks of youth,
just as one believes in the power of fire to burn, even when it is as small as a cow's hair.
The King of Mithilā commanded his attendants to bring forth the bow-ornament,
just as the thousand-eyed Indra commands the clouds to discharge their brilliance for the sake of the celestial bow.

Beholding that [bow] which was as terrifying as a sleeping lord of serpents, the son of Daśaratha took up the bow with which the bull-bannered god (Śiva) had once loosed an arrow that pursued the fleeing deer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Watched by the assembly with eyes fixed in wonder,
he strung his bow without great effort, as easily as the God of Love strings his delicate flower-bow, though it was made of the hardest stone.
As the bow, being broken by that excessive drawing, emitted a harsh sound like a thunderbolt,
it announced to the fiercely indignant descendant of Bhṛgu that the Kṣatriya power had once again been raised up.
Then the King of Mithilā, having observed the essence of the bow of Rudra and rejoiced in the bride-price of valor,
offered his daughter— born not of a womb, like the goddess Śrī incarnate— to the descendant of Raghu.
The King of Mithilā, true to his vow, immediately bestowed his daughter, who was not born from a womb,
upon the descendant of Raghu in the presence of the radiant treasury of asceticism, as if with fire itself as witness.
And the one of great luster dispatched a highly honored priest to the lord of Kosala, saying:
"Because of the acceptance of your daughter as a servant, let this lineage of Nimi be declared [worthy]."
Anxious for the task of providing a son and wife, the Guru arrived before him;
for the son of Gautama, whose speech was agreeable, grants the desires of the virtuous without delay.
He sought out a suitable daughter-in-law, and a twice-born man of pleasing speech found him;
for the desired fruit of those who have performed good deeds ripens instantly, possessing the nature of the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree.
Having heard the words of that elder brother, who had performed the prescribed rites of honor,
the self-controlled Valabhit set forth, obscuring the rays of the sun with the dust raised by his army.
Surrounding Mithilā with his forces and pressing down upon the trees of its groves, he reached the city;
yet that city, like a woman, could not endure the long enjoyment of her lover, for it offered a resistance born of affection.
Having come together and established their agreement, both kings, who resembled Varuṇa and Vāsava,
performed the marriage rites for their daughter and son in a manner befitting their own majesty.
The scion of Raghu married Pārthivī, and Lakṣmaṇa, his younger brother, married her younger sister Urmilā;
those two, endowed with excellent vigor, were the husbands of the slender-waisted daughters of Kuśadhvaja, who were the youngest of the [four] sisters.
Those three sons, together with the fourth, were accompanied by their young brides;
they appeared like the personified successes of that king—namely, conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and war.

The daughters of the lord of men attained their purpose through those princes, and they likewise through her; that union of bridegroom and bride was like the conjunction of the elements with their respective properties.
Thus, having established those four sons there— finding his own delight in them—
Daśaratha, who had bestowed the kingdom of Mithilā upon them, returned to his own city, having relinquished his attachment to the three periods of time.
Once, the Maruts, blowing against him on their paths and uprooting the trees that served as his banners,
greatly distressed his army, just as the currents of a river overflowing its banks afflict the dry land.
Immediately thereafter, the sun was seen with its orb encircled by a formidable halo,
like a jewel fallen from the body of a serpent slain by Vainateya and still entwined within its coils.
With their tresses greyed by the wings of hawks and their garments drenched in the blood of evening clouds,
the quarters of the sky became like women in their menses, unfit for our gaze.
And the sun occupied that quarter of the sky toward which the jackals, taking refuge there, howled with terror,
as if urging Bhārgava on toward the ancestral rites for the Kṣatriyas with their blood.

Observing those portents, such as adverse winds, the lord of the earth, who was skilled in what ought to be done, consulted his preceptor regarding a means of pacification; and the preceptor, resolving that it would have a happy end, allayed his distress.
Suddenly, a mass of splendor rose and appeared at the head of the army,
which the soldiers, after rubbing their eyes, finally recognized as having the form of a person.
Wearing the paternal portion characterized by the sacred thread and the maternal wealth of a mighty bow,
he was like the sun accompanied by the moon, or like a sandalwood tree possessed of two tongues [the leaf and the resin].
By him— who, though standing firm even against his father’s command despite its harshness born of anger—
first conquered his own compassion by cutting off the head of his trembling mother, and thereafter the earth.
He shone with a circle of seed-syllables placed upon his right ear,
as if bearing the preliminary count for the twenty-one [incarnations] that bring about the end of the Kṣatriyas.

Beholding that descendant of Bhṛgu— who, consumed by the wrath born of his father’s murder, was consecrated for the destruction of the royal lineage— and beholding his own wretched state, the king despaired.

The name "Rāma," though identical when applied to his own son and to his cruel enemy, became pleasing to his heart in one case and terrifying in the other, just as a collection of jewels brings delight to a necklace and fear to a serpent.

Without looking at the king who was crying out, "The water-offering! The water-offering!", the elder brother of Bharata fixed upon him a gaze with its pupils dilated, like a flame from the fire of his kshatriya wrath.
With his fist still fixed upon the bow, Rāghava, free from fear, stood before him as the other,
eager for combat, drew an arrow through the space between his fingers and spoke.
The entire class of Kshatriyas was my harmful enemy; having subdued them many times, I attained peace.
Yet, like a sleeping serpent provoked by the strike of a staff, I have been incensed by the report of your prowess.
"You have indeed broken the bow of the King of Mithilā, which had never before been bent by other monarchs;
hearing that, I consider it to be like the shattered peak of my own prowess."
On another occasion, as soon as this word "Rāma" was uttered in the world, it reached me;
but now that you are about to rise, that same word, its application altered, brings me shame.
In my view, there are two enemies who bear weapons that remain unblunted even against immovable objects and who are equal in their offenses:
the Haihaya king, on account of his abduction of the sacrificial cow, and you, who are intent on taking away my daughter.
Though his valor is capable of ending the Kṣatriyas, it does not protect me as long as you remain unconquered;
for that is considered the greatness of fire which burns even in the ocean, just as it does in dry grass.
Know that your own strength was surpassed by the power of Hari, since his divine bow was broken by you;
for even a gentle wind, having undermined the roots with the force of river currents, causes even a tree on the bank to fall.
Therefore, let this weapon of mine be fitted with a string and drawn with an arrow;
let the battle itself cease, for even so, I have been defeated by you whose strength of arm is equal to my own.

If you are timid, having been threatened by the upraised flame of the edge of my axe, then let this palm-joined gesture of yours, which begs for safety, be bound in vain— your fingers already hardened by the strike of the bowstring.
When the descendant of Bhrigu, of fearsome appearance, had spoken thus, Rāghava, his lips trembling with a smile,
accepted the taking up of that very bow as a capable response.
Having been joined with his bow from a previous birth, he became exceedingly handsome to behold;
for even a single fresh cloud is beautiful, how much more so when marked by the rainbow of the gods?
By him, that bow, one end of which was fixed in the ground, was strung by the powerful one;
and the enemy of the kings became lusterless, like a fire reduced to nothing but smoke.
At the close of day, the people beheld those two standing side by side, their splendor waxing and waning respectively, like the full moon and the sun at the end of the fortnight.

Beholding that descendant of Bhṛgu softened by compassion and his own prowess blunted within himself, Rāghava— who resembled the son of Hara— spoke to him regarding his own unerring, well-aimed arrow.
"I am not able to strike you out of compassion, O Brahmin," he said, even though you have transgressed;
tell me, shall I destroy with this arrow your future destiny or the world you have earned through sacrifices?
The sage replied to him: "I do not know you in truth as that ancient Puruṣa;
for while you had gone to the earth, your Vaiṣṇava abode, you were provoked by me who was desirous of seeing you."

Even the reversal of victory that has been inflicted upon me by you, the Supreme Lord, is indeed praiseworthy— for you have reduced my enemies, the haters of my father, to ashes and turned the earth together with its oceans into a mere vessel.
Therefore, O best among the wise, protect for me that desired path for traveling to sacred pilgrimage sites;
for the path to heaven, though neglected, will not cause pain to one who is not greedy for sensual enjoyments.
Rāghava agreed, saying "So be it," and facing the east, he released his arrow;
though Bhārgava was a man of virtuous deeds, that shaft became an insurmountable bar across the path to heaven.
Rāghava, saying "Forgive me," touched the feet of that treasure-house of asceticism;
for when enemies have been swiftly conquered by the powerful, prostration alone leads to glory.
When, having cast off my kingly nature, I was brought by you to the tranquility of my maternal and paternal heritage,
then surely even this punishment of mine was turned into a favor by you, resulting in blameless fruit.
"Excellent! I shall depart; may there be no obstacle for you as you accomplish the task of the gods.
Having spoken these words to the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, who was accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, the seer vanished from sight.
Having entrusted his own Vaiṣṇava abode to Rāghava, who was well-acquainted with the splendor of Viṣṇu,
Bhārgava then departed for his own hermitage, having performed the rite for the granting of imperishable blessings.
When he had gone, the father embraced the victorious Rāma with affection and considered him born once again;
for him, who had been momentarily sorrowful, there came the attainment of joy, like the falling of rain upon a tree scorched by a forest fire.

Then, having spent several nights in a well-prepared and delightful lodging on the road, the king, who was like Śarva himself, entered the city of Ayodhyā; there, the windows were made blue by the eyes of the women, which were intent on beholding Maithilī.
Having experienced his attachment to sense objects and having reached the end of his life's stages,
he was on the verge of extinction like the flame of a lamp at dawn.
Having approached the root of his ear, old age—under the guise of grey hair—spoke as if out of fear of Kaikeyī: "Let the royal fortune depart from Rāma."
That news of the prosperity of Rāma, who was beloved by the citizens,
gladdened each of the townspeople individually, just as a canal irrigates the trees in a garden.
With cruel resolve, Kaikeyī defiled the preparations for his consecration with the king’s tears, hot with grief.
Having been thus consoled by her husband, the fierce woman vomited forth those two boons she had promised,
like the earth, drenched by Indra, disgorging two serpents buried in its chasms.
With one of those two [sons], he caused Rāma to go forth into exile for fourteen years;
with the second, he desired for his son a royal fortune whose sole fruit was widowhood.
Weeping, Rāma first received the earth as it was offered by his father;
afterwards, he joyfully accepted the command, "Go to the forest."
As he wore both the auspicious silken garments and the bark robes,
the people gazed at his countenance with wonder, seeing that its expression remained the same.
Accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, and not violating his vow of truth toward his elder,
he entered the Daṇḍaka forest, which was like the heart of every virtuous man.
The king too, afflicted by separation from her and remembering that the curse was born of his own karma,
considered that purity would be attained merely through the abandonment of the body.
That kingdom, its princes gone abroad and its sovereign deceased,
became a prey for enemies skilled in seeking out vulnerabilities.
Then the subjects, being without a protector, had their lord— who was residing with his maternal kinsmen—
brought back by the hereditary ministers, while they held back their tears.
Having heard of his father's death in such a manner, the son of Kaikeyī turned his back not only on his mother, but on his own sovereignty as well.

Accompanied by his army, he followed after Rāma, shedding tears as he gazed upon the trees where they had dwelt, which were pointed out to him by the inhabitants of the hermitages along with Saumitri.
Having announced his father’s departure to heaven, he invited the Guru, who was staying in the Citrakūṭa forest, with an abundance of wealth that required no further refinement.
For he, upon that first-born son who had not yet accepted the royal glory,
considered himself a "parivettṛ" (one who marries before his elder brother) because of his own appropriation of the earth.
Since it was impossible to remove him because of the command of his father, who had ascended to heaven,
he subsequently requested the two sandals to serve as the presiding deities of the kingdom.
Having been dismissed by his brother with the words "So be it," he did not enter the city at all;
having gone to Nandigrāma, he protected his kingdom as if it were a trust.
Possessing firm devotion to his elder brother and turning away from any thirst for the kingdom,
he performed what was like an act of penance for the sake of purifying his mother’s sin.
Rāma too, together with Vaidehī and his younger brother, lived as a youth observing the ancient vow of the Ikṣvākus; dwelling peacefully in the forest, he sustained himself on forest fare.
Once, having taken refuge under a tree whose shade was rendered motionless by his supernatural power,
he lay for a moment on Sītā’s lap as if from slight fatigue.
It is said that a bird of Indra tore at her breasts with its claws,
as if displaying a spirit of rivalry toward the marks of her lover's enjoyment.
Then, while Sītā stood in the heat protecting the deer meat,
a crow violently attacked it with blows from its wings, beak, and claws.
In that moment, Rama, instructed by Rama, took up the arrow-weapon;
he released himself from it at the cost of the loss of one eye.
But Rāma, suspecting that Bharata might arrive once again due to the proximity of the location,
abandoned the grounds of Citrakūṭa, where the deer were now restless with anxiety.
Dwelling among the families of sages who offered hospitality,
he proceeded toward the southern direction, like the sun moving among the stars of the rainy season.
Following him, the daughter of the lord of Videha shone forth,
even though forbidden by Kaikeyī, like the Goddess Lakṣmī who is ever inclined toward virtuous qualities.
With the fragrant unguent bestowed by Anasūyā, she made the forest—
where bees were rising up from the flowers— into a place of anointed body-scent.
There, a Rākṣasa named Virādha, tawny like the clouds at twilight,
stood blocking the path of Rāma, as an eclipse obstructs the moon.
Between those two, that witherer of the world seized Maithilī,
just as a drought takes away the rain between the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya.
Having crushed him, the two descendants of Kakutstha buried him in the earth,
thinking that he might otherwise defile the land with his foul odor.
Then, at the command of the pot-born sage, Rāma remained at Pañcavaṭī,
maintaining his vow of not eating cooked food, like the Vindhya mountain remaining in its natural state.
There, the younger sister of Rāvaṇa, afflicted by love,
approached Rāghava like a female serpent tormented by the heat of summer approaches a sandalwood tree on Mount Malaya.
In the very presence of Sītā, she chose him after her lineage had been proclaimed;
for the amorous passion of women is excessively intense and knows no proper time.
"I am already married, O young girl; resort to my younger brother," so Rama, whose shoulders were like those of a bull, commanded her as she was filled with lustful desire.
Before she could approach her elder brother, she was again rejected by him;
thus, that beautiful woman once more became dependent on Rāma, like a river flowing between both banks.
The laughter of Maithilī brought that gentle woman, who had been agitated for a moment, to stillness,
just as the rising of the moon brings the ocean tide, which had been motionless in the absence of wind, to rest.
Behold me; you shall receive the fruit of this mockery immediately.
Know that what you have done is an insult offered to a tigress by a deer.
Having spoken thus to Maithilī, who sat upon her husband’s lap out of fear,
she assumed a form resembling that of the one named Śūrpaṇakhā.
Having first heard the female jackal speaking as sweetly as a cuckoo, Lakṣmaṇa subsequently realized that she was actually making an ominous sound and had become transformed.
Then, having quickly entered the leaf-hut with his sword drawn,
he made it terrifying through its disfigurement and redundancy.
With her finger, which bore a curved nail, was as hard as a bamboo joint,
and was shaped like a goad, she threatened them both from the sky.
Having quickly reached Janasthāna, he reported to Khara and the others that such a new humiliation of the Rākṣasas had occurred, initiated by Rāma.
That very head which the Nairṛtas had placed before them, severed from its limbs,
became an ill omen for those who were advancing against Rāma.
Beholding those arrogant men rushing forward with uplifted weapons, Rāghava placed his hope for victory upon his bow and Sītā in the care of Lakṣmaṇa.
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, was alone, while the Yātudhānas were by the thousands; yet however many there were in the battle, he saw himself as being exactly as many as they were.
Then Kakutstha, whose conduct was virtuous, could not endure the calumny uttered by the wicked man,
just as one cannot endure a blemish upon oneself.
He received him with arrows, as well as Khara and Tishiras;
those three then flew forth from his bow simultaneously, as it were.
With those three sharp arrows, purified according to their respective order,
his life-force was drunk up by the birds as they pierced through his body, while his blood was likewise consumed.
When that great host of Rākṣasas had been cut down by Rāma’s arrows,
nothing else was seen to rise up from the headless trunks.
Having fought with Rāma, who was raining down arrows,
that army of the enemies of the gods fell asleep in the shade of the vultures, never to wake again.
Among those Rākṣasas who had been torn apart by the weapons of Rāghava in the presence of Rāvaṇa,
Śūrpaṇakhā alone was able to report the wicked deed.
Due to the humiliation of his sister-in-law and the slaughter of his kinsmen,
the younger brother of Kubera felt as though his ten heads had been struck down by Rāma.
Having deceived the two descendants of Raghu with the form of a deer,
that Rākṣasa carried off Sītā, his attempt thwarted for a moment by the exertion of the Lord of Birds.
Seeking Sītā, the two of them saw the vulture with his wings clipped,
who had become free from his debt to Daśaratha’s affection by means of his life-breaths lingering in his throat.
He informed the two of them that Maithilī had been carried off by Rāvaṇa,
and having revealed his own great feat through his wounds, he remained silent.
For those two, who were grieving over the death of their paternal uncle and the abduction of his daughter by Rāvaṇa,
all further rites ceased after the cremation of the body, as if they had already been performed for their own fathers.
Through the instruction of Kabandha, whose curse had been shaken off by the slaying [of Dūṣaṇa],
Rāma formed a friendship with Hari, who shared his same misfortune.
Having slain Vālin, that hero installed Sugrīva in his long-desired position, just as a substitute is placed in the stead of a verbal root.
Urged by their lord, the monkeys roamed here and there in search of Vaidehī,
like the yearnings of the distressed Rāma.
When his mission was accomplished through the sight of Sampāti,
the son of the Wind crossed the ocean as one free from possessiveness crosses the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
While searching through Laṅkā, which was swarming with ogresses, he beheld Jānaki,
like a great medicinal herb surrounded by poisonous creepers.
The monkey gave her that signet ring from her husband,
which seemed to be met by cool drops of tears of joy.
Having consoled Sītā with the messages of his beloved, he— exultant at the slaying of Akṣa and having momentarily endured the subjugation of his enemy— burnt the city of Laṅkā.
The skillful king showed the jewel of recognition to Rāma,
which was like the very heart of Vaidehī returned to him in bodily form.
With his eyes closed by the touch of the jewel placed upon his heart,
he attained the bliss of his beloved’s embrace, though it was devoid of contact with her breasts.
Having heard the pleasant news, Rāma, eager for reunion with her,
considered the encircling moat of the great ocean surrounding Laṅkā to be as insignificant as a mere ditch.
He set out for the destruction of his enemies, pursued by the monkey hosts moving in close formation not only upon the surface of the earth but also in the sky.
When he had reached the shore of the ocean, Vibhīṣaṇa approached him,
impelled by the very Fortune of the Rākṣasas, who out of affection had directed his mind [toward him].
To him, Rāghava promised the sovereignty over the night-stalkers;
for indeed, policies undertaken at the proper time bear fruit.
He caused a bridge to be built across the salt waters by the monkeys,
appearing like the serpent Śeṣa rising from the netherworld to serve as a couch for the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Having crossed over by that path, he blocked Lanka with tawny monkeys who were like a second golden wall being constructed.
There, a terrible battle broke out between the monkeys and the rākṣasas,
which proclaimed the victory of the descendant of Kakutstha and the descendant of Pulastya as they stretched across the quarters of the sky.
With iron bars shattered by his feet, with mallets crushed by his stones,
with the application of claws sharper than weapons, and with elephants broken by his mountain-like strength.
Then Trijaṭā, declaring that it was an illusion, restored Sītā to life, whose consciousness had been bewildered by the sight of the severed head of Rāma.
"May my lord live!"—with these words she cast off her grief;
yet, having previously believed his end to be certain, she was now ashamed that she herself remained alive.
With his bonds from Meghanāda’s weapon shattered by the swoop of Garuḍa,
the momentary distress of the two sons of Daśaratha became like a dream-event.
Then the descendant of Pulastya pierced Lakṣmaṇa in the chest with a spear;
though he himself remained unhurt, Rāma’s heart was rent asunder with grief.
His pain having been dispelled by the great medicinal herbs brought by Māruti,
he once again made the women of Laṅkā his pupils in the art of lamentation with his arrows.
Like the autumn season does with a cloud, he left nothing remaining of Meghanāda’s roar and his bow, which shone like Indra’s weapon.
Rāvaṇa dispatched his younger brother, who was difficult to defeat in battle, having been forced by great affliction to abandon sleep, to go forth for combat.
At his command, he then struck down many fierce monkeys and entered the city of Laṅkā, taking the lord of the monkeys with him.
Kumbhakarṇa, reduced to a state equal to that of his sister by the lord of monkeys,
obstructed Rāma like a horned mountain whose red arsenic has been shattered by a chisel.
"Because you were awakened at an improper time by your brother, you, who love sleep, have been rendered useless;
as if by the arrows of Rāma, he has been sent into a long sleep."
Other rākṣasas also fell upon the millions of monkeys,
like the dust raised in battle falling upon those who delight in the blood of rākṣasas.
Then the descendant of Pulastya emerged once more from his palace for battle,
resolved that today the world shall be either devoid of Rāvaṇa or devoid of Rāma.
Seeing that Rāma was on foot while the lord of Laṅkā was accompanied by his army,
Purandara dispatched to him a chariot yoked with monkeys.
Holding onto the arm of the celestial charioteer, the descendant of Raghu ascended that victorious chariot, whose banner-cloth was shaken by the winds from the waves of the celestial Ganges.
Mātali released for him that armor of Mahendra,
wherein the weapons of the enemies of the gods attained the feebleness of lotus petals.
The battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa, for which the opportunity for their prowess had long been awaited through mutual sight, finally became one that fulfilled its purpose.
Due to the abundance of his arms, head, and thighs, even though he was but one, that younger brother of Danda appeared unprecedented,
standing like a veritable lineage of mothers.
Rāma highly esteemed his enemy, who had conquered the world-protectors, whose lord was worshipped by his own mouths,
and who had lifted up Mount Kailāsa.
As that [arm] throbbed, foretelling Sītā’s reunion,
Rāvaṇa, his anger intensified, plunged an arrow into his right arm.
The swift arrow discharged by Rāma, having pierced the heart of Rāvaṇa as well,
entered the earth as if to announce the pleasant news to the serpents.
As they struck down each other’s words with words and missiles with missiles,
the fury for mutual victory increased like that of two debaters.
As they struck weapon against weapon with a display of mutual prowess,
the Goddess of Victory hovered between them like the sacrificial altar between two elephants in rut.
Delighted by the exchange of blow for blow, the hosts of arrows released by those two could not tolerate the showers of flowers discharged by the gods and asuras.
Then, for the sake of his enemy, he hurled at him a *śataghnī* weapon studded with iron spikes—
a weapon snatched away from the foe as if it were the deceptive *kūṭaśālmali* tree belonging to Vaivasvata.
Before she could reach the chariot, Rāghava, with crescent-headed arrows as pleasant as plantain stalks, severed both her hope and that of the enemies of the gods.
And that wielder of the bow fixed upon his bow the infallible Brahma-weapon, the medicine for extracting the thorn of grief from his beloved.
That radiant face, divided tenfold in the sky,
appeared like the circle of formidable hoods of a great serpent.
By that [arrow] empowered with a mantra, he caused the row of Rāvaṇa's heads to fall in half a blink of an eye, without the pain of a wound being felt.
The succession of severed necks from the body of the Rakshasa shone like the reflection of the rising sun in water, broken by ripples as it was about to fall.
Even as the heads of that [rākṣasa] fell while the Maruts were looking on, their minds did not fully trust [the sight], for they suspected they might be joined together again.

Then, a fragrant rain of flowers released by the gods fell upon the head of the enemy of Paulastya— whose crest-jewel was now being bound— following the swarms of bees that had abandoned the temples of the world-protectors' elephants due to their heavy rutting ichor.
The charioteer of Hari, having immediately slackened the string of his bow and taken leave of Rāghava— who had thus accomplished the task of the gods—
led upward the chariot yoked to a thousand horses, its flagstaff marked by the name of Rāvaṇa inscribed upon it with the tips of his arrows.
The Lord of the Raghus, having taken his beloved— who had been purified by the fire— and having bestowed the fortune of his enemy upon his dear friend Vibhīṣaṇa,
set out for his city, mounted upon the jewel among celestial chariots won by the strength of his own arms, followed by that son of the Sun along with the son of Sumitrā.

Then, as he who knew the qualities of things was traversing by celestial chariot that region whose quality is sound yet lacks a mind, the one named Hari beheld the ocean, the mine of jewels, and spoke thus to his wife in private: Ragh_13.1 //
O Vaidehī, behold the foamy ocean divided by my bridge,
like the autumn sky, clear and bright with stars, divided by the path of the moon.
When the horse intended for sacrifice was sent down to the netherworld by Kapila,
our ancestors, while digging up the earth for its sake, indeed caused this [tree] to grow.
From him the rays of the sun receive their conception, and here the riches attain their full growth;
he bears the fire that requires no fuel, and by him was produced the light that brings delight.
Assuming various states and pervading the ten directions with his majesty,
his form— like that of Viṣṇu— could not be determined either by its specific nature or by its extent.
Praised by the Primordial Creator seated upon the lotus sprouted from his navel,
that Puruṣa, who is the abode of Yoga appropriate for the end of the age, having withdrawn these worlds, lies transcendent.
Having had their wings clipped and their fragrance taken by the Mountain-Cleaver who split the mountains, hundreds of peaks seek refuge in this [mountain] as their protector;
just as kings threatened by enemies take shelter with a neutral king who excels in righteousness.
For this earth, whose act of being carried upward was undertaken by the Primeval Being from the netherworld (rasātala),
the clear waters swollen during the dissolution became a veil for his face for a mere moment.
Naturally bold in offering his face [to the sea], he himself is skilled in bestowing the lower lip of the waves;
devoted exclusively to his own wife, he drinks from the rivers and causes them to drink him.
Carrying along living beings with the water from the mouths of rivers, these timi fish, closing their wide-open mouths,
discharge streams of water upward through the apertures in their heads.
Behold the sea foam split in two by the suddenly leaping crocodiles;
O Karṇa, as it glides across their temples, it momentarily becomes a fly-whisk for them.
The serpents, which had extended themselves toward the coastal breeze and were indistinguishable from the surging of great waves,
were revealed by the jewels upon their hoods, whose brilliance was intensified by contact with the rays of the sun.
This multitude of conchs, having been cast upon the coral trees by the force of a thousand waves,
somehow manages to escape with difficulty as their openings are impaled upon the upward-pointing shoots.
Merely by its setting out to drink the waters,
this ocean appears as if it were once again being churned by a cloud whirling with the force of a whirlpool, as if by a mountain.
From afar, the slender shore of the salt-water ocean, dark with rows of groves of *tamāla* and *tālī* trees, appears like a streak of tarnish upon a wheel of iron.
O long-eyed one, the sea breeze, laden with the pollen of *ketaka* flowers, honors your face;
it seems to know that I am incapable of waiting for the time of adornment, as my thirst is fixed upon your bimba-like lips.

By the speed of our celestial chariot, we have reached in a mere moment the shore of the ocean, where heaps of pearls are scattered from oyster shells split open on the sands, and where rows of betel-nut trees are bent down by their fruit.
"Wait a moment, O lady with thighs like a young elephant's trunk, you who glance like a deer at the path; cast your gaze behind you!
This earth, together with its forests, seems to be rushing forth from the receding ocean."
In some places it moves along the path of the gods, in some places that of the clouds, and in others that of those falling;
behold how this celestial chariot proceeds according to the specific inclination of my mind.
This wind from the sky, scented by the ichor of Mahendra’s elephant and cooled by contact with the waves of the triple-pathed river (the Gaṅgā),
sips the drops of perspiration upon your face arising from the vigor of midday.
O fierce one, touched by you as you dangle your hand out of curiosity from the window,
that cloud, with its flashing circles of lightning, seems to don a second ornament.
Considering Janasthāna to be free from obstacles, these bark-clad sages have begun constructing new huts and occupy their respective long-abandoned hermitage circles as before.
This is that very spot where, while searching for you, I beheld a single anklet fallen upon the ground;
it seemed as though it had become silent out of grief from the separation from your lotus-like foot.

O timid one, these creepers, out of compassion, have shown me by means of their branches with drooping shoots the very path along which you were carried away by the *rākṣasa*, though they themselves were unable to speak.
And the does, indifferent to the tips of the *darbha* grass, alerted me— who was ignorant of your whereabouts—
by directing their eyes, with rows of lashes upturned, toward the southern quarter.
Before this Mount Mālyavat, there appears a peak that reaches to the sky,
from which fresh clouds have been released by me, along with tears shed during our separation from you.
In that place, the fragrance of ponds struck by rain showers, the kadamba flower with its filaments half-emerged,
and the soft cries of peacocks became unbearable to me when I was without you.
O timid one, as I recalled our previous experiences, I somehow endured the thundering of the clouds echoing through the caves while you were held in my embrace, trembling with fear.

There, your beauty— whose eyes were reddened by the smoke of the wedding ceremony— was imitated by young *kandala* shoots whose sheaths had split open, which, through contact with the moisture of the earth drenched by the downpours, seemed to consume me.
My sight, having descended from afar, seems to drink out of exhaustion these waters of the Pampā, which are embraced by groves of cane thickets at their edges and where cranes float about in view.
O beloved, I gazed longingly from afar upon pairs of cakravāka birds that were inseparable, having transferred the filaments of their lotuses to one another.
Desiring to embrace this slender ashoka creeper, which was bent low by its clusters of blossoms as lovely as breasts,
under the impression that it was you, I was stopped with tears by the son of Sumitrā.
Hearing the sound of golden bells hanging from these celestial chariots,
the rows of cranes on the Godāvarī seem to rise up and fly toward you through the sky as if to welcome you.

O you of slender waist, this Pañcavaṭī— where young mango trees were nurtured by water drawn from jars, and where the black antelopes lift their heads to gaze upon it— delights my mind now that I see it after so long.
Here, along the Godāvarī, having returned from the hunt with my fatigue relieved by the breeze from the waves,
I remember sleeping in the reed-huts with my head resting in your lap in secret.

This is the earthly dwelling-place of that sage, who, by a mere contraction of his eyebrows, caused Nahuṣa to fall from the stations of Indra; it serves as the means for the purification of his turbid waters.

Having smelled the fragrance of the sacrificial oblation from that king of irreproachable fame— whose smoke rising from the three sacred fires has ascended to the path of the celestial chariots— my soul, freed from all dust, experiences a sense of lightness.

O proud lady, this bathing pool named Pañcāpsaras belonging to the sage Śātakarṇi shines with its surrounding forest; from afar, it appears like the orb of the moon visible through a gap in the clouds.
In former times, that sage— who subsisted on nothing more than sprouts of darbha grass while wandering with the deer— was reportedly lured by Maghavan,
fearing his meditative absorption, into the snare of the youthful charms of five celestial nymphs.
The sound of the drums accompanying the continuous music of him who dwells in that hidden palace,
reaching into the sky, momentarily makes the moon-chambers of the Puṣpaka chariot resonant with echoes.
Among those four blazing consumers of oblations, there is another ascetic who performs penance with the sun scorching his forehead; he is Sutīkṣṇa by name, self-restrained in his conduct.

The playful gestures of the celestial nymphs— glances cast with smiles and girdles partially revealed under some pretext— were not enough to distract him, for he had already conceived the suspicion that he was Indra.
With his right arm raised, he extends this left hand toward me for my salutation— a hand that holds a rosary of seeds, scratches the deer, and trims the tips of the kusha grass.
Because of his silence, he accepted my salutation with a slight nod of his head;
then, casting his gaze free from the obstruction of the celestial chariot, he fixed it once more upon the thousand-rayed sun.
There lies that purifying hermitage of the one named Śarabhaṅga, who was devoted to the sacred fires and sought refuge therein;
having long satisfied the fire with fuel-sticks, he finally offered even his own body, purified by mantras, as an oblation.
Now, in these trees— which dispel the fatigue of travelers with their shade and promise abundant fruit— the honor of hospitality toward guests rests, as if in well-bred sons.

O lady of graceful limbs, this Citrakūṭa mountain— its cave mouths resounding with the roar of waterfalls and its peaks covered in the mud of clouds clinging to their summits— binds my gaze like a proud bull with a hump.
This river Mandākinī, with its clear and tranquil current, appearing slender due to its great distance,
shines near the foot of the mountain like a string of pearls resting upon the neck of the Earth.
This well-grown tamāla tree on the mountain slope, whose fragrant sprouts I gathered,
has now adorned my cheek— with its sprout placed upon my ear— as with a decorative streak of black aloe-wood paste.

This forest, the means for practicing asceticism belonging to Atri, has manifested a most exalted power; it subdues beings through discipline rather than through the fear of punishment, and its trees bear fruit without the appearance of flowers.

There, for the sake of the ablution of those whose wealth is their asceticism, Anasūyā caused the triple-streamed Ganges— the garland upon the crest of the Three-Eyed God— to flow forth, its golden lotuses being gathered by the hands of the Seven Sages.
These trees, situated in the midst of altars occupied by sages absorbed in meditation through the *vīrāsana* posture,
shine as if they themselves have ascended to the heights of yoga, owing to their immobility in the windless air.
This very banyan tree, known as Śyāma, which you previously entreated,
now shines forth in fruit like a heap of emeralds interspersed with rubies.
In one place, the lunar radiance, freed from darkness, was like a crystal staff;
elsewhere, it was like a garland of white lotuses with blue water-lilies interspersed within its intervals.
In one place, it was as if possessed by the presence of *kādamba* geese, dear to the birds of Lake Mānasa;
in another, it was a white streak of autumn clouds, like a decorative pattern of sandalwood paste upon the earth.
In some places the moonlight was made variegated by shadows merged with the darkness;
elsewhere it was as white as an autumnal streak of cloud through which patches of sky were faintly visible.
And in some places, O lady of faultless limbs, the body of the Lord, with ashes for its unguent, shines like one adorned by black serpents;
behold how the Ganges, with its divided current, gleams as it is joined by the waves of the Yamunā.
The skin was like a bright night divided by darkness, like a jasmine garland with a wreath of blue lotuses,
like the hide of a black antelope upon Śiva’s neck, or like the ash of the Enemy of Smara [Śiva] by the luster of his throat.
With the luster of her drawn sword, she was like a streak of autumn clouds visible through half-opened shutters;
with the columns of smoke from black aloe incense rising from the windows, the palace floor appeared as if freshly plastered with lime.
It was like a mass of snow-stones from the Himalayas beautified by a slab of natural collyrium,
or like a row of Kadamba birds following a flight of geese that had become the object of the minds of winged creatures.
Due to its contact with the luster of lapis lazuli, which is like an exceedingly pure crystal,
the Gaṅgā, joined by the daughter of the Sun, blossoms forth as a magnificent streak of supreme beauty, like a girdle of gems.

It is said that at the confluence of the two wives of the ocean, those whose souls are purified by bathing here do not undergo further bondage to a body, even without the realization of ultimate truth.
This is that city of the lord of the Niṣādas, where Sumantra wept upon binding my matted locks after laying aside his crest-jewel, crying out, "O Kaikeyī, your desires have borne fruit!"

The poets declare that the Brahma-lake, whose waters possess the pollen of golden lotuses enjoyed by the women of the Yakṣas, is the cause of her [the Ganges], just as the unmanifest is said to be the cause of the intellect.
The waters of that river, which flows past the capital Ayodhyā where sacrificial posts are driven into its banks,
have been rendered exceedingly holy by the Ikṣvākus who descended into them after performing the purificatory baths of horse-sacrifices.
She, who was accustomed to the comfort of sandy laps and nurtured with abundant waters,
makes my mind regard her as the common nurse of the people of Uttarakosala.
This very Sarayū, separated from that venerable king as if she were my own mother,
seems to embrace me with her hands of waves as I dwell afar, cooled by the winter breezes.
Since a dust raised from the earth rises ahead, reddish-brown like the twilight of one who has turned away from passion,
I suspect that Bharata, having received news from Hanumān, has come out to meet me with his army.
Surely that virtuous one will restore his unblemished sovereignty to him who has fulfilled his vow,
just as Lakṣmaṇa restored you to me after returning from battle having slain Khara and the others.
Placing his preceptor at the head, with his army stationed behind him,
Bharata approaches me on foot, clad in bark garments, accompanied by aged ministers, with the respectful offering in his hand.
Though young, he has not enjoyed the royal fortune bestowed by his father for my sake while it rested upon his lap;
for all these years, he has been as if practicing a severe vow as sharp as a sword’s edge together with her.
When the son of Daśaratha had spoken thus, the celestial chariot, having understood his wish through its presiding deity,
descended from the path of the stars while being gazed upon with wonder by the subjects following Bharata.
Therefore, with his hand supported by the Lord of the Monkeys, who was skilled in service and guided by Vibhīṣaṇa walking before him,
Rāma descended from the vehicle onto the ground nearby by way of a path paved with variegated crystal.

Having bowed with devotion to his brother Bharata—the preceptor of the Ikṣvāku lineage—at the conclusion of the reception of the guest-offering, he, with tears in his eyes, embraced him and kissed him on the head; for Bharata’s devotion had set aside the great royal consecration that was due to his father.

And he favored with auspicious glances those aged ministers who were bowing down— their countenances distorted by the growth of their beards, appearing like *plakṣa* trees matted with new shoots— and addressed them with words made sweet by inquiries after their welfare.

"This lord of bears and monkeys is my kinsman born of an ignoble womb; this son of Pulastya is the one who strikes first in battles"—when the joy of the Raghus had spoken thus with respect, Bharata bypassed Lakṣmaṇa and paid homage to both of them.

Thereafter, he was embraced by the son of Sumitrā; and having raised him up, the latter closely clasped him with his chest—rough from the wounds of Indrajit’s weapons—as if causing pain to the middle of his arms, while he stood with his head bowed low.
Then, by the command of Rāma, the commanders of the monkey hosts assumed human forms and mounted lordly elephants;
as those elephants exuded streams of ichor in many ways, they experienced the pleasure of ascending mountains.
The lord of the night-stalkers, accompanied by his followers and instructed by the descendant of Daśaratha,
mounted chariots whose artificial splendor and craftsmanship were not equaled even by those constructed through the power of illusion.
Then the Lord of the Raghus, together with his younger brother, ascended a celestial chariot that moved at will and was adorned with shimmering banners;
he appeared like the moon, visible in conjunction with Mercury and Jupiter, amidst a mass of clouds with flickering lightning.

There, Bharata paid homage to the steadfast Sītā, who had been rescued by Rāma from the perils of the Ten-necked one, just as the earth is restored by Īśvara after the dissolution of the worlds, or as the radiance of the moon is recovered from a thick mass of clouds at the end of the rainy season.
The pair of feet of Janaka’s daughter, whose firm vow was the refusal of the prostrations of the Lord of Laṅkā,
and the head of that virtuous man, matted with hair in obedience to his elder brother— both, having come together, became mutually sanctifying.
Having traveled half a *krośa* with the Puṣpaka chariot, which moved with steady speed as the people preceded him,
the noble descendant of Kakutstha took up residence in the magnificent grove of Sāketa, where Śatrughna had prepared a temporary palace.

"Arise, child! Surely those two sons of Daśaratha, along with their younger brother, have simultaneously entered the tenth stage [of life]; for their mothers, not seeing them, are like two creepers on a tree-trunk severed at the base."

Both of them, having slain their enemies, bowed down to both [the parents] in due order; though they were resplendent with valor, they were not clearly seen because of their blindness from weeping, but were recognized by the experience of the pleasure of touching their sons.
The cool, refreshing tears born of joy broke through their warm tears born of grief,
like the descent of the melting snow from the Himalayas into the hot waters of the Gaṅgā and Sarayū.
Gently touching the fresh scars on their bodies left by the weapons of the Nairṛtas,
they— though longing for the title of "mother of a hero," which is so desired by women of the warrior caste— did not desire it for themselves.
Bringing distress to her husband, she who was devoid of auspicious marks announced her own name, "Sītā," and as the bride,
she paid homage to the two queens of her father-in-law, who were established in heaven, with a distinction in devotion.

"Arise, child! Surely this husband of yours, along with his younger brother, has crossed over a great hardship through your very own pure conduct. Thus they spoke pleasant words that were not false to her who was worthy of such affection.
Then the elder ministers performed the consecration of the banner of Raghu’s lineage, which had already been commenced by the tears of joy of his two mothers,
with waters brought from sacred fords in golden jars.
Having traversed rivers, oceans, and lakes, the waters brought by the lord of monkeys and the rākṣasa fell upon the head of that victorious one,
like waters originating from clouds falling upon the Vindhya mountains.
He who was already exceedingly worthy of being beheld even in the guise and conduct of an ascetic became, moreover,
the object of superfluous praise through the splendor of his attire as a lord of kings.
Accompanied by his army led by the hereditary ministers Rakṣa and Hari, and gladdening the multitude of citizens with the sound of musical instruments,
he entered the ancestral capital, which was adorned with triumphal arches and showered with parched grain falling from the palaces.
Mounted upon his chariot, with his tail-feather fan being gently waved by the son of Sumitrā along with his younger brother,
and with the royal parasol held over him by Bharata, he appeared like the personified embodiment of the four means of statecraft in full expansion.
The column of black aloe-wood smoke from the palace, dispersed before her by the force of the wind,
appeared like her own braid released by the scion of Raghu upon his return from the forest.

The women of Sāketa, visible from the windows of the palace, paid homage with joined palms to the wife of the Raghu hero, who was seated in a palanquin and adorned with beautiful attire prepared by her mother-in-law.
Wearing her eternal body-unguent and the girdle of Anasūyā, which radiated a shimmering halo,
she shone with such purity that she appeared as if she had been shown back to her own city by her husband after having entered the fire.
Having bestowed upon his friends houses filled with all luxuries, Rāma, that treasury of affection,
entered the sacrificial hall of his father— who now remained as a mere painting— while shedding tears.
With palms joined in reverence, Bharata said, "O Mother, that our guru did not fall from the fruit of heaven due to his truthfulness—
that very merit of yours, when reflected upon, took away the shame of Bharata's mother."
And so he attended upon Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, and the others with artificial displays;
they, whose supernatural powers arise from mere thought, were filled with wonder in their minds as they observed him.

Placing at their head those divine sages who had come to congratulate him, he heard from them an account of the slain enemy’s origin and history, which served to increase his own sense of pride in his own prowess.

When those rich in asceticism had departed, Rama dismissed the lords of the Rakshasas and monkeys— who, out of comfort, were unaware that half a month had passed— having personally offered them the highest honors with his own hands.
That celestial chariot, the Puṣpaka, which was easily obtained through meditation on the Self, was seized from the enemy of the gods along with his life;
it was then deemed fit to serve as a flower for the sky once more, to be borne by the Lord of Kailāsa.

Having thus completed his forest exile by the command of his father and having obtained the kingdom, Rāma maintained an equal disposition toward virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and likewise conducted himself with impartiality toward his younger brothers.
Out of affection for all his mothers, he behaved toward them without distinction,
just as the leader of armies, the six-faced god, did toward the Kṛttikās when they had not yet drunk from his breasts.

By him, who was turned away from greed, the world became wealthy; by him, who destroyed the fear of obstacles, it became possessed of ritual action; by him, its leader, it had a father; and by him alone, the dispeller of grief, it had a son.
Having attended to the affairs of the citizens at the proper time, he took his pleasure with the daughter of the Lord of Videha;
she, as it were, having assumed that beautiful form out of eagerness for enjoyment, presented herself to him like the Goddess Lakṣmī.
As those two enjoyed the objects of their senses within their variegated palaces according to their desires,
even the sufferings they had endured in the Daṇḍaka forests became pleasures when reflected upon.
Then Sītā, with her face pale as a reed and her eyes exceedingly moist, brought joy to her husband through her longing, which was expressed not by words but by her very appearance.
Lifting that slender-limbed woman onto his lap— her breasts now marked by the change of color— he,
full of confidence, privately asked the bashful lady about her desire.

She desired once more to go to the ascetic groves on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, which abound in kuśa grass and where the daughters of hermit-ascetics are occupied with harmless tasks such as gathering wild rice for offerings.
Having given his promise to her, that hero of the Raghus, followed by his attendants,
ascended a cloud-licking palace, desiring to behold the joyful city of Ayodhyā.
Beholding the prosperous marketplace, the royal highway, the Sarayū being entered by boats,
and the groves on the outskirts of the city inhabited by playful citizens, he took his delight.

That leader of those who speak, whose conduct was pure, whose arms were as long as the king of serpents, and who had conquered his enemies, asked the spy for news concerning his own life, saying, "May it be well with you."
Questioned with persistence, he said everything: "O god among men, the citizens praise all your deeds, except for the taking as a wife of the queen who had dwelt in the abode of a Rakshasa."
Struck thus by the heavy reproach concerning his wife— a reversal of his fame— the heart of the Lord of Vaidehī, like heated iron struck by an iron hammer, burst asunder.
"Should I ignore the talk of self-reproach, or should I abandon my blameless wife?"—
because of his distress in choosing between these two sides, his mental state was as unsteady as a swing.
Having resolved that there was no other way to remove it, he desired to wipe it away by abandoning his wife—
even from his own body, let alone from the objects of the senses— for among those whose wealth is fame, fame is indeed the most precious thing.

Having assembled his younger brothers—whose vigor was diminished and whose joy was lost upon witnessing that transformation—he recounted to them the public scandal concerning himself, and spoke these words to them once more: Ragh_14.36.

Behold what kind of stain has come upon this lineage of royal seers born of the Sun— upon me, who am pure in virtuous conduct— from me, like a blemish upon a mirror from a gust of wind laden with clouds.
I was unable to endure that former censure spreading among the citizens— like a drop of oil upon the waves of water— as the lord of elephants cannot withstand a tethering post.
To dispel that [sorrow], he remains indifferent even when the attainment of the fruit has presented itself;
he will sooner abandon the daughter of Videha than the earth girt by the ocean, as if by his father’s command.
I know her to be sinless; however, public scandal is considered by me to be powerful.
For the shadow of the earth has been attributed as a blemish upon the pure moon by the people.
My exertion, ending with the slaughter of the Rākṣasa, was not in vain, for it was for the sake of avenging my enmity.
Does a two-tongued serpent, impatient and longing for blood, bite one who merely touches him with his foot?
Therefore, this departure of mine should not be forbidden by you whose hearts are moist with compassion,
if you desire that I preserve your lives for long, having extracted the thorns of reproach.
When the Lord had spoken thus, harboring an exceedingly harsh resolve regarding the daughter of Janaka,
there was no one among his brothers capable of either restraining him or persuading him to change his mind.
Having looked at Lakṣmaṇa, he whose birth preceded that of Lakṣmaṇa, whose fame is sung throughout the three worlds,
and who speaks according to the truth, addressed him as "O gentle one" and gave him a separate command while he stood ready to receive his orders.
"O gentle one," said he who speaks the truth, "this pregnant woman, manifesting her longing, yearns for the penance groves;
take her to the abode of Vālmīki and leave her there."

Having heard that his mother had been struck by the descendant of Bhṛgu at his father’s command as if she were an enemy, he accepted that instruction from his elder brother; for the command of elders is not to be questioned.

Then, having helped the daughter of Videha ascend the chariot whose reins Sumantra had taken up, and which was drawn by horses that were unflinching and yoked to their proper task, he set out upon a path made pleasant by agreeable sounds.
As she was being led through beautiful places, she rejoiced, thinking, "My beloved is doing what is dear to me";
she did not realize that he had ceased to be a wish-fulfilling tree and had become for her a sword-leafed tree.
That Lakṣmaṇa concealed [the truth] from her on the road was signaled by his right eye throbbing—
an omen that foretold the heavy sorrow she was to endure, in which the sight of her beloved would be utterly lost.
Her lotus-like face instantly withered from the despair brought on by those ill omens;
yet, through her internal senses, she prayed that all might be well with the king and his younger brothers.
At his preceptor’s command, the son of Sumitrā was about to abandon his virtuous wife in the forest when he was, as it were,
stopped by the daughter of Jahnu appearing before him with her hands of uplifted waves.
Having disembarked his sister-in-law from the chariot whose horses had been restrained by the driver onto the sandy bank, he,
true to his promise, crossed the Gaṅgā in a special boat brought by the Niṣādas, as one keeps his covenant.
Then, having somehow steadied his speech, the son of Sumitrā, with his throat choked with suppressed tears,
vomited forth the king’s command like a portentous cloud disgorging a shower of stones.
Then, violently shaken by the wind of her affliction, with her ornaments falling like scattered blossoms,
Sītā suddenly collapsed to the earth, which had been her source of being when she first received her own form, like a creeper.
