"How could your husband, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage and of noble conduct, suddenly abandon you?"—thinking thus, the Earth, as if filled with doubt, did not yet grant her entrance. Her mother likewise withheld her from entering.
With her consciousness lost, she did not perceive her suffering; but when her life-breath returned, she was tormented within.
For her, the awakening brought about by the efforts of Sumitrā’s son was more painful than the state of unconsciousness.
The noble lady did not speak a word of reproach against her husband, even though he was intent on rejecting her;
instead, she repeatedly censured herself as an evildoer, the seed of enduring sorrow.

Having comforted that virtuous woman and told her the way to Valmiki’s hermitage, the younger brother of Rama bowed low and said, "O Queen, forgive the harshness of my words, which arose from my obedience to my master's command."

Raising Sītā up, he spoke these words: "I am pleased with you, gentle one; may you live for a long time, since you are thus dependent upon your brother, just as Viṣṇu was once dependent upon his elder brother, the son of Virocana."
Convey my salutations in due order to all your mother-in-laws,
informing them that my son’s consecration for procreation is currently taking place and that he holds them in his heart.

"You must say to that king in my name: 'Since you abandoned me—even though I was proven pure before the fire—merely upon hearing public rumor, how can that be worthy of your learning or your lineage? (Raghuvamśa 14.61)
Or rather, this lack of self-restraint on my part toward you, who possess such a virtuous mind, should not be suspected;
it is simply the irresistible thunderclap of the ripening of my own sins from previous births.
Having previously cast aside the Fortune that stood before you, you have entered the forest along with me;
yet, having regained her former abode, she will not endure my dwelling in your palace out of extreme resentment.
Having become a refuge for these ascetic women whose husbands have been ravished by night-stalkers through your grace,
how could I seek another for protection while you are shining forth?
Or rather, what use would I have for indifference toward this wretched life, which is destined for ultimate separation and futility,
were it not for the obstacle of your own splendor residing within me that must be protected?
With my gaze fixed upon the sun, I shall strive to practice asceticism directed toward the heavens,
so that even in another birth you alone may be my husband, and there be no separation from you.
That which consists in the king’s protection of the castes and stages of life is the very dharma ordained by Manu;
therefore, even though I have been exiled, I must be regarded by you as equal to any other ascetic.
Having accepted her words with "So be it," once the younger brother of Rāma had passed from the range of her vision, she,
overwhelmed by the excessive weight of her calamity, wailed aloud like a distressed osprey.
The peacocks ceased their dancing, the trees shed their flowers, and the does abandoned the darbha grass they had gathered;
for when she entered that state of shared sorrow, even the forest itself wept excessively.
The sage Kavi, who had gone out to gather kusha grass and fuel, followed the sound of her weeping and approached her;
his grief, arising from the sight of a bird pierced by a hunter, took the form of a verse.
Wiping away that tear which obscured her eyes, Sītā ceased her lamentation and paid homage;
the sage, perceiving the signs of her pregnancy longing, granted her the blessing of a noble son and spoke thus.
I know that you were abandoned by your husband, who was agitated by false accusations, through his own lack of discernment;
therefore, do not be distressed, O Vaidehī, for you have reached your father’s home, situated in another region.
Although he has uprooted the thorn of the three worlds, although he is true to his promise, and although he is free from boastfulness,
I nevertheless feel indignation toward Bharata’s elder brother for this sudden manifestation of malice against you.
Your father-in-law is Indukīrti, my friend; your father is the one who brings about the cessation of existence for the virtuous;
and you stand at the forefront of those for whom their husband is a deity—what is there that does not entitle you to my compassion?
Dwell here in this penance grove, free from fear, where the minds of beings have been disciplined through association with ascetics;
for you, whose offspring shall be born sinless, there shall arise from here the rites consisting of the sacraments for your child.
Having plunged into that river which dispels darkness and whose banks are not empty of hermitages,
you will attain serenity of mind through the offerings made upon its sandy shores.
Bringing seasonal flowers and fruits, as well as seeds for the sacrificial animals that grow without cultivation,
the daughters of sages, eloquent in speech, will dispel your fresh affliction.
Nourishing the young trees of the hermitage with water-jars suited to your own strength,
you will undoubtedly experience the joy of a nursing mother before the birth of your son.
Taking her, who expressed her gratitude for his favor, Vālmīki— his heart softened with compassion—
led her to his own peaceful hermitage, where deer roamed at evening and rested upon the sides of the sacrificial altars.
And he entrusted her, distressed with grief, to those female ascetics who were delighted by her arrival—
her whose essence had been consumed by her fathers, like the final digit of the moon at the new moon being absorbed by the medicinal herbs.
At the close of day, they assigned her a hut for her residence, where a lamp fed with ingudi oil was lit within and a bed of pure deerskins was spread, following the ritual of hospitality.
There, devoted to her consecration and dwelling while performing worship according to the rules for guests,
she— clad in bark garments from the forest— sustained her husband’s body for the sake of the continuity of their progeny.
"Is the Lord now free from anxiety, even though he is the slayer of Śakra’s conqueror?
Thus did he report to his elder brother that the command had been executed, concluding with Sītā’s lamentations.
Rāma suddenly became bathed in tears, like the moon of the month of Sahasya shrouded in a shower of frost;
yet, though he had banished the daughter of the King of Videha from his home out of fear of public scandal, she was never cast from his heart.

Restraining his grief by himself, the wise king— ever vigilant in overseeing the duties of the social orders and stages of life, his mind free from passion— ruled the prosperous kingdom whose enjoyments were shared with his brothers.
For the king, who had abandoned that virtuous and sole wife out of fear of public censure,
the Goddess of Fortune shone as if she were alone, dwelling upon his chest without the pleasure of physical contact, as if he were now free from a rival wife.
Because the enemy of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa did not marry another woman after abandoning Sītā, but instead performed sacrifices with an image of her as his companion, she was able,
through that news reaching the range of her hearing, to somehow endure the otherwise irresistible pain of her husband's abandonment.
Having abandoned Sītā,
that protector of the earth enjoyed only the earth itself, which has the ocean as its girdle.
When their sacrifices were plundered by Lavaṇa,
the sages dwelling on the Yamunā, seeking refuge, approached Tāmiśra, who was capable of granting protection.
Beholding Rāma, they did not unleash their own splendor;
for those whose weapons are curses expend their ascetic power only when there is no possibility of protection.
The descendant of Kakutstha promised them the removal of obstacles;
for the protection of dharma alone is the purpose of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow on this earth.
Those enemies of the gods told Rāma the means for his destruction:
"Lavaṇa is difficult to conquer; let him be entreated by you when he is without his trident."
Then Rāghava commanded Śatrughna for their protection,
as if making his name true to its meaning by the suppression of his enemies.
For he was the one supreme scorcher of enemies among the Raghus,
capable of setting aside even a general rule as if it were an exception.
Then the son of Daśaratha, the chariot-warrior, having been addressed with blessings by his elder brother,
proceeded along the path, beholding fragrant and fearless trees in full bloom.
Following the command of Rāma, the army followed him for the sake of his success,
just as the prefix *adhi* follows a verbal root for the sake of its specific meaning.
Following the path pointed out by the sages, that best of ascetics shone like the sun accompanied by the Vālakhilyas upon the back of a chariot.
By the power of his path, he had one dwelling place in the ascetic grove of Vālmīki, where the deer were eager for the sound of the chariot.
The sage honored the prince, whose mount was exhausted,
with special marks of hospitality perfected by the power of his asceticism.
On that very night, his pregnant wife Prājāvatī gave birth to two sons, just as the earth brings forth both the treasury and the army.
Having heard news of his brother’s lineage, the son of Sumitrā was filled with joy;
at dawn, having addressed the sage with palms joined in reverence, he departed with his chariot yoked.
And he, the son born from the womb of Kumbhīnasī, reached Madhūpaghna,
having arrived with a multitude of creatures like a tribute brought from the forest.
Smoke-grey and reeking with the stench of fat, with hair tawny like a flame,
he was surrounded by a host of flesh-eaters, like a funeral pyre come to life.
Having reached Lavaṇa, whose cattle had been driven away, the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa besieged him;
for victory belongs to those who strike at the vulnerable when facing their foe.
"Observing that the food for my belly today is not quite sufficient,
by good fortune you have been provided to me by the Creator, as if by a providential act."
Having thus threatened Śatrughna with the intent to kill him, the rākṣasa uprooted him like a tall tree or a clump of musta grass.
Cut to pieces in mid-air by the sharp arrows of Saumitri,
the tree sent forth by the Nairṛta did not even reach his body with its flower-dust.
Upon the destruction of that tree, the rākṣasa hurled a great boulder at him,
which stood apart like the very fist of Kṛtānta.
Struck by Śatrughna with the Aindra weapon,
he was reduced to the state of a subtle atom, even more minute than grains of sand.
Raising his right arm, the Rakshasa rushed toward him like a mountain struck by a wind-driven thunderclap.
Falling with his heart pierced by that black-feathered arrow,
the enemy caused the earth to tremble and robbed the dwellers of the hermitage of their peace.
Flocks of birds fell upon the slain demon,
while divine showers of flowers descended upon the head of his adversary.
Having slain Lavaṇa, that hero then considered himself the true uterine brother of his immensely powerful sibling, who had distinguished himself by the slaying of Indrajit.
As he was being praised by the ascetics who had achieved their goals,
his head— bowed with modesty yet exalted by valor— shone resplendently.
Along the bank of the Kālindī, he who was adorned by his manly prowess,
who was free from attachment to worldly objects, and who possessed a sweet form, built the city of Mathurā.
It shone with the splendors of its citizens, which were radiant with excellent governance,
as if it had been established there after the overflow of heaven itself had been vomited forth.
There, standing upon the palace and beholding the Yamunā filled with ruddy geese,
he rejoiced as if gazing upon a golden braid of hair from the earth.
Then the counselor of Daśaratha and Janaka,
acting out of affection for both, performed the purificatory rites for the two sons of Maithilī according to the prescribed rules.
The poet, because their fetal impurities had been wiped away by Kuśa and Lava, indeed gave them those very names, Kuśa and Lava.
Having taught them the Veda along with its auxiliary branches, once they had somewhat outgrown childhood,
he caused them to sing his own composition, the first path blazed by poets.
Singing the sweet life-story of Rāma before their mother,
the two sons somewhat alleviated the pain of separation from him.
The other three descendants of Raghu as well, possessing the brilliance of the three sacred fires,
each had two sons through their wives who were blessed with husbands.
Longing for his elder brother, he appointed Śatrughna over Śatrughātin and Bahuśruta, and he entrusted Mathurā and Vidīśā to his two sons.
Thinking, "Let there be no further waste of Vālmīki’s ascetic power," he passed by the hermitage where the deer remained motionless at the singing of Maithilī’s sons.
The self-controlled king entered Ayodhyā, which was beautified by the cleaning of its streets,
and was gazed upon with great reverence by the citizens because of his slaying of Lavaṇa.
In the midst of the assembly hall, he beheld Rāma, attended by the members of the court,
who had become the peerless lord of the earth due to his abandonment of Sītā.
The elder brother welcomed the prostrate slayer of Lavana,
as delighted as Indra was upon the killing of Kālanemi when facing the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Being questioned, he reported news from all sides to the king, but not concerning his lineage,
in accordance with the command of the primordial Kavi, who intended to restore it in due time.
Then a brahmin from the countryside, having set down at the king’s gate his infant son who had not yet reached youth and was lying upon his lap, wailed aloud.
O Earth, you are to be pitied, you who, having fallen from Daśaratha and come into the hands of Rāma, have gone from misery to even greater misery.
Having heard the cause of his grief, the protector Rāghava was ashamed;
for untimely death had not yet touched the domain of the Ikṣvākus.
Having comforted the grieving brahmin with the words "Endure for a moment," he called to mind the vehicle of Kubera, desiring to conquer the son of Vivasvat.
Having taken up his weapon and ascended that [chariot], that scion of Raghu stood firm;
then, in a hidden form, Sarasvatī spoke before him.
"O King, some misconduct is occurring among your subjects;
seek it out and suppress it, and thereby you shall have fulfilled your duty."
Thus, according to the words of the authoritative sage, Rāma, intending to remove the transformation of his complexion,
flew through the air on a winged chariot whose banner remained motionless despite his speed.
Then the descendant of Ikṣvāku beheld a certain man performing ascetic penance with his face turned downward, hanging from the branch of a tree, his eyes copper-red from the smoke.
When questioned by the king regarding his name and lineage, that smoke-inhaling man declared himself to be a Śūdra named Śambuka, seeking the status of a god.
Having determined that he was subject to decapitation because his penance was unauthorized for commoners and thus brought misfortune upon them, the Restrainer took up his weapon.
He drew that face from the throat-pipe like a lotus whose filaments are withered by frost,
its beard struck by particles of light.
The Śūdra Kṛtaṇḍa, though personally commanded by the king,
attained the state of the virtuous through difficult penance that did not transgress his own path.
Raghu’s son, too, was united with Agastya, who had revealed his path,
as the autumn season is joined with the moon of great splendor.
The pot-born sage gave him an ornament of divine quality,
which had been presented by the ocean as if it were the ransom for his own release when he was swallowed.
Holding him with an arm that was no longer occupied with the neck of Maithilī, Rāma turned back; meanwhile, the son of the twice-born had already lost his life.
When his son arrived, the brahmin dispelled with praise the reproach he had previously voiced against him— a reproach that would have brought even Yama, the son of Vivasvat, to his rescue.
The lords of the Rakshasas and Kinnaras showered him with gifts for the sacrifice, just as clouds rain upon the grain with water after the horses have been released.
And great seers invited from all directions came to him,
having abandoned not only their terrestrial abodes but even those composed of light.
With them stationed at its outskirts, Ayodhyā, with its four gates as its mouth,
shone like the body of Brahmā, the progenitor of the world, when it has just been created.
Even the abandonment of Vaidehī by her husband, who dwelt in the sacrificial hall, was praiseworthy;
for since he had not lost his other [wife], that golden image alone remained as his wife.
Thereupon the sacrifice proceeded with even greater abundance of materials;
for therein, the Rakshasas themselves, as guardians, were the obstacles to the ritual.
Then, urged by their preceptor, Kuśa and Lava, the two sons of Maithilī, recited the Rāmāyaṇa— the work first conceived by Vālmīki— here and there.
The conduct of Rāma and the composition of Vālmīki— those two, possessing voices like those of Kinnaras—
what is there that would not be sufficient to captivate the minds of those who hear them?
The sweetness of that singing and that instrumental music was described by connoisseurs;
Rāma, along with his younger brother, looked upon it and listened to it with curiosity.
The assembly, its sole focus on hearing that song, shone with tearful faces like a forest glade at dawn, dripping with dew.
Beholding that resemblance between Rāma and the two of them— a likeness that did not conflict with their age or appearance— the people stood motionless, as if rooted to the spot.
The world was not so much amazed by the skill of both of them in the king’s gifts of affection as it was by their freedom from desire.
"By whom were you two trained, or whose work is this?"—
when thus questioned by the king himself, the two of them declared it was Vālmīki's.
Then Rāma, together with his younger brother, approached the son of Pracetas;
casting aside his own body, he offered the kingdom to him.
Having thus informed Rāma that those two sons of Maithilī were his own offspring,
the compassionate poet requested the acceptance of Sītā.
"O father, your daughter-in-law was proven pure before us in the presence of the sacrificial fire;
yet, due to the wickedness of the Rākṣasa, the people here did not believe her."
"Let her convince Maithilī by pointing to her own conduct;
then, at her command, I shall accept her as one who possesses a son."
When the king had thus given his promise, the sage caused Janakī to be brought from the hermitage by his disciples, just as one brings about one's own spiritual success through religious observances.
Then, on another day, the descendant of Kakutstha, having assembled the citizens,
summoned the poet in order to undertake the task at hand.
Accompanied by his two sons and Sītā, and adorned with the refinement of his own voice,
the sage approached Rāma, just as one approaches the sun with a verse to kindle its radiance.
Clad in saffron robes and with her eyes fixed upon her own feet,
she summoned the poet by her very appearance alone, which was so serene.
Then all the people, withdrawing their eyes from the path of his vision, stood with their faces cast down like *sāla* trees laden with fruit.
Seated upon his mat within the range of her husband's sight, the sage commanded her:
"O child, act so that the world may have no doubt regarding your conduct."
Then, having sipped the holy water offered by the disciple of Vālmīki,
he uttered these true words concerning Sītā.
"O Goddess Viśvambharā, just as there has been no transgression against my husband by me in word, thought, or deed, so you ought to grant me concealment."
When this had been said by that virtuous woman, a circle of light, like the celestial ocean, rose up from the earth’s opening that appeared instantly.
There, the Earth herself appeared in person, seated upon a lion-throne raised up by the hoods of serpents, with the ocean as her girdle.
Taking Sītā onto her lap, she gazed intently at her husband; even as he cried out "Do not! Do not!", she plunged into the netherworld.
On the earth, the preceptor, mindful of the power of destiny, quelled the fury of that archer who desired the restoration of Sītā.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, having dismissed the seers and his honored friends,
Rāma directed the affection he had felt for Sītā toward her two children.
At the command of Yudhājit, he, whose subjects were well-governed, gave that region named Sindhu to Bharata, who had been granted sovereign power.
Having utterly defeated the Gandharvas there in battle, Bharata compelled them to take up musical instruments and made them abandon their weapons.
Having consecrated his two sons, Takṣa and Puṣkala— who were worthy of such rites— in the royal capitals named after them, he returned once more to the presence of Rāma.
And Lakṣmaṇa also, by the command of the Lord of the Raghus, made Aṅgada and Candraketu— the two sons born of himself— lords of Kārāpatha and Īśāvara.
Thus, those lords of men, having installed their sons as successors,
performed the funeral offerings in due order for their mothers who had departed to the world of their husbands.
Then Kāla, assuming the guise of a sage, approached the descendant of Raghu and said:
"We two shall drink the secret conversations of anyone who would abandon you; therefore, you must avoid such a person."
When she had agreed, saying "So be it," he revealed his true nature to the king and said,
"By the command of the Supreme Lord, ascend to heaven."
Although he was learned, Lakṣmaṇa, the doorkeeper,
violated the established rule out of fear of Durvāsas’s curse, as the sage was seeking an audience with Rāma.
Having gone to the bank of the Sarayū, that knower of yoga made his brother’s vow from a previous birth come true by means of casting off his body.
When that fourth part of himself had ascended to heaven,
Rāghava stood unsteady upon the earth, like Dharma remaining on three feet.

Firm in resolve, accompanied by his younger brothers and preceded by Agni, he set out for the water; though followed by Ayodhyā out of its devotion to its lord, the city left behind all its domestic life.
The monkeys and rākṣasas, who knew his thoughts, followed in his footsteps,
which were showered with the tears of the subjects, as thick as kadamba buds.
By him, who was compassionate toward his devotees, the Sarayū was made a ladder to heaven for those who followed him as he departed in his celestial chariot.
Because there was a tumultuous crush of those sinking there like a ford for cattle,
that purifying bathing place became renowned on earth by that name.
That Lord, among the gods who had assumed his own form,
fashioned another heaven for the citizens who had become deities.
Having thus accomplished the task of severing the heads of the ten-faced one for the sake of the gods, Viṣvaksena entered his own body, which is the foundation of all the worlds;
and having established both the lord of Laṅkā and the son of the Wind upon the southern and northern mountains like two pillars of fame.

Then the other seven heroes of the Raghu line, out of affection and because he was their eldest by birth, made Kuśa the recipient of the most excellent jewels; for among them, brotherly love followed the tradition of their lineage.
Though they were elevated by fruitful undertakings— chief among them the construction of bridges, trade routes, and elephant-stabling—
they did not overstep the boundaries that divided their respective territories, just as the oceans do not overstep the shoreline.
Born from a portion of the Four-Armed One, the lineage of those who never ceased their practice of giving spread out in eight branches, like the race of celestial elephants descended from Airāvata.
Then, at midnight, while the lamps were still and the people in the bedchamber were asleep,
Kuśa awoke and beheld a woman dressed in the attire of a wife living abroad, whom he had never seen before.
Standing before that king, who possessed the splendor of Indra and whose royal prosperity was shared with the virtuous,
she, the wife of Bandhumat, joined her palms in salutation, preceded by cries of victory over his enemies.

Then the son of Daśaratha, with half his body still resting upon the couch, spoke in wonder to her who had entered the chamber— though its bolt was not pushed back— as a reflection enters the surface of a mirror.
Having gained access even into your guarded dwelling, the power of your yoga is not perceived;
yet you bear the appearance of those who are not at peace, like a lotus plant undergoing a frost-like affliction.
Who are you, O auspicious one, whose possession are you, or what is the reason for your coming to me?
Speak, considering that the minds of the self-controlled Raghus are naturally averse to the wives of others.
The blameless lady, who had been led away by her preceptor intent on returning to his own station, spoke to him:
"O King, know me now to be the presiding deity of that city, which has become protectorless."
Having surpassed Vasvokasārā with my splendor, which is marked by the festivities of excellent governance,
I have fallen into this pitiable state even while you, a scion of the solar dynasty, remain possessed of complete power.
My residence, with its hundreds of shattered couches and seats and its fallen porticos, being without my lord,
mocks the end of day when the sun has sunk behind the setting mountains and the clouds are rent asunder by fierce winds.

The royal highway, which at night was once frequented by women going to meet their lovers with their bright, tinkling anklets, is now traversed by jackals whose gaping mouths are like flickering torches as they hunt for carrion.
That water of the pleasure-pools which, when struck by the fingertips of young women, followed the deep resonance of drums,
now cries out as it is struck by the horns of wild buffaloes.
The elephants of Citradvīpa, having entered the lotus groves and being offered stalks of lotus fiber by their female companions,
bear the blows of enraged lions that split their temples with the goad-like strikes of their claws.
On the pillars, where the sequence of painted colors had faded and grown grey,
the sloughs cast off by serpents became the breast-cloths clinging to the statues of women.
On these palace rooftops, which have turned dark with age and are now covered here and there with sprouting blades of grass,
the rays of the moon no longer shine, even though they remain as pure as a string of pearls.
My garden creepers, from which playful women once compassionately bent the branches to gather flowers,
are now being tormented by monkeys like wild Pulinda hunters.

At night, the windows were deprived of the light of lamps; by day, they were bereft of the beauty of lovely women's faces. With the flow of smoke interrupted, they were obscured by webs of threads spun by insects.

Beholding the waters of the Sarayū, whose sandy banks are devoid of funeral rites, which have not encountered the touch of bathing powders, and whose shores possess reed-huts now standing empty, I am consumed with grief.
Therefore, you ought to leave this dwelling and come to me at my ancestral capital,
casting off that human form which was for a specific purpose, just as your guru [cast off] his supreme spiritual form.
"So be it," the foremost of the Raghus, being pleased, accepted her request;
she too, her countenance clearly radiant with joy, vanished from sight by means of her physical form.
In the morning, the king related that wonderful event which had occurred during the night to the brahmins in the assembly;
having heard it, they congratulated him on being chosen as the actual sovereign of the ancestral capital.
Having bestowed Kuśāvatī upon a learned Brahmin, he set out toward Ayodhyā on an auspicious day for his journey,
accompanied by his harem and followed by his armies like the wind driven by masses of clouds.
With its groves of *ketumālā* trees, its elephants following along as if they were great pleasure-mountains,
and its chariots serving as magnificent houses, that army in its march became a mobile royal capital.
Set forth toward his ancestral home under that canopy with its stainless orb,
the flood of troops shone like the ocean being led to the shore by the rising moon.
As he marched forth, the earth, as if unable to endure the oppression of his armies,
seemed to ascend to a second heaven by means of the dust.
Exerting herself to depart, whether dwelling behind or moving ahead in her quarters or on the road,
she fixed her mind upon the completeness of the king's army wherever it was seen.
On the road, the dust from the elephants' sprinkling of rut-fluid and the trampling of the horses' hooves turned into mud;
and even that mud, under the leader, turned back into dust.
Seeking its path through the mountain ranges of the Vindhya forest, that army, split into many divisions,
made the mouths of the caves resound with echoes, like the Reva river letting out a great roar.
That lord, whose chariot-rims were reddened by the various minerals [of the mountain], with his musical instruments mingling with the sound of his march,
crossed the Vindhya range while observing the tribute offerings presented by the Pulinda tribes.
At that sacred ford, as he crossed the Ganges— which flows westward due to the construction of the elephant-bridge—
the swans, their wings fluttering as they soared into the sky, became his effortless fly-whisks.

He paid homage to the waters of the triple-streamed Gaṅgā, tossed by waves, which served as the means for his ancestors— who had had their bodies reduced to ashes by Kapila out of wrath— to attain the abode of the gods.

Thus, after some days on the journey, Kuśa reached the bank of the Sarayū and beheld hundreds of sacrificial posts belonging to the Raghus, erected upon altars for the performance of extensive sacrifices.
Shaking the branches of the flowering trees and touching the cool waves of the Sarayū,
the breeze from the edge of the grove in the ancestral capital came forth to welcome him whose army was weary.
Then, at the outskirts of that city, King Kuladhvaja— the enemy whose thorn had been extracted—
accompanied by his citizens, caused his powerful forces, with their fluttering banners, to encamp before her.
Appointed by the lord and having gathered all the necessary materials,
the guilds of artisans renovated the city just as clouds restore the earth, parched by the summer heat, with the release of rain.
Then the hero of Raghu’s line had the worship performed before the temple of the supreme image, accompanied by animal offerings,
by those learned in the rules of architecture who had observed fasts.
Having entered her palace— which bore the prefix "king"— just as a lover enters the heart of his beloved,
he honored the other members of the retinue with their respective dwellings.
With horses stationed in the stables and elephants tied to the pillars of their stalls,
and with its market-stands filled with merchandise, the city shone like a woman whose every limb is adorned with jewelry.
Dwelling in that residence of the Raghus, which had been endowed with its former splendor,
the son of Maithilī felt no longing for the Lord of Heaven, nor even for the Lord of Alakā.

Then the summer heat arrived, as if to instruct him in the attire of his beloved: her upper garment was woven with jewels, a necklace hung down upon her exclusively pale breasts, and her fine cloth was easily displaced by her sighs.
When the sun had returned from its northern course near the constellation of Agastya,
it released a snowy shower from the Himalayas, cool as joy, like a rain of tears.
The day was excessively hot, and the night was exceedingly thin;
both were separated by their opposing natures, like a husband and wife burdened with mutual resentment.
Day by day, the water from the household ponds— releasing its steps one by one from below as they became covered with moss and bearing upraised lotuses— attained the girth of a woman’s hips.
In the forest groves, amidst the blossoming and fragrant buds of the evening jasmine,
the bee, alighting on each one with a sound, seemed to count them.
On the cheeks of the amorous women, where there were marks of moist nail-scratches streaked with perspiration and where most of the hair was bitten away,
the *śirīṣa* flower did not suddenly fall even though it had slipped from their ears.

The wealthy spent the heat of the day in fountain-houses, reclining upon special stone slabs from the Malaya mountains that were cooled by the flow of mechanical jets and washed with the essence of sandalwood.

In the hair of the women— now released from being wet after bathing, still fragrant with incense, and adorned with evening jasmine flowers— the God of Love, whose power had been dulled by the end of spring, regained his strength.
The noble cluster of blossoms on the Arjuna tree shone intensely, tawny with its clinging particles of pollen;
it was like the bowstring of the Mind-born God, severed into fragments by Śiva out of wrath even after he had consumed his body.
By providing fragrant mango blossoms, aged spirits, and fresh *pāṭala* flowers to the people,
all the afflictions caused by the heat of summer were wiped away.
At that time, when the people were immersed in grief, two things became exceptionally beautiful:
the king, who stood ready to dispel their suffering with his feet, and the moon, which had ascended the eastern mountain.

Then, in the waters of the Sarayū, which were pleasant in the summer heat, with royal swans sporting in its waves and flowers from the creepers on its banks being carried along, he, accompanied by his wives, desired to sport.
On the riverbank, where a royal pavilion had been prepared by his attendants and the crocodiles driven away, he,
possessing the majesty of a sovereign, proceeded to plunge into the water in a manner befitting the greatness of his glory.
As those women descended the stairways to the riverbank, the swans became agitated by the ladies whose anklets were jingling and whose armlets were clashing against one another.
As they were intent on splashing one another, the king, observing their passion for bathing while remaining on his boat,
spoke to a Kirāta woman standing at his side who was holding a yak-tail fan.
Behold, as it is plunged into by my hundreds of women with their cosmetics washed away,
this current of the Sarayū assumes many hues, like the rising dawn accompanied by clouds.
The collyrium of the beauties of the inner apartments, which had been washed away by the waters tossed by their hands,
was reapplied to their eyes by those women as they sought to restore the splendor of their intoxicating passion.
Unable to support themselves because of the weight of their heavy hips and breasts,
these young women, though sinking under the pressure of their own limbs, cross over the difficulty by swimming through the power of passion.
These ear-ornaments of *śirīṣa* blossoms, falling from the women sporting in the water,
float restlessly in the current of the river and deceive the fish that are eager for moss.
As these women, intent on splashing the water, scatter droplets that rival pearls and rise against their breasts,
their necklaces, though broken, are not even noticed as they fall apart.

The beauty of whirlpools arose from the loveliness of their sunken navels; the waves from the playfulness of their eyebrows; and the pairs of water-fowl from their breasts—these were the comparisons for the limbs of those graceful women, found not far away.
Welcomed by the peacocks on the riverbanks with their tails fanned out and their cries rendered soft,
the sound of the water-drums following their songs mingles with their ears, red with passion.
Upon the hips of the women, where their garments are tightly clung, these girdles— resembling stars obscured by the light of the moon,
their paths of thread filled with water— now observe a profound silence.
These young women, having been sprinkled on their faces by their friends with streams of water squeezed from their hands out of playful pride,
now emit droplets of water reddened by cosmetic powder through their locks of hair, which fall straight down from their otherwise curling tips.
Though disheveled by the water-sport, with hair hanging loose, decorative leaf-patterns washed away,
and pearl ornaments scattered from their settings, the appearance of the women's faces remained nonetheless charming.
Descending from his celestial ship, he sported in the waters with those women,
his necklace dangling, like a lordly wild elephant with female elephants clinging to his shoulders as they pull up lotus stalks.
Then those women, followed by the king, shone with exceeding brilliance;
for how much more so would pearls, already delightful to the eye when set free, appear when they have reached a radiant sapphire?
With water colored by flowers, poured from golden horns, those large-eyed women sprinkled him out of affection;
thus the Tathāgata shone exceedingly, like the king of mountains with its outflow of precious minerals.
Accompanied by the women of the harem, he who delighted in the celestial Gaṅgā was imitated in his grace by Indra, who is surrounded by Apsarases as he plunges into that best of rivers.
That victorious ornament which Rāma, having obtained it from the pitcher-born Agastya, bestowed upon Kuśa along with the kingdom, sank into the water while he was sporting, its fall unnoticed.

Having bathed according to his desire, he, together with his wives, had only just reached the pavilion on the bank when he beheld his arm— its ornaments already applied— bereft of its divine bracelet.
Because it was the charm for winning victory, because it had previously been worn by his preceptor,
and because he could not bear its loss— not out of greed— that steadfast man wore ornaments of equal flowers.
Then he quickly commanded all his scouts, who were experts in river-crossings, to search for him;
having plunged into the Sarayū with their efforts fruitless, they spoke to him with the radiance of their faces dimmed.
"O King, though every effort was made, that supreme ornament of yours was not found;
it has surely been seized out of greed by the serpent Kumuda, who dwells within the depths of the lake."
Then that swift archer, his eyes bloodshot with rage, stood upon the bank, strung his bow,
and took up the Gārutmat weapon for the destruction of the serpents.
At the mere moment it was joined with him, that lake, its wave-hands tossed violently by the agitation,
struck against its banks and, submerged in the abyss, roared harshly like a wild elephant fallen into a pit.
Then, from that ocean as if it were being churned and filled with leaping crocodiles,
the King of Serpents suddenly emerged, placing the maiden before him like the Tree of the Gods accompanied by Lakṣmī.

Seeing him standing before him with his hands offering ornaments as a gift, the lord of the people withdrew the Suparṇa weapon; for the virtuous do not persist in their anger toward those who have surrendered.

Having prostrated with his head before the consecrated king Kuśa— the source of the Lord of the Three Worlds, a goad for his enemies, and skilled in weapons— Kumuda, who was himself honored even by Ananta, spoke.
I recognize you as another body of Viṣṇu, that being who acts for the sake of others, known by the name of a son;
how then could I act toward you, whose very appearance inspires devotion?
Beholding this ball, which had risen from the blow of her hand, the girl, out of great curiosity,
quickly seized your breast-ornament as it fell from the sky like a star.

Therefore, let this powerful arm of yours— marked by the scars of the bowstring's impact reaching down to the knees, and serving as a protective bolt for the earth— be joined with its former place once more.
And you ought not to refuse this younger sister of mine, Kumudvatī,
O King, who for a long time has been washing away her own transgression by serving at your feet.
Having spoken thus, and having offered his ornaments to the lord of the earth who replied, "You are praiseworthy,
you are my own kinsman," Kumuda, whose relatives had assembled, duly united him with his daughter through that ornament of his lineage.

When the lord of men grasped her hand—encircled by an auspicious woolen thread—for the sake of companionship before the high-flaming fire, the sound of celestial trumpets arose, pervading the ends of the quarters; and wondrous clouds rained down fragrant flowers into that fire.
Thus the Naga, having obtained as his kinsman the legitimate son of the Preceptor of the Three Worlds born of the princess of Mithilā, and Kuśa likewise having obtained Takṣaka’s fifth son,
the former abandoned his fear of the enemy who had slain his father— just as one fears Garuḍa— while the latter, beloved by the citizens, ruled over a land where the serpents were pacified.
From that descendant of Kakutstha, Āpaka and Kumudvatī bore a son named Aithi,
just as consciousness arises from the final watch of the night as a state of clarity.
Possessing a father worthy of his lineage, he purified his father’s line; like the sun, he purified both paths, as the night-lotus plant purifies its offspring.
First, that best among those who know the meaning of things caused him to grasp the hand of the daughters of the royal families— their family lore— before he took the hand of the earthly princesses.
Because of that noble birth, the heroic Kuśa, who possessed valor,
considered himself alone to be many, even though he was self-controlled among the self-controlled.
Having undertaken assistance to Indra as was fitting for his lineage, he slew the Daitya in battle; by that act, he himself was spared.
Kumudvatī, the sister of the Naga king Kumuda,
followed him who delighted the night-lotuses, just as moonlight follows the moon.
Of those two, one was half of the throne of the Lord of Heaven;
the second was a companion of Śacī, sharing in a portion of the Pārijāta tree.
Then the elder ministers established his own son in the kingdom,
remembering the final command of their lord as he departed for battle.
For his consecration, they had craftsmen construct for him a new palatial mansion with a raised terrace supported by four pillars.
There, the subjects waited upon him as he sat upon the auspicious throne, with waters from sacred fords collected in golden jars.
With the lutes sounding smooth and deep and the drums struck by cymbals,
his auspiciousness was inferred through its uninterrupted continuity.
He performed the lustration rites (*nīrājana*) offered by his elder kinsmen, using *dūrvā* grass, barley sprouts, *plakṣa* bark, and unopened leaf-buds as the final offerings.
Led by the family priest, the twice-born first approached Jiṣṇu with victorious Atharvan hymns to consecrate him.
The great torrent of that [army], falling upon his head, shone like the glorious consecration of Śiva, the enemy of Tripura, when the Gaṅgā descends with a roar.
At that moment, being praised by the bards,
he appeared like a rain-cloud intensified by the joyful welcome of cātakas.
As he received the bath with waters purified by sacred mantras,
the luster of his body increased like that of a lightning fire from the drenching of rain.
At the conclusion of his consecration, he bestowed wealth upon the initiated priests until their sacrifices were completed with sufficient sacrificial fees.
The blessing which they, with joyful minds,
pronounced upon him was far surpassed by the fruits resulting from his own past actions.

He decreed the release from bondage for those who were bound, the immunity from execution for those deserving death, the unyoking of the burden for draft animals, and the freedom from milking for cows.
Even his pet birds, such as parrots and others kept in cages,
obtained their release at his command and went wherever they pleased.
Then, for the purpose of dressing, he ascended a pure ivory throne placed within an inner chamber,
which was covered with an upper cloth.
With their hands cleansed by water, the attendants approached him— whose hair-ends were darkened by incense—
with various articles for the performance of his toilette.
They greeted his crown, bound with strings of pearls and containing an inner garland,
with a ruby that shone with a halo of light.
Having completed the body-anointing with sandalwood paste fragrant with musk, they then fashioned the leaf-designs, in which were set inlaid gems.
Adorned with ornaments, wearing garlands, and clad in silken garments marked with the emblem of a swan,
he was exceedingly beautiful to behold as the bridegroom of the royal fortune.
The reflection of him, while he was looking at his attire in a golden mirror,
shone like that of the Kalpavṛkṣa tree upon Mount Meru when the sun has risen.
With his attendants at his sides, their hands occupied with the royal insignia,
he proceeded to the Sudharmā assembly hall, which was unsurpassed and illuminated by the light [of torches].
There he occupied his paternal throne,
which was provided with a canopy and whose footstool had been rubbed by the crest-jewels of kings.
Occupied by him, that great abode of auspiciousness shone like the chest of Viṣṇu, marked with the Śrīvatsa, when it is adorned by the Kaustubha gem.
Having attained supreme sovereignty after his childhood, he shone even more brightly,
like the moon that has reached its full orb after emerging from the crescent phase.
His attendants regarded him, whose facial expression was serene and who spoke preceded by a smile,
as trust itself incarnate.
Possessing the splendor of Indra, he, as he marched, made the city— whose banners resembled the wish-fulfilling tree—
touch the heavens by means of his elephant Airāvata’s prowess.
A single parasol was raised over his head; by him, of stainless luster, the heat born of separation from the former king was removed from the entire world.
Just as the flames of fire arise after smoke, and the rays of the sun after its emergence,
he, having transcended the activity of the [other] luminaries, rose up simultaneously with his virtues.
The women of the city followed him with eyes bright with joy,
as the stars of the autumnal night follow the Pole Star (Dhruva) with their clear radiance.
And the deities of Ayodhyā, who are worshipped in their praised temples, favored him—
who was himself worthy of favor— by manifesting their presence within the images.
As long as the sacrificial altar, drenched with the waters of consecration, had not yet dried,
so long did his unbearable majesty extend to the very edge of the ocean.
The mantras of his preceptor Vasiṣṭha and the arrows of that archer—
what goal is there that these two, when joined together, could not accomplish?
Always accompanied by his ministers of justice, he himself, unwearied, examined the legal disputes of plaintiffs and defendants that required the resolution of doubts.
Thereafter, he engaged his servants with the fruits of their petitions, which were manifested as joy and indicated by their readiness for fulfillment.
The subjects had been nourished by his father as rivers are swollen by the month of Śrāvaṇa;
yet under him, they attained even greater growth, just as those rivers do in the month of Bhādrapada.
What he spoke was never false, and what he gave he never took back;
yet he broke his vow when, having uprooted his enemies, he caused them to be replanted.
Each of his age, beauty, and prosperity was a cause for intoxication; yet, though all these were present in him together, his mind was not overcome by pride.
Thus, although he was still young, he remained unshakable day after day amidst his subjects who were filled with passion for him, like a tree with deeply rooted roots.
Since external enemies are impermanent and remote,
he first conquered those six internal enemies who are constant.
When he was inclined toward grace, Fortune— though fickle by nature—
became unfailing, like a streak of gold upon a touchstone.
"Pure policy is cowardice; valor alone is the behavior of a beast of prey.
Therefore, he sought success through the combination of both. (Raghuvamśa 17.47)
In the realm of that king, whose radiance was his established vow,
nothing remained unseen, just as nothing remains hidden from the sun when it is free from clouds.
Turning his back on all hesitation, he followed with strict discipline that which had been ordained for kings during the various divisions of day and night.
Day after day, his counsel was held with his ministers;
though it was attended to constantly, it remained unobserved, as its entrance was kept secret.
By means of spies— both among his own people and among others— who were stationed there, remained unrecognized by one another,
and kept watch at the proper times even while he slept, he remained vigilant.
Even for his enemies who sought to obstruct him, the passes were difficult to seize;
for a lion that attacks elephants does not dwell in mountain caves out of fear.
His numerous and preeminent undertakings,
which were free from danger and resembled rice grains within a husk, ripened secretly.
Though he had grown great, he never proceeded by an improper path;
for the setting forth of the salt ocean toward its increase occurs only through the mouth of a river.
Granted that he was capable of immediately quelling natural aversion to sensual pleasure;
yet he did not produce that very thing for which a remedy would have been required.
The expedition of that powerful king took place only against the Śakas;
for even a forest fire, though aided by the wind, does not seek water.
He did not obstruct Dharma for the sake of Artha or Kāma, nor did he obstruct those two for its sake;
he did not obstruct Artha for the sake of Kāma, nor Kāma for the sake of Artha—he was equal toward all three.
Since those who are weak are unable to assist, while those who are powerful act perversely,
he therefore established allies of middling strength.

Having distinguished between himself and his enemy the relative strength and weakness of their respective powers and other resources, he remained at ease if he was stronger than the other, but otherwise [he prepared for action].
"Being worthy of reliance because of his treasury"—this is the summary of its meaning;
for a cloud containing water within is welcomed by the cātaka birds.
He was intent on his own duties while thwarting the actions of others;
he guarded his own vulnerabilities while striking at the weaknesses of his enemies.
Constantly nurtured by his father, skilled in weapons, and prepared for battle,
Daṇḍin’s punishment did not spare even his own body.
No one else could seize his three powers, which were like the crest-jewel of a serpent;
yet he drew them from the enemy, just as a magnet attracts iron.
Like streams flowing into ponds, or as caravans move freely through forests and groves,
the people wandered at their own will upon the mountains as if they were their own homes.
Protecting his asceticism from obstacles and his prosperity from thieves,
he caused each of the social orders and stages of life to partake in the six-fold fruits according to their respective duties.
The earth yielded jewels through its mines, grain through its fields, and elephants through its forests;
it bestowed upon him a wage that was truly commensurate with his protection.
Possessing the prowess of six faces, he became an expert in the application of the virtues and the six political expedients toward the objects to be accomplished.
Thus, by applying the fourfold policy of statecraft in due order,
he attained its fruit without obstruction all the way to the sacred bathing-place.
Although he was skilled in the methods of treacherous warfare, he fought only on the path of righteousness;
thus, the Goddess of Victory, who dwells with heroes, took up the role of a woman going to meet her lover.
Because his enemies were generally broken by his majesty, battle was as difficult for him to obtain as it is for a scent-elephant whose rivals have been dispersed by its very odor.
The moon wanes when it has waxed full, and the ocean is likewise;
but he neither increased nor did he suffer decline like those two.

Through their attendance upon that great king, the virtuous suppliants became exceedingly emaciated, yet they attained the status of givers themselves, just as clouds from the ocean become givers of rain.
Though being praised, he felt ashamed while performing only that which was worthy of praise;
nevertheless, the fame of him who detested those who did such things continued to grow.
Destroying misfortune by his very sight and dispelling darkness through the truth of reality,
he made his subjects independent, like the sun ever risen.
The rays of the moon reach the lotus, and those of the sun reach the water-lily;
likewise, the virtues of that virtuous king found a place even among his enemies.
Although his conduct was primarily intent on deceiving others,
that very effort of the one desiring victory for the sake of the horse-sacrifice became entirely consistent with dharma.
Thus, by his majesty and following the path prescribed by the Teacher,
he became a god among gods and a king among kings, like a bull [among bulls].
They spoke of that fifth [state] as belonging to the world-protectors through the yoga of equanimity;
the sixth to the great beings (mahābhūtas), and the eighth to the mountain ranges.
The kings, having set aside their royal parasols from afar, bore upon their heads his command issued as a decree, as if it were the command of Indra himself.
In that great sacrifice, he honored the officiating priests with such liberal sacrificial fees that the name of this king became synonymous with that of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
From Indra, rain came with its excessive flow of pestilence restrained; Yama became the lord of aquatic creatures, making the waters auspicious for the work of seafarers;
thereafter, Kubera, mindful of his former status, increased his treasury; thus the world-protectors adopted the conduct of those who have submitted to punishment.
That conqueror of enemies begot upon the daughter of the lord of the Niṣadhas a son of no inferior strength,
whom they called by the very name Niṣadha, after the king of mountains from which the Niṣadha lands were named.
The father rejoiced in his son, who was now a youth endowed with mature vigor and destined for progeny,
just as the world of living beings rejoices at the arrival of a bountiful rain that yields a harvest of abundant fruit.
Having enjoyed sounds and other pleasures for a long time, and having firmly established the title of "King" therein,
the son of Kaumudvatī ascended to the heaven earned by his deeds, which were as pure as white lotuses.

The grandson of Kuśa, whose eyes were like lotuses, whose mind was as steady as the ocean, and whose long arms were like the bars of an ancient city gate, ruled the earth— encircled by the seas— as the sole hero and the unique sun.
At the end of his reign, his son named Nala, possessing the brilliance of fire, attained the glory of the lineage;
he, whose face was like a lotus, crushed the armies of his enemies as an elephant tramples beds of reeds.

His son, whose dark body was celebrated by the sky-dwellers with a name consisting of the word "Nabhas," was as beloved to the subjects as the month of Nabhas (Śrāvaṇa) is to them. His form was as dark as the expanse of the sky. Ragh_18.6.
Having bestowed upon that sovereign of the Northern Kosalas the sovereignty over his subjects— a sovereignty which,
though naturally undecaying, was worn away by old age— he bound himself once more to the fetters of the body for the sake of further existence.
Thus, Puṇḍarīka was born as one unconquerable among kings, like Puṇḍarīka among elephants;
when his father had passed away, Fortune, having taken up her white lotus, took refuge in him as if he were the lotus-eyed Viṣṇu.
Having caused his son Kṣemadhanvan— who was endowed with forgiveness and skilled in providing for the welfare of his subjects—
to obtain the earth, Amoghadhanvan practiced austerities in the forest with even greater patience.
He also had a son, equal to a god, who was the leader at the head of armies in battle;
even in the third heaven, his name was heard as Devādi, ending with the word "anīka."
Just as that father was devoted to the propitiation of his son,
so too did the son, with even greater affection, become one who truly possessed a father through him.
Having placed the burden of the four castes upon his two sons— who were like himself and born of himself, and who had long been wedded—
he, the performer of sacrifices and sole repository of virtues, departed for the world of those who offer oblations.

His son was self-controlled and, because of his pleasant speech, was as dear to his enemies as he was to his own people; for sweetness, when employed even once, is capable of capturing even the most agitated deer.
He who was named Ahīnagu, possessing unimpaired arms and wealth, ruled the entire earth;
for, by virtue of his aversion to the company of the base, he possessed such sweetness that he could even capture deer.

Immediately after his preceptor, that knower of the inner self became as wise as the primordial Puruṣa descended among men; through four unerring methods of instruction, he became as clever as the Lord of the Four Quarters.

When he had departed on his journey to the other world, the goddess Lakṣmī indeed attended upon his son Pāriyātra— who, by virtue of his lofty head, had conquered the Pāriyātra mountain— as she had once served the Pāriyātra itself as a conqueror of enemies.
He had a son named Śila of noble character, whose broad chest was like a stone slab;
though he had conquered the ranks of his enemies with arrows, he remained modest when being praised.

Having installed that blameless youth as the crown prince, endowed with all personal virtues, he enjoyed pleasures; for the conduct of kings is such that it does not obstruct their own happiness, yet remains itself unobstructed.

While he was still unsatiated with pleasures that bound him with passion— pleasures enjoyed for their exceptional loveliness— old age, though naturally impatient of such indulgence, took him away in vain through its envy.

One named Unnābha, whose name was derived from his elevated navel, became his son; though his navel-cavity was not actually elevated, he was like the lotus-navelled Viṣṇu, the center of the entire circle of kings.
After him, his son Vajraghoṣa, who possessed the power of the wielder of the thunderbolt, became the lord of the earth known as Vajrākarabhūṣaṇā; he was indeed Vajranābha in battle.
When he had departed for heaven, which is attained through meritorious deeds, the earth, bounded by the ocean, attended upon his son Śaṅkhaṇa—
who had uprooted his enemies— with offerings of jewels produced from the mines.
At the end of his life, he who possessed the luster of the sun and bore the form of a horse attained the ancestral station of the Aśvins;
those learned in ancient lore call him Dhyuṣitāśva because his soldiers' horses had stayed upon the shores of the sea.
Having propitiated Viśveśvara, that Lord of the earth begot Viśvasaha;
for he, the friend of the universe, was the very self of the All-sustainer (Viśvaṃbhara), born as his son to protect the entire earth.
When his son Hiraṇyanābha was born—
the son of Hiraṇyākṣa’s enemy and one skilled in policy— he became even more intolerable to his enemies than fire accompanied by the wind.

Having freed himself from his debt to his ancestors, the king— desiring infinite bliss in his final years and having fulfilled his duty— made over the sovereignty to his son, whose arms reached down to his knees, and donned the bark garment.
To him, the lord of the Northern Kosalas and the ornament of the solar dynasty, was born a legitimate son named Kausalya, who, like a second Soma, was a festival for the eyes.
Having installed his own son, who was most devoted to Brahman, in his office as one equally devoted to Brahman, that Kausalya, ruler of the Northern Kosalas, attained the state of union with Brahman.
While he ruled the earth perfectly, marking it with his commands, and was radiant with glory as far as the assembly of Brahmā,
the subjects rejoiced for a long time under that lord of men who possessed noble offspring, their eyes clouded with tears of joy.
Having made himself a worthy vessel through service to his guru, and having been touched by the form of the Lord whose banner bears the king of birds,
that lotus-eyed son placed his father at the very pinnacle of those who possess sons.
Having ensured the continuity of his lineage through that son who would perpetuate the dynasty, he— destined to be a friend of Indra,
having ceased all longing for sensory contact upon touching the waters at Tripuṣkara— attained the state of a god.
On the lunar day of Puṣya, his wife gave birth to Pauṣya, whose splendor surpassed the hue of flowers;
at whose rising, all people attained full nourishment, as if under a second Puṣya constellation.
Having distributed the earth among his sons and surrendered his soul to the wise Jaimini,
he who was fearful of rebirth attained through that union the yoga of liberation and became one who is no longer subject to birth.
After that, his son Dhruvasandhi, who was comparable to Dhruva, obtained the earth;
for while he was the elder, being true to his word, the "firm peace" (dhruva-sandhi) of his bowing enemies became constant.
While his son, named Sudarśana— who was as pleasing to behold as the moon at the end of the new moon— was still but an infant,
that lion among men, whose eyes were as long as those of a deer, met with disaster from a lion while engaged in the sport of hunting.

When he had departed for heaven, the circle of ministers, out of unanimity and observing that the subjects were wretched and without a protector, duly installed his lone descendant as the lord of Sāketa.
With the blooming lotus, the sky was comparable; with the young lion, the forest;
and with the prince Aṣṭaka, Raghu’s lineage became like water with a budding lotus.
He was destined by the world to be equal to his father himself, for he had been honored with the placement of the crown;
indeed, even when no larger than a young elephant, a cloud is seen filling the quarters of the sky upon catching the east wind.
As he proceeded along the royal road on an elephant, supported by his mahout and dressed in the finest attire,
the citizens beheld him with the reverence due to a father, even though he was only about six years old, owing to his majesty.
Granted that he was not physically capable of filling his father’s lion-throne,
yet his soul, enveloped in the majesty of his splendor, pervaded it with its golden-hued radiance.
Therefore, the kings, with their feet slightly descended from above and not quite touching the golden footstool,
yet still stained with red lac, paid homage to his feet with their renowned crowns.
Just as the word "great sapphire" applied to a gem of small dimensions is not false due to its inherent power,
so too was the title "Great King" appropriately applied to that boy.

The dispute uttered from his mouth— whose yak-tail fans were waved at the edges and whose cheeks were brushed by the quivering feathers of both blackbirds— washed away even upon the shores of the oceans.
Wearing a tilaka placed upon his forehead, which was adorned with a band of refined Jāmbūnada gold, he,
with a smiling face, rendered the faces of his enemies' beautiful women empty by that very mark.
Though his tenderness surpassed even that of the śirīṣa flower, he might have succumbed to exhaustion through the study of the scriptures and the company of elders;
yet, by virtue of his majestic power, he bore the exceedingly heavy burden of the earth.
As long as he had not fully mastered writing— its syllables arranged upon the ground of the alphabet—
he nevertheless applied all the fruits of the science of statecraft through his association with those advanced in learning.
Lakṣmī, her portion on his chest not yet fully satisfied and gazing toward him as he was reaching maturity,
embraced him under the pretext of the shade of her parasol, as if overcome with shame.

Even though he had not yet reached the age of youth, his arm— marked by the scars of bowstrings and though it had not yet touched the hilt of a sword— protected the earth as if it were a yoke-bearing bull.
In his time, it was not only his bodily limbs that grew;
indeed, even his hereditary virtues, beloved by the world, though subtle at their inception, attained full expansion.
As if remembering the further shores he had beheld in previous births, he, causing no distress to his elders,
acquired the three branches of knowledge which are the root of attaining the three aims of life, as well as the ancestral hereditary rights.
Standing with his body slightly turned to the left, his topknot raised, and one knee bent, he shone as he was being led forth,
having drawn his bow with its string up to his ear.

Then he attained youth—the honey for the eyes of women, the flower of the tree of the god of love, the sprout of the bond of passion; a natural adornment covering every limb, the very first abode of graceful charm.

The princesses, whose beauty surpassed even those depicted in portraits shown by female messengers, were accepted by the ministers— who desired a pure lineage— for that youth, once the two glorious regions of his body had been first taken possession of.
Having consecrated his son Agniveśya, who possessed the brilliance of fire, upon his own throne, the self-controlled Rāghava,
the last of those learned in the Vedas, retired to the Naimiṣa forest in the final stage of his life.

There, he performed austerities without desire for fruits, forgetting his residence in a palace by means of the water from sacred bathing-places, his couch by means of grass mats spread upon the ground, and his dwelling in a mansion by means of a leaf-hut.
His son felt no weariness in the task of protecting what had been acquired, for the earth had been intended by his father—
having conquered his enemies with his arm— to be enjoyed, not merely to be conquered.
He himself performed for some years the duties appropriate to his lineage with great zeal;
thereafter, having entrusted those responsibilities to his ministers, he became devoted to women in the fresh bloom of youth.
In the palaces of that lover who was accompanied by his beloveds, where the drums resounded, each succeeding festival—
possessing even greater splendor than the former— superseded the preceding celebration.
He was unable to endure even a single moment separated from the objects of his senses;
yet, while dwelling apart during the day and night, he did not disregard his longing subjects.
Even when, out of respect for his ministers, he occasionally granted them an audience that they naturally longed for,
it was accomplished by him merely with one foot hanging down from the opening of a window.
Having prostrated before him, his dependents sought refuge in that hand— which was stained by the hue of its tender nails—
resembling a lotus touched by the rays of the newly risen sun.

With his passion deeply stirred, he plunged into the ponds whose lotuses were tossed by the agitation of the breasts of young, voluptuous women, and which contained hidden chambers for amorous dalliance within their waters.

There, the women further enticed him with faces whose eyes were brightened by collyrium washed away by bathing, whose lips were flushed rosy from the cleansing of their red dye, and which possessed a natural loveliness now fully revealed.
Accompanied by his beloveds, he entered the drinking halls, which attracted him with the fragrance of wine as sweet as that which delights the sense of smell;
he was like an elephant entering flowering lotus ponds accompanied by its mates.
In secret, the women desired to give him more than enough intoxicating drink;
he, whose longing was like that of the *bakula* tree, drank the mouth-liquor offered by them.
Both the lute,
with its heart-pleasing sound, and the fair-eyed maiden, with her charming speech, filled his lap— which was accustomed to being occupied by the turning of a child— with their presence.
That skillful man himself beat the drum, his garlands and bracelets swaying as he captivated the minds [of the audience];
he treated the female dancers—who had surpassed all conventions of dramatic gesture—with no sense of shame before the elders standing nearby.

And at the conclusion of the beautiful dance, his face—its tilaka mark broken by perspiration from exertion—was pressed against her face out of love; thus he lived the life of both the Lord of the Immortals and the Lord of Alakā.

His secret trysts with his beloveds— conducted while he was still under the watchful eye of his attendants and involving attachment to new objects of desire— were rendered incomplete, as their enjoyments were interrupted before they were fully consummated.
Deceiving his beloveds by evading their threats with sprout-like fingertips, their glances curved with the knitting of brows, and their repeated binding with girdles, he attained his goal.
Seated behind his messenger during the nights set aside for dalliance,
he overheard the anxious words of his beloved woman, who was apprehensive of a possible separation.
Having succumbed to passion through his attachment to his wife, he somehow continued to paint her form upon the rare dancers,
using a brush made from a reed pen moistened by the ink flowing from his fingers.

By means of the pretext of festive rites, the queens— having cast aside their anger— brought the king, who was long afflicted by the envy that opposes love and by the pride of passion, to the fulfillment of his desires.
Returning in the morning with a countenance radiant from his amorous dalliance,
he— sluggish in his affection— tormented his beloveds once more as he sought to appease them with folded hands, though they were already pained by the wounds of his lovemaking.
The women, their pain caused by the rejection of their advances through the mere sight of him— who had described his rivals in a dream—
expressed their distress through tossing movements, with tear-drops falling onto the edges of the bedcovers and bracelets broken by their wrathful agitation.
Having entered the vine-cottages where flower-beds were prepared, and with the path shown by female messengers,
he experienced dalliance with the women of his retinue, which was marked by an exceeding tremor born of fear of the harem guards.
"Having obtained even the fortune of your beloved's name, I now long for his very person;
alas, my mind is greedy!"—thus did the women speak to him, faltering in their lineage.

As that lover rose from his bed, it revealed his various amorous disarray: his body tawny with the dust of the bed, his garlands disheveled and tangled, his girdle broken, and his feet marked with red lac.

He himself applied the red dye to his feet, yet he was not so absorbed in it as he was when his eyes were captivated by women with swelling hips, whose garments were loosened and whose girdles left visible traces upon them.
In kissing, when her lower lip was turned away; in the clasp of his hands, when she resisted by clutching her girdle;
and even when his desire was thwarted in every way, the dalliance with his bride became for him fuel for the god of love.
Standing behind them, he playfully asked those brides who were looking at their reflections in mirrors; with his smile, charming to the mind, he caused their faces to close in modesty.
As he rose from bed, his beloveds sought the kiss that concludes the night, with their soft arms entwined around his neck and the soles of their feet placed upon the tops of his feet.
Beholding his own royal attire reflected in the surface of the mirror— more splendid than that of Indra—
he rejoiced not so much at that as a youth would at the manifest signs of enjoyment upon his ornaments.

Under the pretext of performing duties for their friends, his beloveds— knowing him to be fickle and aware that his deceptions in flight were straightforwardly treacherous— seized him by the hair and held him back as he set out from their side.

The women, languid from the exhaustion of merciless lovemaking, reclined upon his broad chest— where the sandalwood paste had been rubbed away by their full breasts— under the pretext of adjusting the neck-threads.
Having gone before him as he moved secretly at night for the sake of a rendezvous, as reported by a female spy,
the women dragged him along, saying, "O lustful one, how will you deceive her while shrouded in darkness?"
Failing to obtain the pleasure of touch from women, as the moon fails to obtain it from the rays of light, he—
who was intent on staying awake at night— ascended to the likeness of a bed of night-lotuses by sleeping during the day.
With their lips pressed by flutes and their thighs marked by nail-scratches from lutes, those women,
urged on by both instruments, enticed him with their sidelong glances as they performed their art.
Displaying a dance performed by women among themselves, which relied upon gestures, expressions, and words,
he vied with performers skilled in technique in the presence of his friends.

During the rainy season, his amorous play took place upon mountains made of artificial peacock-feathers, where he wore garlands of *kuṭaja* and *arjuna* flowers hanging from his shoulders and was anointed with the pollen of *nīpa* blossoms.
He did not hasten to appease those women with gentle words when they lay on their beds turned away from him in anger;
rather, he longed for them to turn back, distressed by the sound of the thunderclouds, and enter his embrace.
In the nights of the month of Kārttika, staying on the roof-terraces of his palace in the company of graceful women,
he enjoyed the moonlight— bright as it was after the clouds had passed— which dispelled the fatigue of amorous dalliance.

And he gazed through the lattice-windows of the palace at the sandy bank of the Sarayū, which, with its girdle of swans, revealed its hips as if they were the riverbank itself, imitating the playful charms of his beloved.

On one side, slender-waisted women captivated him— who was eager to release his fastenings— with winter garments that were rustling, fragrant with the scent of aloe-wood incense, and displayed streaks of visible gold thread.
In the inner chambers of his secluded quarters, where the lamps were fixed and motionless,
the wintry nights served as witnesses to all his amorous dalliances.
Seeing the mango blossom with its leaves stirred by the southern breeze,
the women, casting aside their formal attire, followed him whose separation was so difficult to endure.
Placing them upon his own lap and swinging them on a swing tossed by his attendants, he—
when the ropes were released— seized their necks with his arms tightly, under the pretext of fear.
His beloveds served him with the seasonal rites for the summer, their breasts smeared with sandalwood paste, their lovely ornaments strung with pearls, and jeweled girdles hanging from their hips.
Because he drank that liquor made from crushed mangoes and mixed with red *pāṭala* flowers,
his passion— having been diminished by the departure of the honey-wine— became renewed once more.
Thus experiencing the pleasures of the senses and turning away from other duties,
that king passed the seasons— each announced by its own characteristic signs— driven on by the god of love.
Other kings were unable to overcome him even when he was negligent due to his own power;
yet the disease born of passion for pleasure consumed him, just as the curse of Dakṣa destroyed the moon.
Though its faults were evident, he, being beyond the influence of physicians, did not abandon that object of attachment;
yet, once the collection of sense-faculties has been carried away by sweet sensory objects, it must then be restrained from suffering.
With her pale face, few ornaments, slow and supported gait, and soft voice,
his wasting away from consumption reached a state equal to that of one filled with longing for a beloved.

O Queen, that royal lineage became like the sky with the moon situated in its final digit, or like a summer pond reduced to mere mud, or like a lamp-vessel whose flame has been diminished by exhaustion.
"Indeed, during these days, his labor is being accomplished for the birth of a son"—
thus did the subjects, fearing some calamity, constantly say to the minister, who showed no sign of illness.
Although he was accompanied by many women, he did not escape that purifying lineage—
just as a lamp does not overcome the wind— nor did he transcend the disease that defies even the efforts of physicians.
In the very garden of his palace, the ministers, having assembled with the family priest who was an expert in the final sacrifice,
secretly performed that rite upon the kindled fire under the pretext of a ritual for the pacification of disease.
By means of those who had secured the favor of the chief ministers,
his wife quickly attained the royal fortune of the lord of men, for she was clearly seen to possess the auspicious marks of pregnancy.
Her womb, first scorched by the hot tears from her eyes due to such grief over the king’s calamity,
was cooled by the cool rite of the lineage-consecration poured forth from the mouth of the golden pitcher.
Like the earth holding a handful of seeds hidden within for the sake of future growth,

the queen— seated upon a golden throne together with her hereditary ministers and senior counselors— presided over the kingdom according to law, her commands unimpeded, while awaiting the time of the offspring’s birth for the sake of the people.
It was being filled by forest-dwellers who had come close with fuel-gatherers,
their practice being to rise up to meet the fires that were invisible to them.
Remembering that the queen had just bathed after her menses, he immediately and hastily bypassed the rite of circumambulation, thereby provoking her anger.
Bearing a line upon her coppery forehead that was not white,
she appeared like the twilight pierced by the new moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight.
Accept from me this Gandharva weapon, whose mantras for its employment and withdrawal are clearly distinguished;
like the twilight with the rising of the moon, victory shall be in your own hands without the injury of enemies.
When you had fallen under the power of sleep, Lakṣmī somehow separated herself from your face, which possessed the luster of the moon;
for even at the time of dawn, she remains anxious to behold you, like a lover whose night has been cut short.

The breeze, its cold nature intensified by the frost, blows gently; it mingles with the lotuses split open by the rays of the dawn sun, as if desiring to acquire for itself the fragrance of your breath—the very quality toward which the evening air has been striving.
Thus, his sleep dispelled and his limbs no longer cramped, he left his bed— just as the elephant Supratīka leaves the sandy banks of the Gaṅgā—
and cast aside the edge of the coverlet, which was marked by the jewels of the bracelets of the women of the retinue as they busied themselves at his feet.

There he beheld kings seated upon thrones in palaces resembling celestial chariots, their physical splendor intensified by their ornaments, like magnificent sacrificial pillars standing upon golden altars.
Whenever that princess did not choose a husband from among those previously mentioned,
at each such instance, the creeper of her hope put forth new sprouts upon the branch of Nami.

He covered the ground with the heads of his enemies— heads from which the throats had been severed by broad-headed arrows, filled with the sound of "hum," their brows furrowed into waves upon the forehead, and their lips bitten by the teeth as they gave up their lives.
Then, seeing that his son was firmly established among the subjects through those qualities which win them over,
Raghu took the path leading to the edge of the forest, which indicated his future transformation.
Salutations to you, the triple-formed one, who is the manifestation of the three qualities;
who existed as the solitary Self before creation, and who later attained auspiciousness.
Having quickly understood that [the weapon] was Śambhu’s, they too, intent on the task of withdrawing it,
hurled back at the son of Daśaratha their own bow, which was exceedingly stiff when bent.

O lady with curved eyebrows, this shore of the ocean— which is like a sword and a treasury of waters— shines from afar, dark as a king of *tāla* trees, appearing like a streak of tarnish upon its blade.
Having returned there after a long absence, the two sons of Daśaratha beheld their mothers as the night sky,
with its moonbeams, beholds the night-lotus when it has changed its form and become difficult to recognize.
"O Lakṣmaṇa! O Lakṣmaṇa!"—with these piteous words a woman was weeping aloud in the forest.
"Ah, I know her; she is the daughter of Janaka," the sage reflected, and approached her side.
Having heard those words of the sage, the lotus-eyed Rāma,
who was skilled in statesmanship, was simultaneously overcome by both joy and sorrow.
"Go quickly, Lakṣmaṇa; let there be no violation of dharma.
For the abandonment or even the killing of the virtuous—both are equal."
From him was born a son named Dala, endowed with great strength, whose eyes possessed the luster of lotus petals,
whose teeth were like the tips of kunda flowers, who was a lion to the elephants that were his enemies, and who became the lord of the earth like the moon amidst the clusters of stars.
Then, when the lord of the earth had abandoned enjoyments and attained the third heaven through supreme austerity,
his son— that moon among men, whose mind was as steadfast as the ocean— ruled over the entire world.
